# Overview



This page introduces the **Awesome Foundation Models for Single-Cell** repository — what it contains, how it is architected, and how to navigate it. As the entry point to this documentation, it explains the repository's role as a curated, continuously updated reading list of foundation-model research for single-cell genomics, and gives you the mental model needed before diving into any specific research domain. No prior experience with either machine learning catalogs or computational biology is assumed.

## What This Repository Is

This is an **awesome-list style knowledge base**: a single, carefully maintained reference document rather than a software codebase. The repository's mission, stated directly in its header, is to provide *"a curated, continuously updated reading list of foundation-model research for single-cell genomics"*. Every entry links to an external paper — the repository itself contains no runnable code. It is an open, community-driven project that welcomes contributions via issues and pull requests, as signaled by its "PRs Welcome" badge and explicit contribution note. The project also carries the official [Awesome](https://awesome.re) badge, indicating it meets the quality standards of the awesome-list ecosystem.

For a beginner developer, the key mental model is this: think of the repository as a **living index card catalog** for a fast-moving research field, where the "cards" are paper citations organized by research theme.

Sources: [README.md](/README.md#L1-L16)

## The Evolutionary Tree: Your Field Map

The repository's single visual asset is its **evolutionary tree diagram** (`figs/evo_tree.png`), which charts how single-cell foundation models have branched and evolved over time. The tree design is credited to the [LLMsPracticalGuide](https://github.com/Mooler0410/LLMsPracticalGuide/tree/main) project, adapting a proven visualization pattern from the broader LLM ecosystem. For newcomers, this diagram is the fastest way to grasp the field's shape at a glance: which model families exist, when they emerged, and how they relate to one another. A dedicated documentation page expands this visual into a full guided walkthrough.

![Evolutionary tree of single-cell foundation models](https://github.com/OmicsML/awesome-foundation-model-single-cell-papers/blob/main/figs/evo_tree.png?raw=true)

Sources: [README.md](/README.md#L18-L24)

## Repository Architecture: One File Holds Everything

The physical structure is deliberately minimal — a **single-source-of-truth architecture** where `README.md` (534 lines) contains the entire catalog, supported by one image asset and a license file:

```
awesome-foundation-model-single-cell-papers/
├── LICENSE                    # Open-source license
├── README.md                  # ⭐ The entire knowledge base (534 lines, ~375 papers)
└── figs/
    └── evo_tree.png           # Evolutionary tree visualization
```

Inside `README.md`, the content follows a strict layered pattern: header and mission (lines 1–24), a BibTeX citation block (lines 26–37), a self-navigating Catalog table of contents (lines 39–70), and then nine top-level research domains. The Catalog section is a hyperlinked table of contents, so you can jump directly to any domain from the top of the file.

The architecture below shows how the nine domains organize the field — from **model-centric research** at the top, through **application frontiers** in the middle, to the **supporting ecosystem** (data, evaluation, tooling) and adjacent related fields at the base:

```mermaid
graph TD
    R["README.md<br/>Single Source of Truth — 534 lines"]
    R --> A["Single-Cell Foundation Models<br/>~138 papers"]
    R --> B["Genetic Perturbation<br/>~45 papers"]
    R --> C["Virtual Cell & World Models<br/>~32 papers"]
    R --> D["Pretraining Datasets<br/>~24 papers"]
    R --> E["Benchmarks & Evaluation<br/>~63 papers"]
    R --> F["Infrastructure & AI Agents<br/>~31 papers"]
    R --> G["Surveys & Perspectives<br/>~36 papers"]
    R --> H["Related Domains<br/>Pathology + Bulk ~8 papers"]

    A --> A1["Unimodal<br/>scRNA-seq · scATAC-seq"]
    A --> A2["Multimodal<br/>Spatial · Perturbation · Multi-omics"]
    A --> A3["LLM-based scFMs"]

    subgraph Legend["Domain Roles"]
        L1["Model-centric: A"]
        L2["Application frontier: B · C"]
        L3["Ecosystem: D · E · F · G"]
        L4["Adjacent field: H"]
    end
```

> [!TIP]
> Because everything lives in one file, **the Catalog table of contents at lines 39–70 is your fastest navigation tool** — every domain heading in the README is an anchor link, so you never need to scroll or search to reach a section.

Sources: [README.md](/README.md#L39-L70), [README.md](/README.md#L72-L78)

## Anatomy of a Catalog Entry

Every catalog entry follows one uniform, machine-parseable pattern — which is what makes the list easy to scan, filter, and contribute to:

```
1. [Year Venue] **Model Name: Descriptive paper title** [[paper]](URL-to-publication)
```

| Component | Purpose | Example (from entry for scGPT) |
|---|---|---|
| `[Year Venue]` | Publication year and venue (Nature Methods, NeurIPS, bioRxiv, arXiv…) | `[2024 Nature Methods]` |
| `**Bold title**` | Model name plus paper title | `scGPT: toward building a foundation model…` |
| `[[paper]](URL)` | Direct link to the publication or preprint | `nature.com/articles/s41592-024-02201-0` |
| `[[portal]]`/`[[blog]]`/`[[website]]` | Optional alternate resource link (used sparingly) | CZ CELLxGENE portal link |

Notice that venues span both **peer-reviewed journals** (Nature, Cell, Nature Methods) and **preprint servers** (bioRxiv, arXiv) — the field moves fast enough that preprints are first-class citizens here. Entries are ordered newest-first within each subsection, so scanning the top of any list shows you the research frontier.

> [!TIP]
> Watch for the venue tag as a **credibility signal**: `[bioRxiv]` and `[arXiv]` entries are not yet peer-reviewed, while `[Nature]`, `[Cell]`, or `[NeurIPS]` entries have passed formal review — a useful heuristic when prioritizing what to read first.

Sources: [README.md](/README.md#L81-L124), [README.md](/README.md#L341-L344)

## The Companion Review and Its Classification System

This catalog is not an arbitrary collection — it is the **living companion to a comprehensive review paper**, *"The landscape of single-cell foundation models: design principles, applications, and open challenges"* (currently under review at *Cell*, with full BibTeX provided in the README). The catalog's section structure deliberately mirrors the review's taxonomy, which classifies single-cell foundation models (**scFMs**) along three axes:

1. **By modality** — *unimodal* (one omic type, e.g., scRNA-seq alone), *multimodal* (jointly modeling transcriptomic, epigenomic, proteomic, and spatial data), and *LLM-based* (incorporating large language models or textual biological knowledge).
2. **By pretraining objective** — masked reconstruction, autoregressive generation, contrastive/relational alignment, or supervised prediction.
3. **By research function** — representation learning, perturbation prediction, or world-model simulation.

This is why the domain descriptions in the README read like design-principle statements rather than keyword lists: they are the operational definitions from the review itself.

Sources: [README.md](/README.md#L26-L37), [README.md](/README.md#L74-L78)

## One Navigation Convention to Know

There is exactly one cross-listing rule that could confuse newcomers: **perturbation-trained foundation models are cataloged under Multimodal scFMs, not under the Genetic Perturbation domain**. The README states this explicitly in its Genetic Perturbation introduction, citing models such as X-Cell, SCALE, PerturbGen, STATE, GeneJepa, and Tahoe-x1 as examples. The underlying logic follows the review's classification-first principle: a model's *primary pretraining modality* determines its primary home, while the perturbation domain is reserved for perturbation-*specialized* frameworks, atlases, and benchmarks.

Sources: [README.md](/README.md#L237-L239), [README.md](/README.md#L151-L158)

## Your Path Forward

You now hold the complete mental model: a one-file knowledge base of ~375 papers across nine domains, classified by the taxonomy of its companion review. The recommended reading progression through this documentation follows the catalog's own structure — from orientation, through the core model landscape, outward to applications and ecosystem:

1. **[Quick Start](2-quick-start)** — practical guidance for using and contributing to the repository.
2. **[Evolutionary Tree of Models](3-evolutionary-tree-of-models)** — a guided tour of the visual field map you saw above.
3. **[Taxonomy of Single-Cell Foundation Models](4-taxonomy-of-single-cell-foundation-models)** — the classification system that underpins every section.
4. **Core Model Landscape** — begin with [Unimodal scRNA-seq Models](5-unimodal-scrna-seq-models), the largest and most mature family, then branch into [Single-Cell ATAC-seq Models](6-single-cell-atac-seq-models), [Multimodal and Spatial Models](7-multimodal-and-spatial-models), and [LLM-Based Cell Models](8-llm-based-cell-models).
5. **Application frontiers** — [Perturbation Prediction Frameworks](9-perturbation-prediction-frameworks) and [Virtual Cell Perspectives and Roadmaps](12-virtual-cell-perspectives-and-roadmaps) represent where the field is heading.

If you prefer a top-down grasp of the field before examining individual models, read the Surveys and Perspectives material early via [Surveys and Open Challenges](21-surveys-and-open-challenges); if you are building systems rather than reading theory, the ecosystem layer starting at [Infrastructure and Model Platforms](19-infrastructure-and-model-platforms) is your fast track.


# Quick Start



This page takes you from zero to productively using the **Awesome Foundation Models for Single-Cell** repository. Set your expectations correctly from the start: this is a *curated reading catalog*, not a runnable codebase. There is nothing to `pip install`, no model weights to download, and no API to call. The entire deliverable is a single, carefully structured Markdown document — the `README.md` — that indexes roughly **380 research papers** spanning single-cell foundation models, perturbation prediction, virtual cells, datasets, benchmarks, and AI agents. Your workflow here is browser navigation plus a reference manager, and this page teaches you that workflow in under ten minutes.

Sources: [README.md](/README.md#L1-L12)

## The Repository at a Glance

The project carries the standard [awesome-list](https://awesome.re) badge and welcomes pull requests, signaling that it is a community-maintained index rather than a software product. Its structure is deliberately minimal — three files total — because all informational value is concentrated in one artifact:

```
awesome-foundation-model-single-cell-papers/
├── LICENSE                     # Repository licensing terms
├── README.md                   # The complete catalog: 534 lines, ~380 paper entries
└── figs/
    └── evo_tree.png            # Evolutionary tree visual (clickable → high-res PDF)
```

Think of the repository as a **documentation-as-data** architecture: the README is simultaneously the landing page, the table of contents, and the full database. Every piece of content you will ever consume from this project lives in that one file.

Sources: [README.md](/README.md#L1-L8)

To build a mental model before diving in, here is how the README's eight top-level domains relate to each other. The catalog follows the structure of the team's companion review paper, so model-centric collections sit at the top, resource-centric and evaluation-centric collections in the middle, and tangentially related fields at the bottom:

```mermaid
flowchart TD
    R["README.md — the entire catalog"]
    R --> M["Single-Cell Foundation Models"]
    R --> P["Genetic Perturbation: Models, Atlases, Benchmarks"]
    R --> V["Virtual Cell, World Models & Digital Human"]
    R --> D["Pretraining Datasets and Resources"]
    R --> B["Benchmarks and Evaluation"]
    R --> I["Infrastructure, Platforms and AI Agents"]
    R --> S["Surveys and Perspectives"]
    R --> RW["Related Work: Pathology & Bulk Transcriptomes"]
    M --> M1["Unimodal: scRNA-seq · scATAC-seq"]
    M --> M2["Multimodal: Perturbation · Spatial · Multi-omics"]
    M --> M3["LLM-based scFMs"]
```

The design principle behind this hierarchy is worth internalizing: **models are grouped by pretraining modality, while everything else is grouped by function** (datasets, evaluation, tooling). Once you know which question you are asking — *"which model?"* vs *"which dataset/benchmark/tool?"* — the correct branch of the tree is unambiguous.

Sources: [README.md](/README.md#L39-L70), [README.md](/README.md#L72-L74)

## How to Read a Catalog Entry

Every entry follows one strict format, so once you decode it once, you can scan hundreds of entries at speed. Here is a real entry taken from the scRNA-seq section, broken down component by component:

| Component | Example | What It Tells You |
|---|---|---|
| Position number | `1.` | Sequential list marker; all lists are ordered **newest-first** |
| Year + venue tag | `[2024 Nature Methods]` | Publication year and peer-review venue (`bioRxiv`/`arXiv` = preprint, treat claims accordingly) |
| Bold title | `**scGPT: toward building a foundation model...**` | Model name before the colon; one-line contribution summary after it |
| Link tag | `[[paper]](URL)` | External link — the actual exit point from the catalog |

Applied to the full entry: `1. [2024 Nature Methods] **scGPT: toward building a foundation model for single-cell multi-omics using generative AI** [[paper]](https://www.nature.com/articles/s41592-024-02201-0)` — you can tell at a glance this is a peer-reviewed 2024 model paper published at Nature Methods.

Sources: [README.md](/README.md#L81), [README.md](/README.md#L116), [README.md](/README.md#L125-L136)

A small but important detail: the link tag is not always `[[paper]]`. The catalog uses **four link types** to distinguish what you are about to open, which matters because some entries point at living web services rather than static PDFs:

| Link Tag | Meaning | Example Entry |
|---|---|---|
| `[[paper]]` | Publication (journal, conference, or preprint) | scGPT at Nature Methods |
| `[[portal]]` | Browsable data platform | CZ CELLxGENE Discover — single-cell data portal |
| `[[blog]]` | Vendor/institutional blog post | AIDO Cell simulator announcement |
| `[[website]]` | Directory or project site | Toolome — AI tools for biology directory |

Sources: [README.md](/README.md#L341), [README.md](/README.md#L318), [README.md](/README.md#L443)

> [!TIP]
> The venue tag doubles as a quality filter. When skimming a long section, scan only the bracketed prefixes first: `[2026 bioRxiv]` entries are recent preprints (cutting-edge but not peer-reviewed), while `[2024 Nature Methods]` entries have survived review. This two-second triage lets you decide whether to read deeply or just bookmark.

## Your First Ten Minutes: A Guided Walkthrough

The fastest path from opening the repository to having five relevant papers in your reading queue looks like this:

```mermaid
flowchart LR
    A["Open the repo homepage"] --> B["Scan the Catalog TOC"]
    B --> C["Click the evolutionary tree"]
    C --> D["Pick one section matching your goal"]
    D --> E["Triage entries by year + venue"]
    E --> F["Open paper / portal links"]
    F --> G["Continue to deep-dive pages"]
```

Execute the steps as follows:

1. **Open the repo homepage.** The header, badges, and one-paragraph mission statement tell you immediately what this is.
Sources: [README.md](/README.md#L1-L12)
2. **Jump to the `Catalog` section.** Every top-level heading in the README is a clickable anchor — clicking `[Single-Cell Foundation Models](#single-cell-foundation-models)` in the Catalog teleports you down the page without scrolling. Use this as your navigation hub every visit.
Sources: [README.md](/README.md#L39-L70)
3. **Click the evolutionary tree image.** The embedded image links to a full-resolution PDF (`figs/evo_tree.pdf`), which maps how single-cell foundation models evolved from one another — keep it open on a second screen as your visual map.
Sources: [README.md](/README.md#L22-L24)
4. **Enter exactly one section.** Resist reading everything; pick the branch that matches your current task (see the learning-path table below).
Sources: [README.md](/README.md#L39-L70)
5. **Triage, then open.** Filter by year/venue tags, then open `[[paper]]` links for the three to five entries that survive your filter.
Sources: [README.md](/README.md#L81)

## Choose Your Learning Path

Different readers should enter the catalog at different points. The table below maps common goals to the README section you should open first, an illustrative anchor entry, and the dedicated deep-dive documentation page that expands on that territory. Note how each goal lands in exactly one primary section — that is the payoff of the modality-first / function-first split:

| Your Goal | Start in README Section | Illustrative Entry | Continue Reading At |
|---|---|---|---|
| Understand the model landscape broadly | Single-Cell Foundation Models → scRNA-seq | Geneformer, scGPT, scFoundation | [Taxonomy of Single-Cell Foundation Models](4-taxonomy-of-single-cell-foundation-models) |
| Chromatin accessibility work | Single-Cell Foundation Models → scATAC-seq | GET, EpiAgent | [Single-Cell ATAC-seq Models](6-single-cell-atac-seq-models) |
| Spatial transcriptomics or histology | Multimodal → Spatial, Proteomics and Histology | Nicheformer, OmiCLIP | [Multimodal and Spatial Models](7-multimodal-and-spatial-models) |
| Apply LLMs to cells | LLM-based scFMs | Cell2Sentence, GenePT | [LLM-Based Cell Models](8-llm-based-cell-models) |
| Predict gene perturbation outcomes | Genetic Perturbation → Models and prediction frameworks | GEARS, scGen | [Perturbation Prediction Frameworks](9-perturbation-prediction-frameworks) |
| Find perturbation training data | Genetic Perturbation → Perturbation atlases | Tahoe-100M, Perturb-seq | [Perturbation Atlases and Datasets](10-perturbation-atlases-and-datasets) |
| Know if these models actually work | Benchmarks and Evaluation | PerturBench, scEval | [Benchmarking Studies and Critiques](17-benchmarking-studies-and-critiques) |
| Build your own pretraining pipeline | Pretraining Datasets → Data formats and frameworks | scvi-tools, Scanpy | [Analysis Frameworks and Data Formats](16-analysis-frameworks-and-data-formats) |
| Deploy or serve models | Infrastructure, Platforms and AI Agents | scvi-hub, BioNeMo | [Infrastructure and Model Platforms](19-infrastructure-and-model-platforms) |
| Get oriented fast (theory) | Surveys and Perspectives | Transformers in single-cell omics | [Surveys and Open Challenges](21-surveys-and-open-challenges) |

Sources: [README.md](/README.md#L76-L80), [README.md](/README.md#L125-L117), [README.md](/README.md#L138-L145), [README.md](/README.md#L160-L189), [README.md](/README.md#L203-L235), [README.md](/README.md#L241-L265), [README.md](/README.md#L267-L273), [README.md](/README.md#L275-L290), [README.md](/README.md#L357-L364), [README.md](/README.md#L441-L454), [README.md](/README.md#L478-L517)

> [!TIP]
> Beware one deliberate overlap: perturbation-*trained* foundation models (such as Tahoe-x1 and STATE) are cataloged under Multimodal scFMs, not under the Genetic Perturbation section. The README cross-references this explicitly, so if a perturbation model search comes up empty, check the multimodal branch before concluding the catalog lacks it.

## The Evolutionary Tree: Your Visual Map

![Evolutionary tree of single-cell foundation models](https://github.com/OmicsML/awesome-foundation-model-single-cell-papers/blob/main/figs/evo_tree.png?raw=true)

The repository ships a single visualization — the evolutionary tree of single-cell foundation models, adapted with credit from the LLMsPracticalGuide project. It compresses the catalog's historical narrative into one picture: which model families descended from which, and when major branches (unimodal, multimodal, LLM-based) diverged. For a beginner, this image is the highest-value five minutes in the whole repository — read it *before* reading any paper, because it gives you the vocabulary and lineage context that makes individual entries meaningful. The dedicated page on this topic decodes the tree branch by branch.

## Citing the Project

If this catalog feeds your research, the maintainers ask that you cite their companion review, currently under review at *Cell*. The README includes a ready-to-paste BibTeX block — copy it verbatim into your `.bib` file:

```bibtex
@article{jiang2026landscape,
  title={The Landscape of Single-Cell Foundation Models: Design Principles, Applications, and Open Challenges},
  author={Jiang, Shiyu and Fang, Zhaoyu and Zhang, Yujie and Zhang, Xuting and Kalfon, J{\'e}r{\'e}mie and Wang, Weixu and Fu, Xi and Patel, Aakash and Rizvi, Syed and Lu, Yuancheng Ryan and others},
  year={2026},
  publisher={Preprints}
}
```

This is also an architectural hint about the repository itself: the catalog's section structure mirrors the review's chapter structure, so reading the review alongside the catalog gives you curated narrative plus up-to-date paper links.

Sources: [README.md](/README.md#L26-L37)

## Contributing Back

The repository is explicitly contribution-driven: found a missed paper or a broken link? Open an issue or a pull request. As you use the catalog, you are uniquely positioned to spot the failure modes maintainers care about — a dead `[[paper]]` URL, a new preprint missing from a section, or a model filed under the wrong modality. Because the entire catalog is one Markdown file, contributing requires no build tooling: fork, edit `README.md`, append your entry to the correct section following the exact `[year venue] **Name: description** [[paper]](url)` pattern, and open a PR.

Sources: [README.md](/README.md#L14-L16)

## Where to Go Next

You now know how to navigate, decode, and contribute to the catalog. The recommended progression through this documentation deepens your understanding layer by layer — from the bird's-eye historical view, down into the taxonomy, then into the specific model families and application domains:

1. **[Overview](1-overview)** — if you have not read it yet, it frames why foundation models matter for single-cell genomics.
2. **[Evolutionary Tree of Models](3-evolutionary-tree-of-models)** — a guided decode of the `figs/evo_tree.png` visualization you just downloaded.
3. **[Taxonomy of Single-Cell Foundation Models](4-taxonomy-of-single-cell-foundation-models)** — the classification system that explains *why* the catalog's sections are drawn where they are.
4. **[Unimodal scRNA-seq Models](5-unimodal-scrna-seq-models)** — the largest and most mature branch, and the natural first deep dive.
5. Then branch out to your domain of interest: [Perturbation Prediction Frameworks](9-perturbation-prediction-frameworks), [Virtual Cell Perspectives and Roadmaps](12-virtual-cell-perspectives-and-roadmaps), or [Benchmarking Studies and Critiques](17-benchmarking-studies-and-critiques).

The catalog itself stays useful at every stage: return to it whenever you need the freshest entries, since it is continuously updated with new preprints and publications.


# Evolutionary Tree of Models



This page introduces the **evolutionary tree of single-cell foundation models** — the master visual that maps how the field grew from early transformer experiments into today's sprawling ecosystem of specialized model families. You will learn what the figure shows, how to read it branch by branch, and how each branch connects to the deeper catalog pages. No prior knowledge of single-cell biology or foundation models is required.

Sources: [README.md](/README.md#L10-L24)

## What Is the Evolutionary Tree of Models?

An **evolutionary tree** is a diagram convention borrowed from the large language model (LLM) community: a chronological trunk from which model *families* branch out, with individual models as leaves. This repository adapts that convention — the figure is explicitly credited to the [LLMsPracticalGuide](https://github.com/Mooler0410/LLMsPracticalGuide/tree/main) project, whose famous "Evolutionary Tree of Language Models" popularized this style [README.md](/README.md#L18-L20). Where the LLM tree organizes branches by architecture (encoder-only, decoder-only), this tree organizes branches by **pretraining modality** — the type of biological data a model was trained on.

The figure below is the complete tree, embedded directly from the repository (`figs/evo_tree.png`, the repo's only image asset):

![Evolutionary tree of single-cell foundation models](https://github.com/OmicsML/awesome-foundation-model-single-cell-papers/blob/main/figs/evo_tree.png?raw=true)

Sources: [README.md](/README.md#L18-L24)

> [!TIP]
> The tree is a *navigation aid*, not a genealogy claim. "Family" membership means a model shares a pretraining modality (e.g., all scRNA-seq models form one branch), not that one model literally descends from another. Read it the way you would read a map of a city's districts — by neighborhood, not by street-level history.

## How to Read the Tree: The Taxonomy Behind the Branches

The tree's structure follows the repository's organizing review, *"The landscape of single-cell foundation models: design principles, applications, and open challenges"*. Every model in the catalog is placed into one of three top-level families based on the modalities it was pretrained on [README.md](/README.md#L72-L74):

- **Unimodal scFMs** — trained on a single omic modality (scRNA-seq gene expression, or scATAC-seq chromatin accessibility)
- **Multimodal scFMs** — trained jointly on complementary modalities (transcriptomics + perturbation, spatial/histology, or RNA + ATAC + protein together)
- **LLM-based scFMs** — trained by incorporating large language models or textual biological knowledge into cellular representations

Within the unimodal branches, models further differentiate by their **pretraining objective**: masked reconstruction, autoregressive generation, contrastive/relational alignment, or supervised prediction [README.md](/README.md#L76-L78). The diagram below shows the tree's architecture as the catalog encodes it:

```mermaid
graph TD
    ROOT["🌳 Evolutionary Tree<br/>Single-Cell Foundation Models"] --> UNI["Unimodal scFMs<br/>one omic modality"]
    ROOT --> MULTI["Multimodal scFMs<br/>joint modalities"]
    ROOT --> LLM["LLM-based scFMs<br/>language + cells"]
    UNI --> RNA["scRNA-seq family<br/>scBERT · Geneformer · scGPT · CellFM"]
    UNI --> ATAC["scATAC-seq family<br/>GET · EpiAgent · ChromFound"]
    MULTI --> TP["Transcriptomics +<br/>Perturbation<br/>STATE · Tahoe-x1"]
    MULTI --> SP["Spatial / Proteomics /<br/>Histology<br/>Nicheformer · SpatialFormer"]
    MULTI --> MO["Multi-omics<br/>RNA + ATAC + Protein<br/>SCARF · CLM-X"]
    LLM --> AN["Annotation & Agents<br/>GenePT · Cell2Sentence"]
    LLM --> CH["Chat & Instruction<br/>CellWhisperer · InstructCell"]
```

Sources: [README.md](/README.md#L39-L70), [README.md](/README.md#L72-L78)

## The Main Branches and Their Landmark Models

The table below summarizes each branch of the tree with its defining property and the landmark models you will encounter most often in the literature. Landmarks are listed chronologically within each branch, so each row doubles as a mini evolution history.

| Tree Branch | Pretraining Data | Landmark Models (earliest → latest) | Pretraining Objective Examples |
|---|---|---|---|
| **Unimodal: scRNA-seq** | Single-cell gene expression | scBERT (2022) → Geneformer (2023) → scGPT, scFoundation (2024) → CellFM, TranscriptFormer (2025) → GeneformerV2 (2026) | Masked reconstruction, autoregressive generation |
| **Unimodal: scATAC-seq** | Chromatin accessibility | GET (2025) → EpiAgent, ChromFound, EpiFoundation (2025) → CLM-Access (2026) | Peak-to-gene alignment, reconstruction |
| **Multimodal: Transcriptomics + Perturbation** | Expression under genetic/chemical perturbation | STATE (2026) → Tahoe-x1 (2025, 3B params) | Perturbation-conditioned modeling |
| **Multimodal: Spatial, Proteomics, Histology** | Spatial transcriptomics, tissue images | Nicheformer (2025) → Novae, SToFM (2025) → SpatialFormer (2026) | Cross-modality alignment |
| **Multimodal: Multi-omics (RNA+ATAC+Protein)** | Co-assayed multi-omic cells | SCARF (2025) → CLM-X, CAPTAIN (2026) | Modality-specific reconstruction |
| **LLM-based scFMs** | Cells + natural language knowledge | Cell2Sentence, LangCell (2024) → GenePT, CellWhisperer (2025) → OCellus (2026) | Text-derived embeddings, chat interfaces |

Sources: [README.md](/README.md#L80-L136), [README.md](/README.md#L138-L145), [README.md](/README.md#L151-L201), [README.md](/README.md#L203-L235)

## Evolution Milestones: A Chronological Walk

The trunk of the tree — time itself — shows three distinct growth phases. Each milestone below is a dated catalog entry you can trace back to its paper.

| Phase | Year | Milestone | Why It Matters |
|---|---|---|---|
| **Sprouting** | 2022 | scBERT — early large-scale transformer pretraining for cell-type annotation | Proof that masked-language-model pretraining works on single-cell data |
| **First flowering** | 2023 | Geneformer, tGPT, xTrimoGene, CellPLM | Transfer learning to network biology; scaling and efficiency competition; objectives diversify |
| **Mainstreaming** | 2024 | scGPT and scFoundation published in Nature Methods; GEARS for perturbation; first LLM-cell hybrids (Cell2Sentence, LangCell) | Foundation-model paradigm becomes the field's default; perturbation and language branches emerge |
| **Scaling & specialization** | 2025 | CellFM pretrained on 100M cells; TranscriptFormer spans 1.5B years of evolution; Tahoe-x1 reaches 3B parameters; chat-based CellWhisperer | Scale-up race; spatial and chat sub-branches thicken |
| **Maturation & world models** | 2026 | GeneformerV2, scPRINT-2, universal cell embeddings in Nature; AlphaCell and CellOS target cellular *world models* | Consolidation of flagship families; a new frontier branch grows toward simulated cells |

Sources: [README.md](/README.md#L134), [README.md](/README.md#L124-L127), [README.md](/README.md#L116-L117), [README.md](/README.md#L230-L234), [README.md](/README.md#L263), [README.md](/README.md#L103-L107), [README.md](/README.md#L158), [README.md](/README.md#L222), [README.md](/README.md#L85-L97), [README.md](/README.md#L320-L325)

## Frontier Branches Growing Beyond the Core Tree

Two newer branches extend past the three modality families and are becoming disciplines of their own. The **genetic perturbation branch** covers prediction frameworks, large-scale perturbation atlases, and benchmarks — noting that perturbation-trained scFMs (STATE, Tahoe-x1, GeneJepa) are cataloged under the multimodal branch [README.md](/README.md#L237-L239). The **virtual cell branch** recasts foundation models as cellular *world models* — generative simulators that predict how cells respond to perturbations over time, an emerging paradigm with its own dedicated catalog section [README.md](/README.md#L292-L294).

This history starts earlier than the transformer era: perturbation modeling traces back to Perturb-seq (2016) for scalable pooled genetic screens and scGen (2019) for predicting single-cell perturbation responses — the roots from which today's perturbation branch grew.

Sources: [README.md](/README.md#L237-L239), [README.md](/README.md#L273), [README.md](/README.md#L265), [README.md](/README.md#L292-L294)

Every branch of the tree corresponds to one or more catalog sections, so the figure works as a visual index. Use this mapping table to jump from any branch you find interesting to its detailed page.

| Tree Branch | Catalog Concept | Deep-Dive Page |
|---|---|---|

| Unimodal: scATAC-seq | Unimodal scFMs → scATAC-seq | [Single-Cell ATAC-seq Models](6-single-cell-atac-seq-models) |

Sources: [README.md](/README.md#L39-L70)

> [!TIP]
> Treat the tree as your progress tracker. After reading any deep-dive page, return to the figure and locate that branch — landmark names you just studied will now anchor your mental map, and unexplored branches become your reading queue.

## Suggested Reading Path

For a beginner following the tree from trunk to leaves, the catalog's structure suggests this progression: first understand **why** the field branched this way ([Taxonomy of Single-Cell Foundation Models](4-taxonomy-of-single-cell-foundation-models)), then walk the dominant scRNA-seq trunk ([Unimodal scRNA-seq Models](5-unimodal-scrna-seq-models)) before its epigenomic sibling ([Single-Cell ATAC-seq Models](6-single-cell-atac-seq-models)). From there, widen into joint-modality branches ([Multimodal and Spatial Models](7-multimodal-and-spatial-models), [LLM-Based Cell Models](8-llm-based-cell-models)), then explore the frontier ([Perturbation Prediction Frameworks](9-perturbation-prediction-frameworks), [Cell World Model Implementations](13-cell-world-model-implementations)). If you want the application-oriented view first, jump directly to [Infrastructure and Model Platforms](19-infrastructure-and-model-platforms) or [Benchmarking Studies and Critiques](17-benchmarking-studies-and-critiques).


# Taxonomy of Single-Cell Foundation Models



This page explains the classification system that organizes the model landscape cataloged in this repository. Every entry in the **Single-Cell Foundation Models** section is positioned along two orthogonal axes: the *pretraining modality* the model consumes (the primary axis) and the *learning objective* it optimizes (the secondary axis). Mastering this two-dimensional grid is the key to navigating the four deep-dive model pages that follow, and to predicting where any new paper will land in the catalog.

Sources: [README.md](README.md#L1-L12), [README.md](README.md#L39-L70)

## The Classification Principle: Modality First

The catalog explicitly states its organizing rule: single-cell foundation models "are grouped by the modalities they are pretrained on." This is a deliberate design choice — among all attributes of a single-cell foundation model (architecture, parameter count, downstream task), the pretraining modality is the most stable and consequential one, because it determines what biological information a model can possibly represent. The modality-first principle yields three primary classes: **unimodal** (a single omic), **multimodal** (jointly encoding complementary data types), and **LLM-based** (models where language-model or textual knowledge integration is the defining mechanism). A defining quote from the catalog captures the shared premise of all three classes: these models are "pretrained on large-scale atlases to learn transferable representations of cellular state."

Sources: [README.md](README.md#L72-L74)

The full taxonomy resolves into six leaf categories. The counts below are taken directly from the catalog's entry lists, which are verifiable line-by-line: 56 scRNA-seq entries, 7 scATAC-seq entries, 7 transcriptomics+perturbation entries, 29 spatial/proteomics/histology entries, 10 multi-omics entries, and 29 LLM-based entries — **138 curated model entries** in the core taxonomy alone.

```mermaid
graph TD
    ROOT["Single-Cell Foundation Models<br/>pretrained on large-scale atlases<br/>138 catalog entries"]
    ROOT --> UNI["Unimodal scFMs<br/>single omic modality · 63 entries"]
    ROOT --> MULTI["Multimodal scFMs<br/>jointly encoded modalities · 46 entries"]
    ROOT --> LLM["LLM-based scFMs<br/>language + text knowledge · 29 entries"]
    UNI --> RNA["scRNA-seq · 56 entries"]
    UNI --> ATAC["scATAC-seq · 7 entries"]
    RNA --> RNAEX["Geneformer · scGPT · scFoundation<br/>scBERT · CellPLM · tGPT"]
    ATAC --> ATACEX["ChromFound · EpiFoundation<br/>EpiAgent · GET · ChromBERT"]
    MULTI --> TP["Transcriptomics + Perturbation · 7"]
    MULTI --> SPH["Spatial · Proteomics · Histology · 29"]
    MULTI --> MO["Multi-omics: RNA + ATAC + Protein · 10"]
    TP --> TPEX["STATE · Tahoe-x1 · GeneJepa · X-Cell"]
    SPH --> SPHEX["Nicheformer · Novae · OmiCLIP<br/>SToFM · SPATIA · KRONOS"]
    MO --> MOEX["SCARF · CAPTAIN<br/>scTranslator · scLinguist"]
    LLM --> LLMEX["Cell2Sentence · GenePT · LangCell<br/>CellWhisperer · CELLama"]
```

Sources: [README.md](README.md#L76-L146), [README.md](README.md#L147-L201), [README.md](README.md#L203-L235)

The repository also ships an **evolutionary tree** figure that visualizes the historical lineage of these model families, adapted with credit from the LLMsPracticalGuide project. It complements the taxonomy tree above: the taxonomy classifies models *statically* by design attributes, while the evolutionary tree arranges them *chronologically* by lineage.

![Evolutionary tree of single-cell foundation models](https://github.com/OmicsML/awesome-foundation-model-single-cell-papers/blob/main/figs/evo_tree.png?raw=true)

Sources: [README.md](README.md#L18-L24)

## Primary Class I: Unimodal scFMs

Unimodal models are "trained within a single omic modality (scRNA-seq or scATAC-seq)." This class contains the oldest and largest branch of the landscape — the transcriptomic branch stretches from scBERT (2022) through Geneformer (2023) and scGPT/scFoundation (2024) to the 2026 generation of billion-parameter models — and splits cleanly along the transcriptomic/epigenomic boundary. The catalog assigns this class four learning objectives: "masked reconstruction, autoregressive generation, contrastive/relational alignment, or supervised prediction."

| Sub-family | Pretraining input | Representative entries | Catalog span |
|---|---|---|---|
| scRNA-seq | Gene expression counts per cell | scBERT, Geneformer, xTrimoGene, tGPT, scGPT, scFoundation, CellPLM, CellFM, SCimilarity, TranscriptFormer, GeneMamba | 2022 → 2026 |
| scATAC-seq | Chromatin accessibility peaks | CLM-Access, Atacformer, ChromFound, EpiFoundation, EpiAgent, GET, ChromBERT | 2025 → 2026 |

The asymmetry between the two sub-families (56 vs 7 entries) reflects data availability: scRNA-seq atlases are vastly larger and more standardized than single-cell chromatin accessibility data, so the epigenomic branch matured roughly two years later.

Sources: [README.md](README.md#L76-L146)

## Primary Class II: Multimodal scFMs

Multimodal models "jointly encode complementary modalities — transcriptomic, epigenomic, proteomic, perturbational and spatial — through modality-specific reconstruction, cross-modality alignment, or task-informed supervision." The catalog partitions this class into three sub-categories that correspond to different *pairing strategies* rather than a single schema: expression+perturbation (training signal from genetic or chemical perturbation responses), expression+space/image (aligning transcriptomics with tissue coordinates, protein imaging, or histology), and co-assayed multi-omics (RNA, ATAC and protein measured jointly). Note that several members of the first sub-category — STATE, Tahoe-x1 (scaled to 3B parameters), GeneJepa, X-Cell — are among the largest and most recent models in the entire catalog.

| Sub-category | Modality pairing | Representative entries | Typical objective |
|---|---|---|---|
| Transcriptomics + Perturbation | expression + perturbation response | STATE, Tahoe-x1, GeneJepa, X-Cell, PertGen, SCALE | conditional generation / transport |
| Spatial, Proteomics and Histology | expression + spatial coordinates / images | Nicheformer, Novae, OmiCLIP, SToFM, SPATIA, HEIST, KRONOS, scGPT-spatial | cross-modality alignment |
| Multi-omics: RNA, ATAC and Protein | co-assayed omic layers | SCARF, CAPTAIN, scTranslator, scLinguist, CLM-X, HoloCell | modality-specific reconstruction |

Sources: [README.md](README.md#L147-L201)

## Primary Class III: LLM-based scFMs

The third class is defined not by how many omics a model consumes but *how* it leverages language technology: these models "incorporate large language models or textual biological knowledge into cellular representation learning." Their objective set extends the standard families with a fifth mechanism unique to this class — **text-derived representation**, where biological meaning is injected through natural-language embeddings or instructions. The class spans a wide integration spectrum: Cell2Sentence converts expression profiles into text for direct LLM consumption; GenePT derives gene embeddings from GPT text embeddings; LangCell pre-trains joint language-cell representations; and agentic copilots such as CellWhisperer, scChat and InstructCell wrap LLMs around single-cell workflows for conversational analysis.

| Integration pattern | Mechanism | Representative entries |
|---|---|---|
| Cells-as-text | serialize expression into language tokens | Cell2Sentence, CELLama, C2S-Scale |
| Text-derived gene/cell embeddings | LLM embeddings as biological priors | GenePT, scELMo, sciLaMA, scKITE |
| Joint cell-language pretraining | aligned multimodal (cell+text) training | LangCell, CellHermes, CellTok, OKR-Cell |
| LLM copilots / agents | instruction-following analysis interfaces | CellWhisperer, scChat, InstructCell, scReader |

Sources: [README.md](README.md#L203-L235)

## The Secondary Axis: Learning Objectives

Within every modality class, the catalog's class definitions repeatedly cite the same small set of objective families — the secondary axis of the taxonomy. A model's catalog position is therefore a tuple: *(modality class, objective family)*. The table below maps each objective to concrete, line-verifiable examples across the three classes.

| Objective family | Mechanism | Unimodal example | Multimodal example | LLM-based example |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| Masked reconstruction | mask-and-predict corruption recovery | scBERT, Single-cell Masked Autoencoder, scPRINT | GeneJepa (predictive latent) | — |
| Autoregressive generation | next-token / next-gene prediction | tGPT, scMulan, scGPT | X-Cell (diffusion LM) | PGL, RVQ-Alpha |
| Contrastive / relational alignment | pull related views together | Divide-and-Conquer Contrastive, scConcept, scPROTEIN | scCLIP, OmiCLIP | LangCell |
| Supervised / task-informed prediction | label-driven objectives | scPretrain, scCello (ontology-guided) | STATE | mLLMCelltype |
| Text-derived representation | meaning from natural language | — | scGenePT | GenePT, scELMo |

```mermaid
graph LR
    ENTRY["Catalog entry"] --> MOD
    ENTRY --> OBJ
    subgraph MOD["Primary axis · pretraining modality"]
        M1["Unimodal"]
        M2["Multimodal"]
        M3["LLM-based"]
    end
    subgraph OBJ["Secondary axis · learning objective"]
        J1["Masked reconstruction"]
        J2["Autoregressive generation"]
        J3["Contrastive / relational alignment"]
        J4["Supervised prediction"]
        J5["Text-derived representation"]
    end
```

Sources: [README.md](README.md#L78), [README.md](README.md#L149), [README.md](README.md#L205)

> [!TIP]
> Multi-class membership is a real pattern, not an error: BioM-JEPA and Cell-JEPA appear in both the scRNA-seq list and the Virtual Cell "Models and frameworks" list, and GeneJepa appears in both Transcriptomics+Perturbation and Virtual Cell. The catalog convention is *primary listing by taxonomy class, cross-listing when a model also serves as a world-model implementation*. When searching the catalog, check both locations.

Sources: [README.md](README.md#L90-L91), [README.md](README.md#L157), [README.md](README.md#L323-L329)

## Cross-Cutting Catalog Axes: Where Model Classes End

The taxonomy deliberately separates *what a model is* (the three classes above) from *what it is for and what it needs*. The remaining catalog sections — Genetic Perturbation, Virtual Cell and World Models, Pretraining Datasets, Benchmarks and Evaluation, Infrastructure and AI Agents — are orthogonal slices that can apply to any model class. This is why, for example, perturbation benchmarks and perturbation atlases live outside the model-class section entirely: they describe evaluation instruments and training resources, not models.

> [!TIP]
> The catalog has one explicit disambiguation rule that trips up new readers: **perturbation-trained scFMs (X-Cell, SCALE, PerturbGen, STATE, GeneJepa, Tahoe-x1) are cataloged under Multimodal scFMs, not under the Genetic Perturbation section**. The Genetic Perturbation section holds dedicated perturbation *prediction frameworks* (GEARS, scGen, Squidiff), *atlases* (Tahoe-100M, Perturb-seq, X-Atlas) and *benchmarks* — models whose identity is "multimodal foundation model" stay upstairs.

Sources: [README.md](README.md#L237-L239), [README.md](README.md#L292-L294), [README.md](README.md#L332-L334), [README.md](README.md#L366-L368), [README.md](README.md#L437-L439)

Applying the taxonomy to a new paper reduces to the following decision flow, which mirrors exactly how the catalog's six leaf categories were constructed:

```mermaid
flowchart TD
    A["New single-cell foundation model entry"] --> B{"Pretraining modalities?"}
    B -->|"one omic"| C{"scRNA-seq<br/>or scATAC-seq?"}
    C -->|"gene expression"| D["Unimodal · scRNA-seq"]
    C -->|"chromatin accessibility"| E["Unimodal · scATAC-seq"]
    B -->|"multiple omics /<br/>spatial / histology"| F{"Is an LLM or textual<br/>knowledge the defining<br/>mechanism?"}
    F -->|"yes"| G["LLM-based scFMs"]
    F -->|"no"| H["Multimodal scFMs"]
    H --> I{"Dominant modality pairing?"}
    I -->|"expression +<br/>perturbation"| J["Transcriptomics + Perturbation"]
    I -->|"expression + space /<br/>protein imaging / histology"| K["Spatial · Proteomics · Histology"]
    I -->|"RNA + ATAC + protein<br/>co-assayed"| L["Multi-omics"]
    A --> M{"Perturbation atlas,<br/>benchmark, or dedicated<br/>prediction framework?"}
    M -->|"yes"| N["Genetic Perturbation section<br/>(cross-cutting axis)"]
```

Sources: [README.md](README.md#L39-L70)

Each cross-cutting axis has its own deep-dive page in this documentation set, with scope boundaries matching the catalog's section intros:

| Cross-cutting axis | Catalog scope | Deep-dive page |
|---|---|---|
| Genetic perturbation | prediction frameworks, atlases, benchmarks | [Perturbation Prediction Frameworks](9-perturbation-prediction-frameworks) |
| Virtual cell | perspectives, roadmaps, world-model implementations | [Virtual Cell Perspectives and Roadmaps](12-virtual-cell-perspectives-and-roadmaps) |
| Pretraining data | atlases, multimodal corpora, formats | [Transcriptomic Atlases and Repositories](14-transcriptomic-atlases-and-repositories) |
| Evaluation | benchmarks, critiques, privacy | [Benchmarking Studies and Critiques](17-benchmarking-studies-and-critiques) |
| Ecosystem | infrastructure, platforms, AI agents | [Infrastructure and Model Platforms](19-infrastructure-and-model-platforms) |

> [!TIP]
> Entries within every catalog section are ordered **newest-first** (2026 entries at the top, descending to foundational works like scGen 2019 at the bottom). The taxonomy is therefore also a timeline: the top of each list is the current research frontier, and each section's tail documents the field's origin points.

Sources: [README.md](README.md#L81-L136), [README.md](README.md#L242-L265)

## Navigating Forward

With the taxonomy internalized, the recommended reading path is to descend from the three primary classes into the four leaf deep-dives, in order of increasing integration complexity. Start with the dominant branch, then the epigenomic minority branch, then the multimodal and language-integrated classes.

- [Unimodal scRNA-seq Models](5-unimodal-scrna-seq-models) — the 56-entry transcriptomic branch, oldest and largest
- [Single-Cell ATAC-seq Models](6-single-cell-atac-seq-models) — the 7-entry epigenomic branch
- [Multimodal and Spatial Models](7-multimodal-and-spatial-models) — perturbation-paired, spatial, and co-assayed multi-omics models
- [LLM-Based Cell Models](8-llm-based-cell-models) — language-integrated representation learning and copilots

For historical context on how these classes emerged from one another, revisit the evolutionary tree visualization on [Evolutionary Tree of Models](3-evolutionary-tree-of-models). When you reach the point of choosing or evaluating models for a concrete task, the cross-cutting pages — [Perturbation Prediction Frameworks](9-perturbation-prediction-frameworks) and [Benchmarking Studies and Critiques](17-benchmarking-studies-and-critiques) — provide the application and validation layer on top of this taxonomy.


# Unimodal scRNA-seq Models



This page catalogs foundation models pretrained **exclusively on scRNA-seq data** — the largest and most mature family in the single-cell foundation model landscape. It is extracted directly from the repository's curated reading list, which follows the review *"The landscape of single-cell foundation models: design principles, applications, and open challenges"*. You'll find a taxonomy positioning map, a training-paradigm breakdown, a 56-entry paper catalog organized by era, and architectural signals worth tracking if you're selecting or building on these models.

Sources: [README.md](README.md#L10-L12), [README.md](README.md#L72-L80)

## Position in the Taxonomy

The repository organizes all single-cell foundation models (scFMs) by **the modality they are pretrained on**. Unimodal scFMs sit at one extreme: a single omic input, learned entirely from transcriptomic structure. This page covers only the `scRNA-seq` leaf; the `scATAC-seq` leaf, multimodal families, and LLM-based models are cataloged on their own pages.

```mermaid
flowchart TD
    A["Single-Cell Foundation Models"] --> B["Unimodal scFMs"]
    A --> C["Multimodal scFMs"]
    A --> D["LLM-based scFMs"]
    B --> E["scRNA-seq<br/>★ THIS PAGE (56 entries)"]
    B --> F["scATAC-seq<br/>→ [Single-Cell ATAC-seq Models](6-single-cell-atac-seq-models)"]
    C --> G["Transcriptomics + Perturbation<br/>→ [Multimodal and Spatial Models](7-multimodal-and-spatial-models)"]
    C --> H["Spatial, Proteomics, Histology"]
    C --> I["Multi-omics: RNA, ATAC, Protein"]
    D --> J["→ [LLM-Based Cell Models](8-llm-based-cell-models)"]

    style E fill:#2d6a4f,color:#fff
    style B fill:#95d5b2
```

The catalog's unimodal definition is precise: models trained within a single omic modality, learning representations through one of four mechanisms (detailed in the next section). Note that entries are grouped by **pretraining input**, not downstream task — so several spatial-adjacent or proteomics-adjacent titles appear here because their core representations are transcriptomic.

Sources: [README.md](README.md#L72-L80), [README.md](README.md#L138-L146)

## The Evolutionary Tree

The repository opens with an evolutionary tree of single-cell foundation models, credited to [Mooler0410/LLMsPracticalGuide](https://github.com/Mooler0410/LLMsPracticalGuide/tree/main). The scRNA-seq branch visible on the left side of this tree corresponds to the catalog on this page — it's worth cross-referencing the visual lineage against the entries below. For a guided walkthrough of the full tree, see [Evolutionary Tree of Models](3-evolutionary-tree-of-models).

![Evolutionary tree of single-cell foundation models](https://github.com/OmicsML/awesome-foundation-model-single-cell-papers/blob/main/figs/evo_tree.png?raw=true)

Sources: [README.md](README.md#L18-L24)

## Training Paradigm Landscape

> [!TIP]
> The repository's one-sentence definition of unimodal scFMs encodes the entire design space: **masked reconstruction, autoregressive generation, contrastive/relational alignment, or supervised prediction**. These four objectives determine how a model tokenizes genes, what its pretraining loss looks like, and which downstream fine-tuning strategy it supports — making them the most important axis when comparing papers in this catalog.

```mermaid
flowchart LR
    subgraph INPUT["Raw Input"]
        R["scRNA-seq count matrix"]
    end
    R --> M["Masked Reconstruction"]
    R --> AR["Autoregressive Generation"]
    R --> CL["Contrastive / Relational Alignment"]
    R --> SP["Supervised Prediction"]

    M --> M1["Single-cell MAE"]
    M --> M2["ScDiVa (discrete diffusion)"]
    AR --> A1["tGPT · scGPT · scMulan"]
    AR --> A2["Stack (in-context)"]
    CL --> C1["Divide-and-Conquer CL"]
    CL --> C2["Cell-JEPA · BioM-JEPA"]
    SP --> S1["scBERT · scPretrain"]

    style R fill:#e9c46a
    style M fill:#219ebc,color:#fff
    style AR fill:#fb8500,color:#fff
    style CL fill:#8ecae6
    style SP fill:#90be6d
```

| Paradigm | Mechanism | Representative catalog entries |
|---|---|---|
| **Masked reconstruction** | Corrupt gene tokens, train encoder to recover them | Single-cell Masked Autoencoder, ScDiVa, Exceiver |
| **Autoregressive generation** | Predict next gene/expression token sequentially | tGPT, scGPT, scMulan, TranscriptFormer, Stack |
| **Contrastive / relational alignment** | Pull similar cell representations together without token reconstruction | Divide-and-Conquer Contrastive Learning, scConcept, Cell-JEPA, BioM-JEPA |
| **Supervised / task-informed** | Optimize directly for annotation or classification objectives | scBERT (cell type annotation), scPretrain, scCello (ontology-guided) |

Sources: [README.md](README.md#L76-L80)

## The Paper Catalog by Era

The scRNA-seq list spans **2022–2026** and is maintained in reverse-chronological order. Reading it era-by-era reveals the field's trajectory: early transformer language-model transfers, a 2024 scaling wave, and a 2025–2026 frontier exploring efficiency (Mamba/JEPA), world-model framing, and cross-species generalization.

### Foundational Era (2022–2023) — 12 entries

## Catalog Statistics

> [!TIP]
> When evaluating maturity of a model before adoption, the venue column is a useful proxy: journal acceptance at Nature/Cell-family venues generally indicates peer-validated benchmarks, while arXiv/bioRxiv entries mark active research frontiers you can follow before official release.

| Dimension | Distribution |
|---|---|
| **By year** | 2022: 3 · 2023: 9 · 2024: 13 · 2025: 15 · 2026: 16 — **Total: 56** |
| **By venue type** | Peer-reviewed journals: 23 · Preprints (arXiv/bioRxiv): 23 · ML/CS conferences (NeurIPS, ICLR, ICML, RECOMB): 8 · Other: 2 |
| **Publication velocity** | Pre-2024 entries (12) vs. 2025–2026 entries (31) — the field roughly tripled in the last two catalog years |

Sources: [README.md](README.md#L80-L136)

## Developer's Lens: Architectural Signals Worth Tracking

Beyond individual papers, the catalog reveals four recurring architectural themes. If you're choosing a base model for fine-tuning (see [scPEFT](https://www.nature.com/articles/s42256-025-01170-z)) or designing a successor, these clusters represent the current design space.

| Architecture family | Motivation | Catalog exemplars |
|---|---|---|
| **Transformer scaling** | Capacity via parameter/data scale | scFoundation, CellFM (100M cells), scPRINT (50M cells), scLong (billion-param), GeneformerV2 |
| **Efficient sequence models** | Linear-time or long-context attention | xTrimoGene, scHyena, GeneMamba (bidirectional Mamba) |
| **Graph / network-informed encoders** | Inject gene regulatory or PPI structure | MuSe-GNN, Cell-GraphCompass, RegFormer, scNET, BioM-JEPA |
| **Joint-embedding (JEPA-style)** | Predict in latent space, avoid pixel-level reconstruction | Cell-JEPA, BioM-JEPA, scConcept |

A complementary cross-cutting axis is **organism coverage**: SATURN and SATURN-style universal embeddings target cross-species integration, GeneCompass injects cross-species regulatory knowledge, and TranscriptFormer extends the atlas across 1.5 billion years of evolution — evidence that "unimodal" refers to modality, not to a single training distribution.

Sources: [README.md](README.md#L97-L111), [README.md](README.md#L112-L124), [README.md](README.md#L125-L136)

## Suggested Reading Progression

This page covers the transcriptomic-only subset of the unimodal family. Natural next steps follow the catalog's structure:

1. **[Single-Cell ATAC-seq Models](6-single-cell-atac-seq-models)** — the sibling unimodal branch (chromatin accessibility: CLM-Access, Atacformer, ChromFound, EpiFoundation, EpiAgent, GET, ChromBERT).
2. **[Multimodal and Spatial Models](7-multimodal-and-spatial-models)** — models that jointly encode transcriptomics with perturbational, spatial, proteomic, or epigenomic inputs.
3. **[LLM-Based Cell Models](8-llm-based-cell-models)** — approaches leveraging large language models for cell representation.
4. For the conceptual framework unifying all four families, return to **[Taxonomy of Single-Cell Foundation Models](4-taxonomy-of-single-cell-foundation-models)**.

If your goal is applied work — perturbation response prediction, virtual cell simulation, or benchmark selection — proceed to the dedicated sections starting at [Perturbation Prediction Frameworks](9-perturbation-prediction-frameworks) and [Benchmarking Studies and Critiques](17-benchmarking-studies-and-critiques).


# Single-Cell ATAC-seq Models



This page documents the **unimodal scATAC-seq branch** of the OmicsML catalog of single-cell foundation models — a curated reading list that follows the review *"The landscape of single-cell foundation models: design principles, applications, and open challenges"*. Here you will find the seven foundation models pretrained exclusively on single-cell chromatin accessibility data, their publication venues, the design motifs they declare, and clear boundaries separating them from multimodal work that also consumes ATAC-seq.

Sources: [README.md](/README.md#L10-L12), [README.md](/README.md#L138-L145)

## Scope and Taxonomy Position

The repository organizes single-cell foundation models **by the modality they are pretrained on**: unimodal (a single omic), multimodal (jointly modeling transcriptomic, epigenomic, proteomic, and spatial data), and LLM-based. Within the unimodal branch, models "learn representations through masked reconstruction, autoregressive generation, contrastive/relational alignment, or supervised prediction" — this is the training-paradigm vocabulary that applies to both unimodal sub-branches, scRNA-seq and scATAC-seq.

The diagram below situates this page within the catalog's taxonomy, using the entry counts verified in the README:

```mermaid
graph TD
    FM["Single-Cell Foundation Models<br/>grouped by pretraining modality"]
    FM --> UNI["Unimodal scFMs<br/>one omic modality"]
    FM --> MM["Multimodal scFMs<br/>joint multi-omic encoding"]
    FM --> LLM["LLM-based scFMs<br/>text-informed representations"]
    UNI --> RNA["scRNA-seq<br/>56 catalogued models"]
    UNI --> ATAC["scATAC-seq ★<br/>7 catalogued models"]
    style ATAC fill:#e8f5e9,stroke:#2e7d32
```

The repository also ships a canonical visualization of the field's evolution, useful for anchoring the ATAC branch within the broader model landscape:

![Evolutionary tree of single-cell foundation models](https://github.com/OmicsML/awesome-foundation-model-single-cell-papers/blob/main/figs/evo_tree.png?raw=true)

Sources: [README.md](/README.md#L39-L49), [README.md](/README.md#L72-L78), [README.md](/README.md#L22-L24)

## The Seven-Model Catalog

The `scATAC-seq` section lists exactly **seven entries**. Each entry records a publication year, venue, model name, and a direct paper link — the full verifiable surface of the catalog entry format. The table below is a faithful expansion of that section:

| Model | Year | Venue | Declared focus (from title) | Paper |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| **CLM-Access** | 2026 | AAAI | High-dimensional single-cell ATAC-seq analysis | [link](https://ojs.aaai.org/index.php/AAAI/article/view/37046) |
| **Atacformer** | 2025 | bioRxiv | Transformer-based analysis and interpretation of ATAC-seq | [link](https://www.biorxiv.org/content/10.1101/2025.11.03.685753v1) |
| **ChromFound** | 2025 | NeurIPS | Universal foundation model for chromatin accessibility | [link](https://arxiv.org/abs/2505.12638) |
| **EpiFoundation** | 2025 | bioRxiv | Peak-to-gene alignment | [link](https://www.biorxiv.org/content/10.1101/2025.02.05.636688v2) |
| **EpiAgent** | 2025 | Nature Methods | Single-cell epigenomics | [link](https://www.nature.com/articles/s41592-025-02822-z) |
| **GET** | 2025 | Nature | Foundation model of transcription across human cell types | [link](https://www.nature.com/articles/s41586-024-08391-z) |
| **ChromBERT** | 2025 | Cell Genomics | Interpretable representations of transcriptional regulatory networks | [link](https://www.cell.com/cell-genomics/fulltext/S2666-979X(25)00386-6) |

> [!TIP]
> The catalog quantifies a striking **modality asymmetry**: the scRNA-seq sibling section holds 56 entries versus 7 here — roughly an 8:1 ratio. For developers selecting a starting point, this means the unimodal ATAC-seq landscape is a frontier with fewer, more recent options, not a saturated field where exhaustive benchmarking against dozens of predecessors is required.

Sources: [README.md](/README.md#L138-L145), [README.md](/README.md#L81-L136)

## Publication Timeline and Venue Signal

All seven entries fall within a **two-year publication window (2025–2026)**, confirming this is the youngest branch of the unimodal landscape — the scRNA-seq branch, by contrast, stretches back to 2022. The venue distribution splits cleanly into three classes, each carrying a different signal about maturity and review status:

| Venue class | Models | What the signal means |
|---|---|---|
| High-impact journals | GET (*Nature*), EpiAgent (*Nature Methods*), ChromBERT (*Cell Genomics*) | Peer-reviewed validation at top life-science venues |
| ML conferences | ChromFound (NeurIPS), CLM-Access (AAAI) | Method-driven contributions vetted by the ML community |
| Preprints | Atacformer, EpiFoundation (bioRxiv) | Most recent entries, still under community review |

For an intermediate developer planning adoption, this distribution implies: three models have journal-grade evidence trails, two have ML-conference vetting, and the two preprints represent the current technical frontier whose claims are not yet peer-reviewed.

Sources: [README.md](/README.md#L138-L145)

## Design Motifs: What Distinguishes ATAC-seq Pretraining

Because the catalog encodes each model's positioning in its title, the seven entries reveal distinct **design motifs** — each addressing a known challenge of chromatin accessibility data: extreme dimensionality (hundreds of thousands of sparse peaks), the need to connect accessible peaks to target genes, and the goal of interpretable transcriptional regulation. The table below grounds every motif in the exact title text:

| Design motif | Representative model | Catalog title claim |
|---|---|---|
| Accessibility universality | ChromFound | "Towards A Universal Foundation Model for Single-Cell Chromatin Accessibility Data" |
| High-dimensional efficiency | CLM-Access | "specialized foundation model for high-dimensional single-cell ATAC-seq analysis" |
| Peak-to-gene alignment | EpiFoundation | "A Foundation Model for Single-Cell ATAC-seq via Peak-to-Gene Alignment" |
| Epigenomic generality | EpiAgent | "foundation model for single-cell epigenomics" |
| Cross-cell-type transcription | GET | "A foundation model of transcription across human cell types" |
| Interpretable regulatory networks | ChromBERT | "interpretable representations for context-specific transcriptional regulatory networks" |
| Transformer-based analysis | Atacformer | "transformer-based foundation model for analysis and interpretation of ATAC-seq data" |

The concept map below relates these motifs as a pipeline: raw chromatin accessibility profiles are consumed by the four unimodal training paradigms defined in the catalog, producing embeddings that different models push toward either regulatory interpretation or cell-level analysis:

```mermaid
graph LR
    A["Single-cell chromatin<br/>accessibility profiles"] --> B["Unimodal training paradigms:<br/>masked reconstruction ·<br/>autoregressive generation ·<br/>contrastive/relational alignment ·<br/>supervised prediction"]
    B --> C["Cell and peak<br/>embeddings"]
    C --> D["Peak-to-gene alignment<br/>EpiFoundation"]
    C --> E["Regulatory network<br/>interpretation<br/>GET · ChromBERT"]
    C --> F["Cell-level analysis<br/>CLM-Access · Atacformer ·<br/>ChromFound · EpiAgent"]
```

> [!TIP]
> **Peak-to-gene alignment** is the only explicitly named biological prior across all seven titles. When evaluating EpiFoundation against accessibility-only approaches, this is the architectural differentiator to scrutinize: it directly links open chromatin regions to putative target genes, bridging the epigenomic input modality toward transcriptomic semantics.

Sources: [README.md](/README.md#L138-L145), [README.md](/README.md#L76-L78)

## Boundary: Where Multimodal ATAC Work Lives

Several cataloged models combine ATAC-seq with other omics — for example **SCARF** ("Single Cell ATAC-seq and RNA-seq Foundation model") and **CLM-X** (a "flexible multi-way Transformer for unified scRNA-seq and scATAC-seq analysis"). These are deliberately **excluded from this page**: the catalog files them under the *Multi-omics: RNA, ATAC and Protein* subsection of the multimodal branch, and they are covered in depth on the multimodal page. Keeping this boundary sharp prevents misclassification when you cite or benchmark against this catalog.

Sources: [README.md](/README.md#L191-L201)

## Suggested Reading Progression

To build complete context around this branch, follow the catalog's own structure:

1. **[Taxonomy of Single-Cell Foundation Models](4-taxonomy-of-single-cell-foundation-models)** — the modality-based grouping logic that defines what "unimodal" means here.
2. **[Unimodal scRNA-seq Models](5-unimodal-scrna-seq-models)** — the sibling branch; its 56 entries are the maturity benchmark against which the seven ATAC models should be read.
3. **[Multimodal and Spatial Models](7-multimodal-and-spatial-models)** — the mandatory next stop for RNA+ATAC joint models such as SCARF and CLM-X.
4. **[Evolutionary Tree of Models](3-evolutionary-tree-of-models)** — the visual companion to the taxonomy if you prefer a top-down view first.


# Multimodal and Spatial Models



This page documents the **multimodal branch** of the single-cell foundation model landscape: models that jointly encode complementary modalities — transcriptomic, epigenomic, proteomic, perturbational and spatial — through modality-specific reconstruction, cross-modality alignment, or task-informed supervision. The catalog currently curates **46 entries** in this family, organized into three sub-families: *Transcriptomics and Perturbation* (7), *Spatial, Proteomics and Histology* (29), and *Multi-omics: RNA, ATAC and Protein* (10). Because the source repository is a curated reading list rather than a codebase, this page treats the catalog itself as the architecture under analysis — reconstructing the design space, the integration patterns, and the boundaries that separate this family from its neighbors.

Sources: [README.md](README.md#L147-L150)

## Position in the Model Taxonomy

Before reading the diagram below, note two prerequisites: the catalog's top-level grouping criterion is the **set of modalities a model is pretrained on** — unimodal (a single omic), multimodal (jointly modeling transcriptomic, epigenomic, proteomic, and spatial signals), and LLM-based (models incorporating text or language-model priors). Within the multimodal branch, the catalog applies a second axis: the *specific modality pairing* being coupled. The diagram makes both axes explicit.

```mermaid
graph TB
    subgraph TAX["scFMs — grouped by pretraining modality"]
        UNI["Unimodal scFMs<br/>(scRNA-seq · scATAC-seq)"]
        MULTI["Multimodal scFMs<br/>◀ this page"]
        LLM["LLM-based scFMs"]
    end

    subgraph FAM["Multimodal sub-families (by modality pairing)"]
        TP["Transcriptomics + Perturbation<br/>7 entries"]
        SPH["Spatial + Proteomics + Histology<br/>29 entries"]
        MO["Multi-omics: RNA + ATAC + Protein<br/>10 entries"]
    end

    subgraph STRAT["Integration strategies (orthogonal axis)"]
        REC["Modality-specific<br/>reconstruction"]
        ALN["Cross-modality<br/>alignment"]
        SUP["Task-informed<br/>supervision"]
    end

    UNI --- MULTI
    MULTI --- LLM
    MULTI ==> TP
    MULTI ==> SPH
    MULTI ==> MO
    STRAT -. applies to all three sub-families .-> FAM
```

The three integration strategies — reconstruction, alignment, and task-informed supervision — are declared by the catalog as applying across the whole multimodal family rather than being owned by any single sub-family. You can verify this from titles alone: alignment appears in spatial models (`ST-Align`, `OmiCLIP`, `scCLIP`), reconstruction in multi-omics (`CellWorld`, `HoloCell`), and task-informed supervision in perturbation coupling (`STATE`, `PertFormer`).

| Sub-family | Entries | Modality coupling | Defining signal in titles |
|---|---|---|---|
| Transcriptomics + Perturbation | 7 | Expression ↔ genetic/compound perturbation | "predicting perturbation responses", "conditional transport" |
| Spatial + Proteomics + Histology | 29 | Expression ↔ tissue coordinates ↔ image ↔ protein | "spatial transcriptomics", "from histology", "spatial proteomics" |
| Multi-omics: RNA + ATAC + Protein | 10 | Transcriptome ↔ chromatin ↔ proteome | "unified scRNA-seq and scATAC-seq", "translating transcriptomes to proteomes" |

Sources: [README.md](README.md#L72-L74), [README.md](README.md#L147-L150), [README.md](README.md#L151-L201)

## Sub-family I: Transcriptomics and Perturbation

This is the smallest sub-family (7 entries) and the one with the most deliberate catalog placement. The perturbation section header explicitly notes: *"Perturbation-trained scFMs such as X-Cell, SCALE, PerturbGen, STATE, GeneJepa and Tahoe-x1 are listed under Multimodal scFMs"* — meaning these models are treated as **transcriptome–perturbation multimodal models first**, and only their downstream prediction frameworks belong to the dedicated perturbation section. For an advanced reader, this placement encodes a real architectural claim: these systems bake perturbation response into pretraining, rather than layering prediction on top of a frozen expression model.

> [!TIP]
> When searching this repository for STATE, Tahoe-x1, or SCALE, look here — not in the Genetic Perturbation section. The catalog's own cross-listing note (README.md#L239) is the authoritative placement rule.

| Model | Venue / Year | Coupling signal (from title) |
|---|---|---|
| [scDEBART](https://openreview.net/forum?id=pJyidZg93y) | 2026 ICML | In silico perturbation responses via large-scale differential expression learning |
| [X-Cell](https://www.biorxiv.org/content/10.64898/2026.03.18.712807v1) | 2026 bioRxiv | Causal perturbation prediction across cellular contexts via diffusion language models |
| [SCALE](https://arxiv.org/abs/2603.17380) | 2026 arXiv | Conditional atlas-level endpoint transport for virtual cell perturbation prediction |
| [PerturbGen](https://www.biorxiv.org/content/10.64898/2026.03.04.709254v1) | 2026 bioRxiv | Predicting how perturbations reshape cellular trajectories |
| [STATE](https://www.cell.com/cell/fulltext/S0092-8674(26)00921-9) | 2026 Cell | Cellular responses to perturbation across diverse contexts |
| [GeneJepa](https://www.biorxiv.org/content/10.1101/2025.10.14.682378v1) | 2025 bioRxiv | Predictive world model of the transcriptome |
| [Tahoe-x1](https://www.biorxiv.org/content/10.1101/2025.10.23.683759v1) | 2025 bioRxiv | Perturbation-trained scFM scaled to 3B parameters |

Note the methodological spread visible in the titles alone: diffusion-based generation (X-Cell), optimal-transport-style endpoint modeling (SCALE), trajectory prediction (PerturbGen), and joint-embedding predictive architectures (GeneJepa). Tahoe-x1's title also signals the scale dimension — it is the perturbation counterpart to the parameter-scaling race documented in the unimodal branch.

Sources: [README.md](README.md#L151-L158), [README.md](README.md#L237-L239)

## Sub-family II: Spatial, Proteomics, and Histology

The largest sub-family (29 entries) spans a verifiable **scale axis** that its own titles make explicit: from *subcellular molecular* to *multicellular landscapes* ([SpatialFormer](https://www.nature.com/articles/s43588-026-01016-7)), *single-cell resolved* brain atlases ([BrainBeacon](https://www.biorxiv.org/content/10.1101/2025.07.08.663729v1)), *across scales* spatial proteomics ([VirTues](https://www.nature.com/articles/s41586-026-10884-y)), and *multi-scale* tissue modeling ([SToFM](https://arxiv.org/abs/2507.11588), [TERRA](https://www.biorxiv.org/content/10.64898/2026.07.29.741565v1)). Analytically, the entries cluster into five distinguishable engineering patterns, each verifiable from title semantics: **native spatial pretraining**, **graph/topology-based modeling**, **vision–omics translation** (inferring molecular profiles from histology), **spatial proteomics**, and **spatial multimodal generation**.

The vision–omics translation pattern deserves its own module-level view, since it dominates recent entries. The prerequisite for reading the diagram: these systems pair an image encoder (histology/H&E) with an omics encoder (spatial expression), couple them in a joint latent space, then either retrieve or decode *virtual* molecular measurements at locations where only the image exists.

```mermaid
graph LR
    subgraph INPUT["Observed inputs"]
        IMG["Histology / H&E image"]
        ST["Measured spatial<br/>transcriptomics"]
    end
    subgraph CORE["Joint encoding"]
        IE["Image encoder"] --> LAT["Shared latent<br/>alignment space"]
        OE["Omics encoder"] --> LAT
    end
    LAT -->|"retrieval-based prediction"| OUT1["In-situ expression<br/>(VOICE)"]
    LAT -->|"generative decoding"| OUT2["Virtual spatial transcriptomics<br/>(DeepSpot-M, STPath)"]
    LAT -->|"virtual proteomics"| OUT3["Biomarker discovery<br/>(HEX, VirTues)"]
```

The following tables decompose all 29 entries by pattern. Placement follows the catalog exactly; pattern labels are derived strictly from title text.

**Native spatial transcriptomics pretraining** — models pretrained on spatially resolved expression as a first-class signal:

| Model | Venue / Year | Scope signal (from title) |
|---|---|---|
| [SpatialFormer](https://www.nature.com/articles/s43588-026-01016-7) | 2026 Nat. Comput. Sci | Subcellular molecular → multicellular landscapes |
| [CellWorld](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.06659) | 2026 arXiv | Gene-level reconstruction → latent cell prediction |
| [TERRA](https://www.biorxiv.org/content/10.64898/2026.07.29.741565v1) | 2026 bioRxiv | Multi-scale human tissue modeling |
| [xVERSE](https://www.biorxiv.org/content/10.64898/2026.04.12.718016v1) | 2026 bioRxiv | Transcriptomics-native universal cell representation, virtual cell synthesis |
| [STORM](https://arxiv.org/abs/2604.03630) | 2026 arXiv | Spatial transcriptomics + histology for discovery and clinical prediction |
| [OmniCell](https://www.biorxiv.org/content/10.64898/2025.12.29.696804v1) | 2025 bioRxiv | Unified single-cell and spatial transcriptomics |
| [scGPT-spatial](https://www.biorxiv.org/content/10.1101/2025.02.05.636714v1) | 2025 bioRxiv | Continual pretraining of a unimodal scFM for spatial data |
| [SToFM](https://arxiv.org/abs/2507.11588) | 2025 ICML | Multi-scale spatial transcriptomics |
| [Nicheformer](https://www.nature.com/articles/s41592-025-02814-z) | 2025 Nat. Methods | Single-cell and spatial omics |
| [AIDO.Tissue](https://www.biorxiv.org/content/10.1101/2025.07.04.663102v1) | 2025 bioRxiv | Spatial cell-guided pretraining |
| [stFormer](https://www.biorxiv.org/content/10.1101/2024.09.27.615337v7) | 2024 bioRxiv | Foundation model for spatial transcriptomics |
| [BrainBeacon](https://www.biorxiv.org/content/10.1101/2025.07.08.663729v1) | 2025 bioRxiv | Cross-species, single-cell resolved brain spatial transcriptomics |

Two entries in this group encode an architectural transition worth noting: `scGPT-spatial` demonstrates **continual pretraining** (extending an existing unimodal checkpoint into the spatial domain), while `OmniCell` demonstrates **unified pretraining** (single-cell and spatial jointly from the start).

Sources: [README.md](README.md#L160-L189)
