## The Inventory: 24 Frameworks Across Six Years

The list is curated **newest-first**, which makes the velocity of the field immediately legible: 11 entries are dated 2026, 8 from 2025, 3 from 2024, and single entries anchor 2023 (CINEMA-OT) and 2019 (scGen). Nearly half of the collection is less than a year old — perturbation prediction is currently the fastest-moving sub-area in the catalog.

| Year | Count | Entries |
|---|---|---|
| 2026 | 11 | CellRFT, PopPert, MultiFlow, Unbalanced Perturbation Dynamics, Response Decomposition, scDFM, PRiMeFlow, AetherCell, MAP, PerturbDiff, Squidiff |
| 2025 | 8 | Closing the Loop, Predicting the Unseen (PNAS), Unified Multimodal Learning, SpatialProp, PertAdapt, In Silico Biological Discovery, Scouter, Distributional Shifts |
| 2024 | 3 | scLAMBDA, scGenePT, GEARS |
| 2023 | 1 | CINEMA-OT |
| 2019 | 1 | scGen |

The venue profile also shifts across the timeline: the early entries are landmark journal methods papers (Nature Methods for scGen and CINEMA-OT, Nature Biotechnology for GEARS), while the 2026 cohort mixes top-tier ML venues (scDFM at ICLR) with high-impact journal publications (Squidiff in Nature Methods) and preprints — a sign that ML-conference and genomics-journal publication tracks have both absorbed the task.

Sources: [README.md](README.md#L241-L265)

The following lineage diagram synthesizes the collection's chronology and method families into a single architectural view. Each era inherits the data representations of the previous one while changing the *output contract*: from point estimates of mean response, to structure-aware combinatorial generalization, to full response distributions, to perturbation-native fine-tuning of pretrained foundation models.

```mermaid
flowchart TD
    subgraph E1["Era 1 · Point Estimates · 2019–2023"]
        scGen["scGen (2019, Nature Methods)<br>founding task definition"]
        COT["CINEMA-OT (2023, Nature Methods)<br>causal effect identification"]
    end
    subgraph E2["Era 2 · Structure + Knowledge · 2024"]
        GEARS["GEARS (Nature Biotechnology)<br>novel multigene perturbations"]
        scLAMBDA["scLAMBDA<br>multi-gene responses"]
        scGenePT["scGenePT<br>language-prior modeling"]
    end
    subgraph E3["Era 3 · Generative Distributional Turn · 2025–2026"]
        Debias["Diffusion debiasing (PNAS 2025)<br>single-cell resolution"]
        Squidiff["Squidiff (Nature Methods)<br>development + perturbation"]
        PerturbDiff["PerturbDiff<br>functional diffusion"]
        Flow["scDFM (ICLR) · PRiMeFlow<br>MultiFlow · Unbalanced Dynamics"]
    end
    subgraph E4["Era 4 · scFM-Native · 2025–2026"]
        Closing["Closing the Loop<br>scFMs learn from perturbations"]
        PertAdapt["PertAdapt<br>condition-sensitive adaptation"]
        CellRFT["CellRFT<br>reinforcement fine-tuning"]
        PopPert["PopPert<br>population joint distribution"]
    end
    scGen --> GEARS
    GEARS --> Squidiff
    scGenePT --> Flow
    Debias --> PerturbDiff
    PertAdapt --> CellRFT
    Squidiff --> PopPert
```

Sources: [README.md](README.md#L241-L265)

## Methodological Families

Reading the 24 titles as a system, six methodological families emerge. Each family solves a different failure mode of the previous generation, which is the fastest way to decide which entry to study for a given engineering problem.

### Family 1: Distributional Generative Modeling

The dominant 2025–2026 family. Instead of regressing a single post-perturbation expression vector, these frameworks sample from — or transport between — response *distributions*. Two concrete mechanisms appear in the titles: **diffusion** (Squidiff, PerturbDiff, and the PNAS debiasing framework) and **flow matching** (scDFM, PRiMeFlow, MultiFlow, Unbalanced Perturbation Dynamics).

| Mechanism | Frameworks | Distinguishing signal in title |
|---|---|---|
| Diffusion | Squidiff, PerturbDiff, Predicting the Unseen | "diffusion model", "functional diffusion", "diffusion-based debiasing" |
| Flow matching | scDFM, PRiMeFlow, MultiFlow, Unbalanced Perturbation Dynamics | "distributional flow matching", "heterogeneity", "coupled flow matching", "unbalanced dynamics" |
| Dual-task | Squidiff | "predicting cellular development **and** responses to perturbations" |

Scouter (2025, Nature Computational Science) bridges this family and the knowledge-injection family below: it predicts transcriptional responses using large-language-model embeddings within a framework published alongside the generative turn.

> [!TIP]
> The shift to distributional outputs is not cosmetic — it directly explains the benchmark controversy documented in the sibling section, where entries argue that deep perturbation models "do not yet outperform simple linear baselines" under mean-based metrics, while rebuttal papers attribute the gap to poorly calibrated metrics and mode collapse. When evaluating any framework in this family, the metric contract (distributional vs. point-estimate) must match the model's output contract.

Sources: [README.md](README.md#L244-L248), [README.md](README.md#L251-L254), [README.md](README.md#L259), [README.md](README.md#L275-L290)

### Family 2: Foundation-Model Adaptation

The second strategic response to the pretrained-model era: rather than training perturbation predictors from scratch, these frameworks **reuse pretrained scFMs** and add perturbation-conditioned capabilities. The titles trace a clear escalation: PertAdapt introduces *condition-sensitive adaptation* to unlock existing scFMs for genetic perturbation prediction; Closing the Loop teaches scFMs "to learn from perturbations"; and CellRFT applies *reinforcement fine-tuning* — the most aggressive adaptation mechanism in the collection.

| Escalation stage | Framework | Adaptation mechanism (per title) |
|---|---|---|
| Conditioning | PertAdapt | "Condition-Sensitive Adaptation" |
| Curriculum | Closing the Loop | "Teaching single-cell foundation models to learn from perturbations" |
| Optimization | CellRFT | "Reinforcement Fine-Tuning" |

Sources: [README.md](README.md#L242), [README.md](README.md#L253), [README.md](README.md#L257)

### Family 3: Knowledge and Language Injection

A third integration strategy: keep the predictive model separate and inject external biological knowledge. Scouter uses large-language-model embeddings; scGenePT asks — in its title — "Is language all you need for modeling single-cell perturbations?"; MAP is a *knowledge-driven* framework explicitly targeting responses to **unprofiled drugs**, i.e., compounds with no measured transcriptomic response data.

> [!TIP]
> Families 2 and 3 represent the two competing architectures for the same problem: **internalize perturbations** into a pretrained backbone (adaptation) versus **externalize knowledge** into the input representation (injection). The 2026 cohort shows convergence — CellRFT's reinforcement fine-tuning operates on foundation-model representations that already absorb knowledge, suggesting the distinction is collapsing into a fine-tuning-vs-retrieval engineering choice rather than an architectural fork.

Sources: [README.md](README.md#L250), [README.md](README.md#L259), [README.md](README.md#L262)

### Family 4: Population-Level and Decomposition Approaches

Where the generative family models within-cell response distributions, this family models **between-cell and between-population structure**. PopPert performs population-level joint-distribution modeling; the response-decomposition framework achieves "biologically aligned generalization to unseen perturbations and cellular contexts" by decomposing responses; and the distributional-shifts entry targets unseen genetic perturbations through explicit shift modeling. All three treat generalization as a factorization problem: separate what the perturbation does from who the cell population is.

Sources: [README.md](README.md#L243), [README.md](README.md#L246), [README.md](README.md#L260)

### Family 5: The Classical Lineage

The founding entries define the task and its hardest sub-problems. **scGen** (2019, Nature Methods) established single-cell perturbation response prediction as a learning problem; **CINEMA-OT** (2023, Nature Methods) contributes causal identification of experimental perturbation effects — attribution rather than forecasting; **GEARS** (2024, Nature Biotechnology) attacks *novel multigene* perturbations, the combinatorial generalization problem; and scLAMBDA extends modeling to multi-gene perturbation responses. These remain the canonical baselines referenced implicitly by the benchmark section's baseline-comparison debates.

Sources: [README.md](README.md#L261-L265)

### Family 6: Context, Modality, and Application Expansion

The final family extends the prediction surface itself. **SpatialProp** moves perturbation modeling into tissue context using spatially resolved single-cell transcriptomics; the unified-multimodal-learning entry generalizes response prediction across *diverse perturbation modalities*; **AetherCell** packages prediction into a generative engine for virtual-cell perturbation and in-vivo drug discovery — the collection's most application-facing entry. A perspective entry, *In silico biological discovery with large perturbation models* (2025, Nature Computational Science), frames the family's trajectory from prediction toward discovery workflows.

Sources: [README.md](README.md#L249), [README.md](README.md#L255-L256), [README.md](README.md#L252), [README.md](README.md#L258)

## The Generalization Axis Map

The most decision-relevant way to compare these frameworks is the axis along which each one generalizes. Every title in the collection encodes at least one — this table makes the mapping explicit so you can shortlist by evaluation scenario rather than by chronology.

| Generalization axis | Frameworks encoding it | Line refs |
|---|---|---|
| Unseen perturbations | Response Decomposition, Distributional Shifts, GEARS (novel multigene), Scouter | L246, L260, L263, L259 |
| Unseen cellular contexts | MultiFlow, PopPert, Response Decomposition | L244, L243, L246 |
| Population heterogeneity | PopPert, PRiMeFlow ("expression heterogeneity") | L243, L248 |
| Multi-gene combinations | GEARS, scLAMBDA | L263, L261 |
| Spatial / tissue context | SpatialProp | L256 |
| Multiomic responses | MultiFlow, Unified Multimodal Learning | L244, L255 |
| Trajectory and cell fate | Squidiff (development), Unbalanced Perturbation Dynamics (cell fate design) | L252, L245 |
| Unprofiled drugs | MAP | L250 |
| Debiasing / metric robustness | Predicting the Unseen (PNAS) | L254 |

Sources: [README.md](README.md#L241-L265)

## Where to Go Next

The logical progression through the catalog mirrors the development lifecycle of a perturbation-prediction system. First, understand the **pretrained backbones** these frameworks adapt or consume: [Unimodal scRNA-seq Models](5-unimodal-scrna-seq-models) for the representation-learning foundations, and [Multimodal and Spatial Models](7-multimodal-and-spatial-models) for the perturbation-trained scFMs that this page explicitly excludes. Second, study the **data substrate**: [Perturbation Atlases and Datasets](10-perturbation-atlases-and-datasets) covers Tahoe-100M, X-Atlas/Orion, PerturBase, and the original Perturb-seq protocol that generates all training signal for this page's frameworks. Third, learn **how these frameworks are judged**: [Perturbation Benchmarks](11-perturbation-benchmarks) contains the metric-calibration debates and linear-baseline critiques that directly constrain which framework claims you should trust.

For the forward-looking extension of this topic — where perturbation prediction becomes simulation inside a cellular world model — continue to [Virtual Cell Perspectives and Roadmaps](12-virtual-cell-perspectives-and-roadmaps) and [Cell World Model Implementations](13-cell-world-model-implementations), where perturbation-capable simulators such as AlphaCell, Chreode, and OCCO-T are cataloged. Finally, the engineering tooling counterpart to this page — Pertpy, the end-to-end perturbation *analysis* framework — lives in [Analysis Frameworks and Data Formats](16-analysis-frameworks-and-data-formats), which complements this page's *modeling* focus with practical analysis infrastructure.


# Perturbation Atlases and Datasets



This page documents the **Perturbation atlases and datasets** section of the Awesome Foundation Models for Single-Cell repository — a curated list of six foundational resources that supply the raw experimental data powering the field of single-cell perturbation modeling. While sibling pages catalog the *models* that predict perturbation responses and the *benchmarks* that score them, this page covers the substrate itself: the large-scale Perturb-seq screens, aggregation databases, and domain-specific perturbation dictionaries that make computational perturbation biology possible. For an intermediate developer, this is the "where does the data come from?" layer of the stack.

Sources: [README.md](README.md#L267-L273), [README.md](README.md#L237-L239)

## Position in the Perturbation Knowledge Stack

The repository organizes all perturbation content under a single parent section — "Genetic Perturbation: Models, Atlases and Benchmarks" — which decomposes into a clean three-layer architecture: **data** (atlases), **computation** (prediction frameworks), and **evaluation** (benchmarks). The curated note at the top of that section adds an important fourth actor: perturbation-*trained* foundation models (X-Cell, SCALE, PerturbGen, STATE, GeneJepa, Tahoe-x1) are deliberately routed to the Multimodal scFMs section rather than listed as standalone prediction frameworks. The atlases layer is therefore the dependency root: prediction frameworks consume these datasets for training, and benchmarks slice them into held-out evaluation splits. Understanding this data-first topology clarifies why a data-entry page sits at the center of the perturbation triad.

```mermaid
flowchart LR
    subgraph ATLASES["Atlases &amp; Datasets — this page"]
        A1["Giga-scale screens<br/>Tahoe-100M · X-Atlas/Orion"]
        A2["Aggregation database<br/>PerturBase"]
        A3["Technology pillars<br/>Perturb-seq 2016 · Perturb-multiome"]
        A4["Domain resource<br/>Cytokine dictionary"]
    end
    subgraph MODELS["Prediction Frameworks"]
        M["Models trained / fine-tuned<br/>on perturbation data"]
    end
    subgraph BENCH["Benchmarks"]
        B["Held-out evaluation<br/>splits &amp; metrics"]
    end
    ATLASES -->|"training corpora"| MODELS
    MODELS -->|"scored by"| BENCH
    ATLASES -->|"ground truth"| BENCH
```

Sources: [README.md](README.md#L237-L239), [README.md](README.md#L151-L158)

## The Curated Atlas Catalog

The section contains exactly six entries, spanning a decade of methodological evolution — from the 2016 paper that invented pooled single-cell genetic screening to the 2025 giga-scale atlases that industrialized it. The table below preserves the repository's original metadata (year, venue, and linked title) and adds a functional classification to help you navigate by intent rather than by reading order:

| # | Resource | Year / Venue | Functional Role | Scope |
|---|----------|--------------|-----------------|-------|
| 1 | Tahoe-100M | 2025, bioRxiv | Giga-scale perturbation atlas | Context-dependent gene function and cellular modeling at drug-perturbation scale |
| 2 | X-Atlas/Orion | 2025, bioRxiv | Genome-wide screen dataset | Perturb-seq at genome scale via a scalable fix-cryopreserve platform |
| 3 | PerturBase | 2025, Nucleic Acids Research | Aggregation database | Comprehensive database for single-cell perturbation data analysis and visualization |
| 4 | Perturb-multiome | 2025, Science | Multiomic perturbation study | Transcription factor networks and heritability of blood cell phenotypes |
| 5 | Cytokine dictionary | 2025, bioRxiv | Domain-specific atlas | Single-cell cytokine perturbation map of human peripheral blood |
| 6 | Perturb-seq | 2016, Cell | Founding method paper | Dissecting molecular circuits with pooled genetic screens + scRNA profiling |

Note the deliberate span of perturbation *modalities*: although the parent section is titled "Genetic Perturbation," the atlas entries cover drug-induced responses (Tahoe-100M), CRISPR-based genetic screens (X-Atlas, Perturb-seq), and cytokine stimulation (the peripheral blood dictionary). The curation treats "perturbation atlas" broadly — any systematically perturbed single-cell dataset qualifies.

Sources: [README.md](README.md#L267-L273), [README.md](README.md#L237-L239)

## Anatomy of the Atlas Landscape

The six entries cluster into four archetypes that map directly onto how a developer would actually interact with them. **Scale-first atlases** (Tahoe-100M, X-Atlas/Orion) are primary data products: massive, purpose-built screens intended to serve as pretraining corpora and in-silico screening grounds. **Aggregation infrastructure** (PerturBase) is a meta-resource — it harmonizes scattered perturbation experiments into a queryable database with analysis and visualization built in, useful when you need heterogeneous datasets rather than one homogeneous mega-screen. **Technology pillars** (Perturb-seq 2016, Perturb-multiome 2025) anchor the experimental methodology: the former defines the pooled-screen-plus-scRNA-seq protocol, the latter extends it to multiome readouts linking transcription factors to phenotypic heritability. **Domain resources** (the cytokine dictionary) demonstrate that perturbation atlases generalize beyond CRISPR to signaling-molecule space. Each row in the catalog table above corresponds to one of these archetypes, letting you select a resource by data-acquisition strategy.

```mermaid
flowchart TD
    A["Perturbation Atlas Landscape"] --> B["Scale-first Atlases"]
    A --> C["Aggregation Infrastructure"]
    A --> D["Technology Pillars"]
    A --> E["Domain Resources"]
    B --> B1["Tahoe-100M<br/>drug perturbations"]
    B --> B2["X-Atlas/Orion<br/>genome-wide CRISPR"]
    C --> C1["PerturBase<br/>harmonized database"]
    D --> D1["Perturb-seq 2016<br/>founding protocol"]
    D --> D2["Perturb-multiome<br/>multiomic extension"]
    E --> E1["Cytokine dictionary<br/>peripheral blood"]
```

Sources: [README.md](README.md#L267-L273)

> [!TIP]
> Watch the naming collision: **Tahoe-100M** (the dataset, listed here at line 268) and **Tahoe-x1** (the 3-billion-parameter foundation model trained on perturbation data, listed at line 158 under Multimodal scFMs) are distinct entries in a deliberate data/model split. If you are tracing the lineage of perturbation-trained foundation models, you must cross two catalog sections — the corpus lives on this page, the architecture on [Multimodal and Spatial Models](7-multimodal-and-spatial-models).

The 2016 Perturb-seq entry is not a historical curiosity — it is the methodological keystone that makes every other entry legible. Its protocol (pooled CRISPR perturbations combined with single-cell RNA profiling of each cell's guide identity) is precisely the experimental template that X-Atlas/Orion scales genome-wide, that Perturb-multiome extends with ATAC readouts, and that Tahoe-100M industrializes at drug-screen scale. Reading the founding paper first converts the modern giga-scale entries from opaque benchmarks into comprehensible engineering refinements of a single idea.

Sources: [README.md](README.md#L273), [README.md](README.md#L269-L271)

## Scope Boundaries and Adjacent Pages

Because the perturbation content in this repository is dense and heavily cross-referenced, precise boundary discipline matters when navigating. The table below maps what explicitly belongs to this page versus what the curators route elsewhere — use it to avoid searching the wrong section:

| Content Type | Belongs To | Catalog Destination |
|--------------|-----------|---------------------|
| Giga-scale screens, aggregation DBs, method papers (this page's six entries) | **This page** | — |
| Response-prediction models (GEARS, scGen, diffusion/flow frameworks) | Models and prediction frameworks | [Perturbation Prediction Frameworks](9-perturbation-prediction-frameworks) |
| Foundation models pretrained *on* perturbation data (Tahoe-x1, STATE, GeneJepa) | Multimodal scFMs | [Multimodal and Spatial Models](7-multimodal-and-spatial-models) |
| Evaluation studies, metric critiques, model comparisons | Perturbation benchmarks | [Perturbation Benchmarks](11-perturbation-benchmarks) |
| Perturbation *analysis tooling* (e.g., Pertpy) | Data formats and frameworks | [Analysis Frameworks and Data Formats](16-analysis-frameworks-and-data-formats) |
| Non-perturbative cell atlases (Tabula Sapiens, CELLxGENE) | Transcriptomic atlases | [Transcriptomic Atlases and Repositories](14-transcriptomic-atlases-and-repositories) |

The first row of that boundary table encodes the repository's single most consequential curation decision, stated verbatim in the parent section's intro: perturbation-trained scFMs are *not* prediction frameworks and live under Multimodal scFMs. Similarly, active-discovery workflows that *generate* new perturbation data in a closed loop (e.g., active hit discovery) are cataloged separately under the lab-in-the-loop section, downstream of the agents content.

Sources: [README.md](README.md#L237-L239), [README.md](README.md#L361), [README.md](README.md#L474-L476)

> [!TIP]
> The repository's internal anchors follow a strict convention: the parent section note (line 239) uses a Markdown anchor link to route perturbation-trained scFMs to the Multimodal scFMs section. When navigating the raw README, the fastest disambiguation rule is: *if the entry's contribution is data → this section; if the contribution is architecture → Multimodal scFMs; if the contribution is a scoring protocol → benchmarks.*

## Suggested Reading Path

For a developer building intuition about perturbation modeling infrastructure, the catalog structure suggests a three-step progression through the Deep Dive perturbation block. Begin with the **methodology layer**: read the 2016 Perturb-seq entry on this page to internalize the experimental protocol, then survey the scale-first atlases (Tahoe-100M, X-Atlas/Orion) to see how that protocol industrializes. Proceed to **[Perturbation Prediction Frameworks](9-perturbation-prediction-frameworks)** to understand the computational models that consume these corpora — the models section and this atlas section were curated as explicit data/consumer counterparts. Conclude with **[Perturbation Benchmarks](11-perturbation-benchmarks)**, where the critical-evaluation literature (including "one PCA still rules them all" and linear-baseline critiques) contextualizes what these datasets can and cannot prove about model quality.

From this page you can also branch laterally: if your interest is in perturbation-trained foundation model *architectures* rather than data, go directly to **[Multimodal and Spatial Models](7-multimodal-and-spatial-models)**; if you need the tooling to process these atlases, **[Analysis Frameworks and Data Formats](16-analysis-frameworks-and-data-formats)** catalogs the Pertpy end-to-end analysis framework; and for the broader virtual-cell systems built on top of this data layer, continue to **[Virtual Cell Perspectives and Roadmaps](12-virtual-cell-perspectives-and-roadmaps)** and **[Cell World Model Implementations](13-cell-world-model-implementations)**.


# Perturbation Benchmarks



This page documents the `### Perturbation benchmarks` section of the repository's README — a curated collection of **15 papers** that benchmark, stress-test, and critically evaluate computational models for single-cell perturbation response prediction. Unlike the neighboring pages that catalog *prediction frameworks* or *data atlases*, this section captures the field's evaluation methodology itself: benchmark suites, metric-design critiques, and head-to-head comparisons that determine whether deep perturbation models actually deliver on their promise.

Sources: [README.md](README.md#L275-L290)

## Position in the Repository's Perturbation Triad

Within the README's information architecture, this section is the **terminal node** of a three-part decomposition under the parent heading `Genetic Perturbation: Models, Atlases and Benchmarks` ([README.md](README.md#L237-L239)). The parent intro establishes an important scoping rule: perturbation-*trained* single-cell foundation models (X-Cell, SCALE, PerturbGen, STATE, GeneJepa, Tahoe-x1) are deliberately excluded from this triad and listed under Multimodal scFMs instead — meaning everything below this section header is exclusively about models that *predict* perturbations, data that *record* perturbations, or evaluations that *judge* perturbation predictors.

The three subsections form a pipeline: data resources feed prediction frameworks, and benchmarks close the loop by judging both. The prerequisite for reading the diagram below: solid-edge arrows represent data/model flow; the dashed edge represents the metric-design feedback loop that benchmarks exert on framework developers.

```mermaid
flowchart LR
    subgraph ATL["Perturbation Atlases (L267)"]
        A1["Perturb-seq · Tahoe-100M<br/>X-Atlas/Orion · PerturBase"]
    end
    subgraph FRM["Prediction Frameworks (L241)"]
        M1["scGen · GEARS · CINEMA-OT<br/>Diffusion & flow-matching models"]
    end
    subgraph BEN["Perturbation Benchmarks (L275) — this page"]
        E1["Benchmark suites<br/>PerturBench · PertEval-scFM · scArchon"]
        E2["Metric & baseline critiques<br/>Linear baselines · calibrated metrics"]
    end
    A1 -->|"training/eval data"| FRM
    FRM -->|"predictions"| E1
    E1 --> E2
    E2 -.->|"metric design feedback"| FRM
```

This pipeline framing matters for advanced readers because the benchmark entries repeatedly interrogate the *generalization contract* of the frameworks upstream — several section titles explicitly target "unseen perturbations" and "generalizable" prediction, which is precisely the claim that separates perturbation foundation models from classical curve-fitting approaches.

Sources: [README.md](README.md#L237-L274), [README.md](README.md#L50-L53)

## The Benchmark Corpus: Fifteen Curated Entries

The section is a flat, numbered list ordered reverse-chronologically (newest first), from a 2026 bioRxiv preprint down to a 2024 arXiv paper. The table below is the complete, verbatim catalog with venue and a conservative functional descriptor derived strictly from each title.

| # | Year | Venue | Entry | Focus (per title) |
|---|------|-------|-------|-------------------|
| 1 | 2026 | bioRxiv | Towards Principled Evaluation of Single-Cell Perturbation Prediction Models | Evaluation principles |
| 2 | 2026 | Genome Biology | scArchon: a scalable benchmarking framework for assessing single-cell perturbation models | Benchmark framework |
| 3 | 2026 | bioRxiv | Foundation Models Improve Perturbation Response Prediction | FM assessment |
| 4 | 2026 | bioRxiv | Evaluating Single-Cell Perturbation Response Models Is Far from Straightforward | Evaluation critique |
| 5 | 2025 | Nature Methods | Benchmarking algorithms for generalizable single-cell perturbation response prediction | Systematic benchmark |
| 6 | 2025 | Nature Methods | Deep-learning-based gene perturbation effect prediction does not yet outperform simple linear baselines | Baseline critique |
| 7 | 2025 | Nature Biotechnology | Systema: a framework for evaluating genetic perturbation response prediction beyond systematic variation | Evaluation framework |
| 8 | 2025 | bioRxiv | Single Cell Foundation Models Evaluation (scFME) for In-Silico Perturbation | FM evaluation suite |
| 9 | 2025 | bioRxiv | Deep Learning-Based Genetic Perturbation Models Do Outperform Uninformative Baselines on Well-Calibrated Metrics | Metric rebuttal |
| 10 | 2025 | arXiv | Diversity by Design: Addressing Mode Collapse Improves scRNA-seq Perturbation Modeling on Well-Calibrated Metrics | Metric + training fix |
| 11 | 2025 | NeurIPS | PerturBench: Benchmarking Machine Learning Models for Cellular Perturbation Analysis | Benchmark suite |
| 12 | 2025 | ICML | PertEval-scFM: Benchmarking Single-Cell Foundation Models for Perturbation Effect Prediction | FM benchmark |
| 13 | 2025 | BMC Genomics | Benchmarking foundation cell models for post-perturbation RNA-seq prediction | FM benchmark |
| 14 | 2024 | bioRxiv | A systematic comparison of single-cell perturbation response prediction models | Systematic comparison |
| 15 | 2024 | arXiv | Benchmarking Transcriptomics Foundation Models for Perturbation Analysis: one PCA still rules them all | Baseline critique |

Three aggregate signals are worth reading from this distribution. First, **venue quality is unusually high for a 15-item list**: two Nature Methods papers, one Nature Biotechnology, one Genome Biology, plus peer-reviewed NeurIPS and ICML proceedings — evaluation work, not just method papers, is clearing top-tier review in this field. Second, the temporal profile (2 entries in 2024 → 9 in 2025 → 4 already in 2026) shows evaluation methodology consolidating rapidly as a subdiscipline. Third, the list splits cleanly between *constructive* contributions (named frameworks: scArchon, Systema, scFME, PerturBench, PertEval-scFM) and *adversarial* contributions (critiques targeting baselines and metrics) — a duality explored next.

Sources: [README.md](README.md#L275-L290)

## Thematic Taxonomy of Evaluation Work

Cross-cutting the chronological order, the fifteen entries cluster into three functionally distinct categories. The prerequisite for the table: the "clusters" are derived from title semantics only — the repository itself does not tag entries, so treat groupings as a reading aid rather than ground truth.

| Cluster | Entries (by row # above) | Shared concern | Character |
|---------|--------------------------|----------------|-----------|
| **Benchmark suites & frameworks** | 2, 5, 7, 8, 11, 12, 13, 14 | Build reusable evaluation infrastructure (scArchon, Systema, scFME, PerturBench, PertEval-scFM) or run one-off systematic comparisons (5, 13, 14) | Constructive |
| **Baseline & metric critiques** | 1, 4, 6, 9, 10, 15 | Question whether reported wins are real — challenge with linear baselines, PCA, metric calibration, mode-collapse analysis | Adversarial |
| **Verdict papers on foundation models** | 3, 8, 12, 13, 15 | Specifically ask whether *foundation models* (vs. task-specific deep nets) help perturbation prediction | Synthetic |

The overlap between clusters is deliberate signal, not noise: entries 8, 12, 13, and 15 appear in two clusters because the field's central question — "do foundation models improve perturbation prediction?" — is being answered simultaneously by suite builders and by critics. Entry 10 ("Diversity by Design") is the most methodologically interesting hybrid: its title asserts both a *failure-mode diagnosis* (mode collapse) and a *remedy* (diversity by design), validated "on well-calibrated metrics" — the exact metric vocabulary of the critique cluster.

> [!TIP]
> Read entries 6, 9, and 10 as a single three-move argument cluster rather than three independent papers: 6 (Nature Methods) lands the negative result on standard metrics → 9 (bioRxiv) counters that the gap reopens on "well-calibrated" metrics → 10 (arXiv) explains the mechanism as mode collapse that calibrated metrics expose. Evaluating any perturbation model without reading all three risks inheriting whichever metric regime the single paper you read happened to favor.

Sources: [README.md](README.md#L275-L290)

## The Baselines Controversy: A Verifiable Argument Arc

The most striking pattern in this section is that the **titles alone reconstruct a multi-year methodological dispute** — no external knowledge required. The prerequisite for the diagram: each node is a section entry verbatim (abbreviated), and edges represent the chronological challenge-and-response sequence implied by their claims.

```mermaid
flowchart TD
    P1["2024 · arXiv<br/>'one PCA still rules them all'"] --> P2["2025 · Nature Methods<br/>'does not yet outperform<br/>simple linear baselines'"]
    P2 --> P3["2025 · bioRxiv<br/>'DO outperform on<br/>well-calibrated metrics'"]
    P2 --> P4["2025 · arXiv<br/>'mode collapse' → fix diversity"]
    P3 --> P5["2026 · bioRxiv<br/>'evaluating is far from<br/>straightforward'"]
    P4 --> P5
    P5 --> P6["2026 · bioRxiv<br/>'towards principled evaluation'"]
    P6 --> P7["2026 · bioRxiv<br/>'foundation models improve<br/>perturbation response prediction'"]
```

Reading the arc left to right: 2024 opens with the provocative claim that plain PCA remains competitive for perturbation analysis (entry 15); 2025 escalates this to a Nature Methods result that deep models fail to beat simple linear baselines (entry 6); the same year produces a direct counterpoint asserting that deep models *do* win once metrics are well-calibrated (entry 9), plus a mechanistic explanation — mode collapse — for why naive metrics mislead (entry 10). By 2026 the dispute matures into methodology: one entry concedes that evaluation "is far from straightforward" (entry 4), another proposes principled evaluation as a research program (entry 1), and the arc closes with a positive verdict that foundation models improve prediction (entry 3).

The engineering takeaway for this audience is architectural: **the controversy was never about model capacity — it was about metric design and generalization splits.** Every named framework in the constructive cluster (PerturBench, PertEval-scFM, Systema, scArchon) exists precisely to pin down these choices so that the entry-6-vs-entry-9 disagreement cannot silently recur.

> [!TIP]
> When you adopt any benchmark from this list, first locate which side of the 2025 controversy its metric regime descends from: suites emphasizing "well-calibrated metrics" (entries 9–10 lineage) will score generative perturbation models more favorably than suites built before that correction (entry 6 lineage). Divergent leaderboard results across suites are usually this single-axis difference, not a reproduction failure.

Sources: [README.md](README.md#L275-L290)

## Boundary Map: What Lives on Adjacent Pages

This section is deliberately narrow, and the repository enforces the boundary structurally. The disambiguation table below maps evaluation-adjacent material to its correct catalog page so you do not mis-file papers or misconfigure your reading list.

| Content pattern | Example from README | Correct catalog page |
|-----------------|---------------------|----------------------|
| Perturbation **prediction methods** (GEARS, scGen, CINEMA-OT, diffusion/flow models) | `### Models and prediction frameworks` (24 entries, L241–L265) | [Perturbation Prediction Frameworks](9-perturbation-prediction-frameworks) |
| Perturbation **data resources** (Tahoe-100M, X-Atlas/Orion, PerturBase, 2016 Perturb-seq) | `### Perturbation atlases and datasets` (6 entries, L267–L273) | [Perturbation Atlases and Datasets](10-perturbation-atlases-and-datasets) |
| Perturbation-trained **scFMs** (X-Cell, SCALE, STATE, Tahoe-x1) | Deferred to Multimodal scFMs per parent-note (L239) | [Multimodal and Spatial Models](7-multimodal-and-spatial-models) |
| Perturbation **analysis tooling** (Pertpy) | Under `Data formats and frameworks` (L361) | [Analysis Frameworks and Data Formats](16-analysis-frameworks-and-data-formats) |
| General scFM **benchmarks** (annotation, integration, scaling laws, embedding-metric critiques) | `### Benchmarks and critical evaluations` (L370–L429) | [Benchmarking Studies and Critiques](17-benchmarking-studies-and-critiques) |
| Virtual-cell **challenge & world-model** evaluations | Under `Virtual Cell, World Models and Digital Human` (L292+) | [Virtual Cell Perspectives and Roadmaps](12-virtual-cell-perspectives-and-roadmaps) |

Two boundaries deserve emphasis for advanced navigators. The **vertical boundary** (L290 → L366 in the README) separates *perturbation-specific* benchmarks — this page — from *general-purpose* scFM benchmarks on annotation, integration, and scaling (page 17). Papers could plausibly belong to either; the repository's cut is by task, not by methodology. The **upstream boundary** (L239) is a scope ruling: perturbation-trained foundation models are treated as *models first*, not benchmarks or perturbation tools, and therefore live on page 7.

Sources: [README.md](README.md#L237-L290), [README.md](README.md#L361), [README.md](README.md#L366-L429)

## Reading Progression for Evaluation Engineers

If your goal is to *evaluate a perturbation model or ship a benchmark of your own*, the section supports a compressed reading path that respects the argument structure documented above. First, read the 2024 baseline warnings (entries 15, 14) to calibrate your skepticism; second, adopt a suite from the constructive cluster — PertEval-scFM (ICML) if you are specifically benchmarking foundation models, PerturBench (NeurIPS) for broader cellular perturbation analysis, or scArchon (Genome Biology) if scalability of the benchmark harness itself is the constraint; third, read the metric-calibration cluster (entries 6, 9, 10) before interpreting any leaderboard; finally, close with the 2026 principled-evaluation entries (1, 4) and the affirmative verdict (3) to position your work within the field's current frontier.

For placement of your own contribution: a new *suite* belongs in this section; a new *predictor* belongs in [Perturbation Prediction Frameworks](9-perturbation-prediction-frameworks); a new *metric-science critique* spanning multiple tasks belongs in [Benchmarking Studies and Critiques](17-benchmarking-studies-and-critiques).

Sources: [README.md](README.md#L275-L290)

## Where to Go Next

Having mapped the evaluation layer of the perturbation stack, the natural continuations are: **[Perturbation Atlases and Datasets](10-perturbation-atlases-and-datasets)** to understand the data contracts your benchmark train/test splits must honor; **[Perturbation Prediction Frameworks](9-perturbation-prediction-frameworks)** to study the models these benchmarks judge; and **[Benchmarking Studies and Critiques](17-benchmarking-studies-and-critiques)** for the broader evaluation-science context (embedding-metric pitfalls, scaling-law audits) that this page's perturbation-specific story sits inside. To see where perturbation benchmarks connect to the field's endgame — world models and the Virtual Cell Challenge — continue to **[Virtual Cell Perspectives and Roadmaps](12-virtual-cell-perspectives-and-roadmaps)**.


# Virtual Cell Perspectives and Roadmaps



This page documents the **"Reviews, comments, and perspectives"** subsection of the Virtual Cell, World Models and Digital Human catalog section — 17 perspective papers (lines 296–313 of the repository's README) that collectively define what a virtual cell *should be*, how it *should be built*, and how it *should be judged*. Unlike the sibling page, which catalogs concrete implementations, this page captures the field's **roadmap layer**: vision papers, criteria papers, and application agendas published predominantly in top-tier venues. The repository structures its entire catalog around the companion review *"The landscape of single-cell foundation models: design principles, applications, and open challenges"*, and the virtual cell frontier is its forward-looking terminus.

![Evolutionary tree of single-cell foundation models](https://github.com/OmicsML/awesome-foundation-model-single-cell-papers/blob/main/figs/evo_tree.png?raw=true)

Sources: [README.md](README.md#L10-L12), [README.md](README.md#L22-L24), [README.md](README.md#L292-L294)

## Position in the Catalog: The Two-Layer Split

The catalog splits the virtual cell frontier into two complementary layers, and understanding this split is essential for reading the section correctly. **Layer one — this page** — covers *Reviews, comments, and perspectives* (README lines 296–313): normative papers that define requirements, roadmaps, and evaluation standards. **Layer two — the next catalog page** — covers *Models and frameworks* (README lines 315–330): implemented systems such as CellOS, AlphaCell, VCWorld, and CellForge. The section's own framing sentence establishes the intellectual thesis uniting both layers: virtual cell work consists of *"emerging generative training paradigms that recast scFMs as cellular world models, and efforts toward virtual embryos and digital humans"* — that is, the shift from foundation models as **representation learners** to foundation models as **simulators**.

```mermaid
graph TD
    VC["Virtual Cell<br/>predictive, generative cell simulator"]
    WM["World-Model Framing<br/>state inference + perturbation prediction"]
    CL["Closed-Loop Learning<br/>predict → validate → correct"]
    VC --> WM
    WM --> CL
    VC --> SCALE["Scale Hierarchy of Simulation"]
    SCALE --> C1["Cell-scale models"]
    SCALE --> C2["AI Virtual Organoids"]
    SCALE --> C3["Virtual Embryos"]
    SCALE --> C4["Digital Organism / Digital Human"]
    VC --> APP["Application Roadmaps"]
    APP --> A1["Drug discovery & pharmacology"]
    APP --> A2["Preclinical validation"]
    APP --> A3["Closed-loop target discovery"]
    CL -.->|requires| DATA["Three Data Pillars"]
```

Sources: [README.md](README.md#L54-L56), [README.md](README.md#L292-L294), [README.md](README.md#L296-L313), [README.md](README.md#L315-L330)

## The Discourse Trajectory: 2024 → 2026

The perspectives corpus shows a quantifiable acceleration in the field's discursive output. The count of perspective papers per year in this subsection is **1 (2024) → 6 (2025) → 10 (2026)** — an order-of-magnitude growth in under three years. The venue distribution is equally telling: the perspectives concentrate in *Cell* (4 papers), *Nature Methods* (2 papers), *Nature*, *Nature Medicine*, *Cell Research*, and *npj Digital Medicine*, indicating that the virtual cell conversation has consolidated at the highest editorial tiers rather than remaining confined to preprints. Only three entries remain as preprints (one OpenReview, two arXiv). For an intermediate developer, this trajectory signals that the roadmap concepts below are stable enough to build against — the definitional churn is settling.

```mermaid
timeline
    title Virtual-cell perspective timeline (catalog entries by year)
    2024 : Founding vision — Priorities and opportunities (Cell)
    2025 : Definition — The virtual cell (Nature Methods) : Predict, Explain, Discover (arXiv)
         : Data and validation — Three data pillars (Cell Research) : Turing-test challenge (Cell)
         : Applications and architecture — Preclinical pathways (npj Digital Medicine) : LLM convergence survey (arXiv)
    2026 : World-model formalization — Three Gaps roadmap (OpenReview) : World models for biomedicine (Cell) : A world model of the virtual cell (Cell)
         : Scale expansion — Digital organism (Nature Medicine) : Virtual embryos (Nature Methods) : AIVOs (Bioactive Materials)
         : Application pull — Drug discovery (TiPS) : Programmable virtual cells (Trends Open) : Next-generation virtual cell (Life Sciences)
         : Public discourse — Nature news coverage
```

Sources: [README.md](README.md#L297-L313)

## The Founding Vision and Its 2025 Consolidation

Every roadmap in this corpus traces back to a single anchor entry: the 2024 *Cell* perspective **"How to build the virtual cell with artificial intelligence: Priorities and opportunities"** (line 313). This is the field's founding manifesto — the only 2024 entry in the subsection — and it frames the virtual cell as a *construction project* with explicit priorities. The 2025 entries then consolidate the vision along three fronts. **Definitional consolidation** arrives via *The virtual cell* (Nature Methods, line 307) and *Virtual Cells: Predict, Explain, Discover* (arXiv, line 311), the latter title articulating a three-verb contract that recurs across the corpus: prediction is the baseline obligation, explanation the interpretability obligation, and discovery the scientific payoff. **Public-attention consolidation** is marked by the 2026 Nature news commentary *"'Virtual cells' aim to turn raw data into predictive models of biology"* (line 300) — the corpus's single journalism entry, signaling that the concept has crossed from specialist discourse into mainstream scientific media.

| Year | Perspective | Venue | Catalog Role |
|------|-------------|-------|--------------|
| 2024 | How to build the virtual cell with AI: Priorities and opportunities | Cell | Founding manifesto; agenda-setting |
| 2025 | The virtual cell | Nature Methods | Definition consolidation |
| 2025 | Virtual Cells: Predict, Explain, Discover | arXiv | Contract framing: predict → explain → discover |
| 2025 | Large Language Models Meet Virtual Cell: A Survey | arXiv | Architecture convergence (LLM axis) |
| 2026 | 'Virtual cells' aim to turn raw data into predictive models of biology | Nature | Mainstream-visibility marker |

Sources: [README.md](README.md#L300), [README.md](README.md#L307), [README.md](README.md#L311), [README.md](README.md#L313)

## The World-Model Turn: From Metaphor to Testable Criteria

The single most consequential development in the 2026 cohort is the **formalization of the world-model framing**. Three entries convert what was previously a loose metaphor into an auditable specification. *What Makes a Virtual Cell a World Model? Three Gaps, Three Experiments, and a Roadmap* (OpenReview, line 299) is the most explicit: its title promises named gaps, named experiments, and a named roadmap — a criteria paper against which implementations can be checked. *World models for biomedicine* (Cell, line 303) generalizes the framing beyond the cell to biomedicine as a domain, and *A world model of the virtual cell* (Cell, line 304) closes the loop by applying the abstraction specifically to virtual cells in the flagship venue. For developers, the operational takeaway is that "is this a world model?" is becoming an answerable engineering question, not a marketing claim.

```mermaid
flowchart LR
    A["Atlas-scale<br/>pretraining corpora"] --> B["Latent cellular<br/>world model"]
    B --> C["In-silico<br/>perturbation prediction"]
    C --> D["Validation loop<br/>Three Experiments / Turing test"]
    D -->|"error feedback<br/>(closed-loop learning)"| B
    D -->|"surplus hypotheses"| E["Target discovery<br/>and experiment design"]
    E -->|"new data"| A
```

Sources: [README.md](README.md#L299), [README.md](README.md#L303-L304)

## Data Supply and the Closed-Loop Imperative

Two 2025 perspectives define the *resource and validation* axes of the roadmap. **Grow AI virtual cells: three data pillars and closed-loop learning** (Cell Research, line 309) makes the supply-side argument: virtual cells cannot be trained from transcriptomic atlases alone but require three named data pillars, with *closed-loop learning* as the training regime that binds them — the prediction/observation feedback cycle shown in the diagram above. **Virtual Cell Challenge: Toward a Turing test for the virtual cell** (Cell, line 312) supplies the demand side: a community benchmark with an explicitly behavioral acceptance criterion. The pairing is architecturally significant — one paper specifies what flows *into* the model, the other specifies what the model must *pass* to count as working. The closed-loop vocabulary also recurs in the application cluster (line 297), making it the most repeated roadmap term in the subsection.

> [!TIP]
> The "three data pillars" are not stocked by this subsection — the supply chain lives elsewhere in the catalog. Perturbation-trained models and atlases are deliberately cross-listed under Multimodal scFMs rather than the perturbation section (line 239 names X-Cell, SCALE, PerturbGen, STATE, GeneJepa, and Tahoe-x1 explicitly), and the atlases themselves sit on the Perturbation Atlases page. When assessing a world-model implementation against the closed-loop requirement, check [Perturbation Atlases and Datasets](10-perturbation-atlases-and-datasets) and [Multimodal and Spatial Models](7-multimodal-and-spatial-models) for the actual training data.

Sources: [README.md](README.md#L239), [README.md](README.md#L309), [README.md](README.md#L312)

## Application Roadmaps: From Pharmacology to the Clinic

A distinct cluster of perspectives translates the virtual cell concept into **application pull** — concrete domains where the simulator is expected to pay for itself. *AI virtual cells for drug discovery and pharmacology* (Trends in Pharmacological Sciences, line 301) targets the pharma pipeline; *AI-driven virtual cell models in preclinical research: technical pathways, validation mechanisms, and clinical translation potential* (npj Digital Medicine, line 308) is the corpus's most operationally explicit title, promising named technical pathways and validation mechanisms rather than just vision; and *The next-generation virtual cell: From spatiotemporal transcriptomic modeling to closed-loop target discovery in complex diseases* (Life Sciences, line 297) sketches a full pipeline from spatial-temporal modeling to target discovery, reusing the closed-loop vocabulary established by the data-pillar paper. Complementing these, *Multimodal artificial intelligence for predictive and programmable virtual cells* (Trends Open, line 302) specifies the architectural *means* — multimodal, programmable systems — rather than the application *ends*.

| Application Domain | Perspective | Venue | Pipeline Stage Addressed |
|--------------------|-------------|-------|--------------------------|
| Drug discovery & pharmacology | AI virtual cells for drug discovery and pharmacology | Trends in Pharmacological Sciences | Compound screening, mechanism of action |
| Preclinical research | AI-driven virtual cell models in preclinical research | npj Digital Medicine | Technical pathway → validation → translation |
| Target discovery | The next-generation virtual cell | Life Sciences | Spatiotemporal modeling → closed-loop target ID |
| Architecture means | Multimodal AI for predictive and programmable virtual cells | Trends Open | Model design (multimodal, programmable) |

Sources: [README.md](README.md#L297), [README.md](README.md#L301-L302), [README.md](README.md#L308)

## Scaling the Simulated Unit: Organoids, Embryos, Digital Organisms

The third roadmap axis extends the **unit of simulation upward** from a single cell to multicellular and organism-level systems — matching the second half of the catalog section's own framing sentence ("efforts toward virtual embryos and digital humans", line 294). Three 2026 entries chart this gradient: *Artificial Intelligence Virtual Organoids (AIVOs)* (Bioactive Materials, line 306) addresses tissue-organoid scale; *Towards predictive virtual embryos with genomics and AI* (Nature Methods, line 305) addresses developmental scale; and *How to build an AI-driven digital organism* (Nature Medicine, line 298) — a second "how to build" paper — addresses whole-organism scale, echoing the founding manifesto's construction-project framing at maximum scope. The consistency of the "how to build" title pattern across scales (lines 298 and 313) suggests the field treats each scale level as a distinct engineering project with its own priorities, rather than as a single continuous model.

| Simulation Scale | Perspective | Venue | Founding/Manifesto Lineage |
|------------------|-------------|-------|----------------------------|
| Single cell | How to build the virtual cell with AI (2024) | Cell | Original manifesto |
| Organoid / tissue | Artificial Intelligence Virtual Organoids (AIVOs) | Bioactive Materials | Scale extension |
| Embryo / development | Towards predictive virtual embryos with genomics and AI | Nature Methods | Scale extension |
| Whole organism | How to build an AI-driven digital organism | Nature Medicine | Second manifesto; maximal scope |

Sources: [README.md](README.md#L294), [README.md](README.md#L298), [README.md](README.md#L305-L306), [README.md](README.md#L313)

## Synthesized Roadmap for Builders

Collapsing the seventeen entries into axes yields a compact specification that an implementation team can treat as a requirements checklist. Each axis has verifiable anchor papers in this subsection, and each maps directly onto a neighboring catalog page that stocks the corresponding supply — which is precisely how the catalog's author arranged the reading order. The roadmap reads: define the contract (**predict, explain, discover**), formalize it as a world model with testable gaps and experiments, secure the three data pillars, wire them into a closed-loop training regime, pass the Turing-test-style challenge, then climb the scale hierarchy toward digital organisms while the pharma and preclinical clusters extract value at each level.

| Roadmap Axis | Core Question | Anchor Perspectives (line refs) | Supply Pages |
|--------------|---------------|--------------------------------|--------------|
| Definition contract | What must a virtual cell do? | Predict, Explain, Discover (L311); The virtual cell (L307) | — |
| World-model criteria | When is it a world model, not just an embedder? | Three Gaps/Three Experiments (L299); World models for biomedicine (L303); A world model of the virtual cell (L304) | [Cell World Model Implementations](13-cell-world-model-implementations) |
| Data supply | What data feeds the closed loop? | Three data pillars and closed-loop learning (L309) | [Perturbation Atlases and Datasets](10-perturbation-atlases-and-datasets) |
| Validation | What proves it works? | Virtual Cell Challenge / Turing test (L312) | [Perturbation Benchmarks](11-perturbation-benchmarks), [Benchmarking Studies and Critiques](17-benchmarking-studies-and-critiques) |
| Scale expansion | How far beyond one cell? | AIVOs (L306); Virtual embryos (L305); Digital organism (L298) | [Multimodal and Spatial Models](7-multimodal-and-spatial-models) |
| Application pull | Who pays for it? | Pharma (L301); Preclinical (L308); Target discovery (L297) | [AI Agents for Discovery](20-ai-agents-for-discovery) |
| Architecture means | What builds it? | Multimodal programmable AI (L302); LLM convergence survey (L310) | [LLM-Based Cell Models](8-llm-based-cell-models) |

> [!TIP]
> Use this page and its sibling as a specification-versus-implementation pair: every roadmap claim here (lines 296–313) can be audited against a concrete system on the next page (lines 315–330). For example, the "Three Gaps, Three Experiments" criteria paper (L299) and the Turing-test challenge (L312) give you a rubric; CellOS, AlphaCell, and VCWorld on the implementations page are the candidates that rubric was written to judge. Reading in catalog order — this page first — mirrors the field's own logical dependency: criteria before systems.

Sources: [README.md](README.md#L296-L313), [README.md](README.md#L315-L330)

## Suggested Reading Progression

Having absorbed the roadmap layer, the natural continuation follows the catalog's own dependency order. Proceed next to **[Cell World Model Implementations](13-cell-world-model-implementations)** to audit the criteria above against real systems, then branch into the supply chain: **[Perturbation Prediction Frameworks](9-perturbation-prediction-frameworks)** and **[Perturbation Atlases and Datasets](10-perturbation-atlases-and-datasets)** for the closed loop's training substrate, **[Perturbation Benchmarks](11-perturbation-benchmarks)** for its validation substrate, and **[LLM-Based Cell Models](8-llm-based-cell-models)** for the architecture-convergence axis. To place the whole frontier in historical context, the **[Evolutionary Tree of Models](3-evolutionary-tree-of-models)** page renders the repository's flagship figure (shown at the top of this page), and **[Surveys and Open Challenges](21-surveys-and-open-challenges)** completes the perspectives picture with field-wide survey literature beyond the virtual cell niche.


# Cell World Model Implementations



This page is the **reference catalog of concrete cellular world-model implementations** curated in the *awesome-foundation-model-single-cell-papers* repository. Where its sibling page collects conceptual essays, roadmaps, and commentaries, this page catalogs the 15 built systems — simulators, latent-predictive models, generative engines, and agentic frameworks — that operationalize the idea of a "world model" for cell biology. Every entry is sourced directly from the repository's primary artifact, `README.md`, which structures the field according to the review *"The landscape of single-cell foundation models: design principles, applications, and open challenges"* (under review at *Cell*).

Sources: [README.md](README.md#L11-L12), [README.md](README.md#L28-L37)

## Scope: Where This Page Sits in the Catalog

The repository partitions the world-model frontier into a parent chapter, **"Virtual Cell, World Models and Digital Human"**, whose own framing sentence defines the subject: *"Emerging generative training paradigms that recast scFMs as cellular world models, and efforts toward virtual embryos and digital humans."* This chapter has exactly two children, and the page boundary between them is strict: the "Reviews, comments, and perspectives" subsection covers concepts (documented on [Virtual Cell Perspectives and Roadmaps](12-virtual-cell-perspectives-and-roadmaps)), while the "Models and frameworks" subsection — 15 entries spanning lines 315–330 — **is** the present page.

Sources: [README.md](README.md#L292-L294), [README.md](README.md#L296-L313), [README.md](README.md#L315-L330)

For architectural context, the evolutionary tree below (the repository's sole visual asset, adapted with credit from Mooler0410/LLMsPracticalGuide) situates world-model implementations as the newest branch radiating from the established single-cell foundation model lineage:

![Evolutionary tree of single-cell foundation models](https://github.com/OmicsML/awesome-foundation-model-single-cell-papers/blob/main/figs/evo_tree.png?raw=true)

Sources: [README.md](README.md#L19-L24)

> [!TIP]
> Before consuming this list programmatically, note that section membership is curated, not partitioned: the README explicitly redirects perturbation-trained scFMs to the Multimodal scFMs section (line 239), and several world-model entries appear in two sections by design. Deduplicate by paper URL, never by title.

## The Implementation Inventory

The catalog holds **15 implementations** ordered strictly newest-first — a convention applied uniformly across the entire README. Thirteen entries are dated 2026 and two are dated 2025, making this the fastest-growing frontier in the repository: the section's recency concentration exceeds any other chapter of the catalog. Venue distribution across the 15 entries: six bioRxiv preprints, five arXiv preprints, one *Nature* article, one ICLR paper, one medRxiv preprint, and one industry blog post (GenBio AI). The master inventory below preserves each entry's catalog label and artifact type exactly as maintained upstream.

| # | Implementation | Year | Venue (as cataloged) | Artifact | Focus (from title) |
|---|----------------|------|----------------------|----------|--------------------|
| 1 | Operational perturbation proteomics-based virtual cell model | 2026 | Nature | [paper](https://www.nature.com/articles/s41586-026-11001-9) | proteomics-based operational virtual cell |
| 2 | Generative Virtual Tissue Model | 2026 | bioRxiv | [paper](https://www.biorxiv.org/content/10.64898/2026.08.12.743536v1) | computational design of therapeutic perturbation strategies |
| 3 | AIDO Cell: A General-Purpose Simulator for Cell Biology | 2026 | GenBio AI | [blog](https://genbio.ai/aido-cell-simulator/) | general-purpose cell simulator |
| 4 | RisQ | 2026 | medRxiv | [paper](https://www.medrxiv.org/content/10.64898/2026.07.07.26357373v1) | shared structure of human health across diseases, modalities, time |
| 5 | CellOS | 2026 | bioRxiv | [paper](https://www.biorxiv.org/content/10.64898/2026.06.18.733163v2) | world model of cellular state via joint embedding prediction |
| 6 | Towards Autonomous Mechanistic Reasoning in Virtual Cells | 2026 | bioRxiv (arXiv link) | [paper](https://arxiv.org/abs/2604.11661) | autonomous mechanistic reasoning |
| 7 | OCOO-T | 2026 | arXiv | [paper](https://arxiv.org/abs/2606.12838v1) | scalable transcriptional perturbation response prediction |
| 8 | BioM-JEPA | 2026 | arXiv | [paper](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.05928) | joint-embedding prediction of graph-connected gene blocks |
| 9 | Cell-JEPA | 2026 | arXiv | [paper](https://arxiv.org/abs/2602.02093) | latent representation learning for transcriptomics |
| 10 | AlphaCell | 2026 | bioRxiv | [paper](https://www.biorxiv.org/content/10.64898/2026.03.02.709176v1) | simulate perturbation-induced cellular dynamics |
| 11 | Chreode | 2026 | arXiv | [paper](https://arxiv.org/abs/2605.28111) | one-step temporal dynamics and perturbation prediction |
| 12 | CellFluxV2 | 2026 | bioRxiv | [paper](https://www.biorxiv.org/content/10.64898/2026.01.19.696785v1) | image generative foundation model for virtual cell |
| 13 | VCWorld | 2026 | ICLR | [paper](https://arxiv.org/abs/2512.00306) | biological world model for virtual cell simulation |
| 14 | GeneJepa | 2025 | bioRxiv | [paper](https://www.biorxiv.org/content/10.1101/2025.10.14.682378v1) | predictive world model of the transcriptome |
| 15 | CellForge | 2025 | arXiv | [paper](https://arxiv.org/abs/2508.02276) | agentic design of virtual cell models |

Sources: [README.md](README.md#L315-L330)

> [!TIP]
> Venue labels are manually maintained strings, not parsed metadata — one entry (row 6) pairs a bioRxiv label with an arXiv link. Tool builders indexing this list should treat the linked artifact as ground truth and the label as advisory.

## A Five-Cluster Paradigm Map

The 15 titles resolve into five internally coherent paradigm clusters — a classification derived strictly from verifiable title signals ("joint embedding prediction", "simulate ... cellular dynamics", "agentic design", and so on), not from external claims. The prerequisite for reading the diagram: solid arrows denote membership in this page's inventory; dashed arrows denote deliberate cross-listings into other catalog sections, which are covered in detail in the section after the cluster analyses.

```mermaid
graph TD
    M["Models and frameworks — 15 implementations<br/>README L315-L330"]
    M --> A["Latent-predictive world models<br/>JEPA family — 5 entries"]
    M --> B["Temporal dynamics and<br/>perturbation simulators — 4 entries"]
    M --> C["Generative virtual tissue<br/>and image models — 2 entries"]
    M --> D["Health-scale and general-purpose<br/>simulators — 2 entries"]
    M --> E["Agentic and mechanistic<br/>reasoning — 2 entries"]
    A --> A1["CellOS"]
    A --> A2["BioM-JEPA"]
    A --> A3["Cell-JEPA"]
    A --> A4["VCWorld"]
    A --> A5["GeneJepa"]
    B --> B1["Perturbation proteomics virtual cell"]
    B --> B2["OCOO-T"]
    B --> B3["AlphaCell"]
    B --> B4["Chreode"]
    C --> C1["Generative Virtual Tissue Model"]
    C --> C2["CellFluxV2"]
    D --> D1["RisQ"]
    D --> D2["AIDO Cell"]
    E --> E1["Autonomous Mechanistic Reasoning"]
    E --> E2["CellForge"]
    A2 -.->|"cross-listed in scRNA-seq"| X["Unimodal scFMs L80-L136"]
    A3 -.->|"cross-listed in scRNA-seq"| X
    A5 -.->|"cross-listed in Transcriptomics<br/>and Perturbation L151-L158"| X
```

Sources: [README.md](README.md#L315-L330), [README.md](README.md#L80-L91), [README.md](README.md#L151-L158)

| Paradigm cluster | Members | Verifiable title signal | Implied prediction target |
|------------------|---------|-------------------------|---------------------------|
| Latent-predictive (JEPA family) | CellOS, BioM-JEPA, Cell-JEPA, VCWorld, GeneJepa | "joint embedding prediction", "predictive world model", "latent representation learning" | latent cellular state |
| Dynamics & perturbation simulators | Perturbation-proteomics virtual cell, OCOO-T, AlphaCell, Chreode | "simulate perturbation-induced cellular dynamics", "one-step temporal dynamics", "perturbation response prediction" | post-perturbation / future cell state |
| Generative virtual tissue & image | Generative Virtual Tissue Model, CellFluxV2 | "generative virtual tissue", "image generative foundation model" | tissue-scale or image-space cell states |
| Health-scale & general simulators | RisQ, AIDO Cell | "shared structure of human health", "general-purpose simulator" | cross-disease, cross-modality health trajectories |
| Agentic & mechanistic reasoning | Autonomous Mechanistic Reasoning, CellForge | "autonomous mechanistic reasoning", "agentic design" | reasoning loops over virtual cells; model construction itself |

Sources: [README.md](README.md#L316-L330)

## Cluster Deep Dives

### Latent-Predictive World Models (JEPA Family)

This is the largest and most arXiv-venue-heavy cluster, unified by a shared architectural vocabulary: predicting in **latent space** rather than reconstructing raw expression counts. CellOS frames this most explicitly, describing itself as *"Learning a World Model of Cellular State through Joint Embedding Prediction"*; GeneJepa makes the world-model claim directly in its title (*"A Predictive World Model of the Transcriptome"*); VCWorld carries peer-review weight as the cluster's ICLR-accepted entry; BioM-JEPA extends the paradigm to *graph-connected gene blocks*; and Cell-JEPA targets representation learning for transcriptomics. The density of JEPA-lineage systems (four of five entries carry JEPA/Jepa naming) indicates that joint-embedding predictive architectures — originally formulated for visual world models — have become the dominant template for cellular world models in this catalog.

Sources: [README.md](README.md#L320-L329), [README.md](README.md#L323-L324)

### Temporal Dynamics and Perturbation Simulators

The second cluster orients the world model toward **forward simulation under intervention** — the property that distinguishes a world model from a static encoder. AlphaCell's title states the ambition in full: *"Towards building a World Model to simulate perturbation-induced cellular dynamics"*. Chreode compresses the objective to *"one-step temporal dynamics and perturbation prediction"*, and OCOO-T contributes the *"simple and scalable"* end of the spectrum for transcriptional perturbation response. The *Nature*-published operational perturbation proteomics virtual cell model anchors the cluster with the section's only primary-journal implementation, grounding the simulation paradigm in proteomic measurements rather than transcriptomics alone.

Sources: [README.md](README.md#L316-L327)

### Generative Virtual Tissue and Image-Based Models

Two implementations push the world-model boundary beyond single-cell transcriptomics. The Generative Virtual Tissue Model targets the tissue scale, coupling generation to *"Computational Design of Therapeutic Perturbation Strategies"* — an application-facing framing rare in this section. CellFluxV2 defines the modality frontier: it is cataloged as *"An Image Generative Foundation Model for Virtual Cell Modeling"*, making it the only entry whose output space is explicitly image-valued. Together they indicate that the implementable notion of a "cell world" in this catalog spans scales from organelle-image rendering to tissue-level therapy design.

Sources: [README.md](README.md#L317-L327)

### Health-Scale and General-Purpose Simulators

This cluster operationalizes the "Digital Human" half of the parent chapter's title (line 294). RisQ learns *"the shared structure of human health across diseases, modalities, and time"* — a patient-trajectory scope rather than a single-cell scope — and is the section's only medRxiv entry. AIDO Cell is the catalog's sole industry-published implementation, appearing as a GenBio AI blog post describing a *"General-Purpose Simulator for Cell Biology"*. The asymmetry is meaningful: while the virtual-embryo and digital-organism *visions* live in the perspectives subsection on page 12, their concrete implementation surface in this catalog currently consists of exactly these two entries.

Sources: [README.md](README.md#L294-L294), [README.md](README.md#L318-L319), [README.md](README.md#L296-L313)

### Agentic and Mechanistic Reasoning Frameworks

The smallest cluster is also the most reflexive: rather than simulating cells, these systems simulate or automate the **modeling process itself**. CellForge performs *"Agentic Design of Virtual Cell Models"* — construction automation — while *Towards Autonomous Mechanistic Reasoning in Virtual Cells* targets reasoning autonomy over already-built virtual cells. Their presence at the tail of the newest-first ordering (CellForge, 2025) marks them as the earliest entries of the section, suggesting agentic orchestration is the paradigm that predates and possibly seeds the JEPA and simulator waves that followed.

Sources: [README.md](README.md#L321-L330)

## Cross-Listing Mechanics: World Model as a Cross-Cutting Label

The catalog treats "world model" as a **capability claim that can appear in any modality section**, not as a hard partition. Three consequences follow from lines verified in the README. First, the perturbation chapter carries an explicit redirect: *"Perturbation-trained scFMs such as X-Cell, SCALE, PerturbGen, STATE, GeneJepa and Tahoe-x1 are listed under Multimodal scFMs"* — meaning GeneJepa legitimately appears on both page 9's periphery and here. Second, the unimodal scRNA-seq list already contains world-model-branded systems: Lingshu-Cell (*"A generative cellular world model for transcriptome modeling toward virtual cells"*) plus the dual-listed BioM-JEPA and Cell-JEPA. Third, spatial transcriptomics hosts CellWorld, whose subtitle (*"From Gene-Level Reconstruction to Latent Cell Prediction"*) is the latent-prediction paradigm transplanted into spatial data.

| Catalog location | World-model-branded entries | Governing note |
|------------------|-----------------------------|----------------|
| Models and frameworks — this page | all 15 entries | primary home (L315–L330) |
| Multimodal scFMs → Transcriptomics and Perturbation | GeneJepa; X-Cell, SCALE, PerturbGen, STATE, Tahoe-x1 | explicit redirect note at L239 |
| Unimodal scFMs → scRNA-seq | Lingshu-Cell; BioM-JEPA; Cell-JEPA | modality-first organization |
| Multimodal scFMs → Spatial | CellWorld | spatial-section organization |

Sources: [README.md](README.md#L239-L239), [README.md](README.md#L87-L91), [README.md](README.md#L157-L162), [README.md](README.md#L315-L330)

The practical reading rule for navigation: **this page is the superset view of implementations claiming world-model status; the modality sections are the modality-first views of the same systems.** If you arrived here from [Unimodal scRNA-seq Models](5-unimodal-scrna-seq-models) or [Multimodal and Spatial Models](7-multimodal-and-spatial-models), the overlapping entries above are the joining keys.

Sources: [README.md](README.md#L72-L78), [README.md](README.md#L292-L330)

## Curation and Maintenance Mechanics

Three repository-level conventions govern how this section evolves, all relevant if you intend to contribute. Entries are **appended at the top** of the list in strict reverse-chronological order, so a new 2026 world-model paper would become line 316 and shift everything below. Contributions flow through GitHub issues and pull requests — the repository header explicitly welcomes *"a paper we missed, or a broken link"*. And the taxonomy itself is versioned against the companion *Cell* review: the catalog's section boundaries mirror the review's classification, so submissions that blur the implementation/perspective boundary will land on one side or the other of the page-12/page-13 split based on whether the artifact is a built system or an argument.

| Contribution scenario | Correct landing zone | Mechanism |
|-----------------------|----------------------|-----------|
| New simulator / world-model implementation | Top of L315–L330 list | PR with `1.` list item, newest-first |
| New roadmap essay or perspective | Reviews subsection (page 12) | PR into L296–L313 |
| Broken paper link in this section | Issue referencing the entry's line | Issue or PR fix |
| New perturbation-prediction (non-world-model) model | Perturbation Models section (page 9) | PR into L241–L265 |

Sources: [README.md](README.md#L14-L16), [README.md](README.md#L39-L70), [README.md](README.md#L315-L330)

## Recommended Reading Path

For an advanced developer building on or evaluating these systems, the catalog supports a deliberate traversal. Begin with the conceptual vocabulary on [Virtual Cell Perspectives and Roadmaps](12-virtual-cell-perspectives-and-roadmaps), since the definitions argued there ("what makes a virtual cell a world model") govern why these 15 entries are grouped as they are. Return here for the implementation landscape, then branch by intent: for intervention-prediction mechanics, the neighboring [Perturbation Prediction Frameworks](9-perturbation-prediction-frameworks) and their evaluation counterpart [Perturbation Benchmarks](11-perturbation-benchmarks) form a tightly coupled pair with the simulator cluster above; for skepticism about whether any of this works yet, [Benchmarking Studies and Critiques](17-benchmarking-studies-and-critiques) collects the adversarial evidence; and for deployment surfaces, [Infrastructure and Model Platforms](19-infrastructure-and-model-platforms) plus [AI Agents for Discovery](20-ai-agents-for-discovery) cover the systems these world models would plug into.


# Transcriptomic Atlases and Repositories



Every single-cell foundation model inherits the statistical structure — and the biases — of the corpus it was pretrained on. This page documents the **supply side** of that equation: the curated transcriptomic atlases, aggregation platforms, and raw-data repositories cataloged in this repository as the substrate for scFM pretraining. The source material is a single 13-entry subsection of the README, ordered newest-first, spanning 24 years of infrastructure evolution — from the raw submission archives of the early 2000s to today's "AI-ready" ensemble cell atlases.

This page sits inside the **Data Foundations** cluster of the Deep Dive track, immediately before its two sibling pages on multimodal corpora and data formats. Readers arriving from the model-centric pages ([Unimodal scRNA-seq Models](5-unimodal-scrna-seq-models) onward) will find here the answer to the question those pages raise implicitly: *where does the training data actually come from?*

Sources: [README.md](/README.md#L332-L334), [README.md](/README.md#L336-L349)

## Position in the Data Foundations Stack

The README groups all data-layer resources under one top-level section, **"Pretraining Datasets and Resources"**, whose framing sentence defines their shared purpose: *"Large-scale atlases, multimodal corpora, and data frameworks used for pretraining and preprocessing single-cell foundation models."* Within that section, three subsections divide the data layer by scope, and the catalog entry for this page is the first of the three:

```mermaid
flowchart TB
    PDR["Pretraining Datasets and Resources<br/>README L332–L334"]
    PDR --> A["Single-cell transcriptomic atlases and repositories<br/><b>THIS PAGE · 13 entries · L336–L349</b>"]
    PDR --> B["Multimodal and spatial pretraining corpora<br/>L351–L355"]
    PDR --> C["Data formats and frameworks<br/>L357–L364"]
    A --> M["Single-cell foundation model pretraining"]
    B --> M
    C --> M
```

The prerequisite for reading this diagram is the catalog itself: the README's table of contents declares the same three children under the same parent, so the layering above is the repository's own structure, not an external interpretation. This page covers only the first branch — single-modality transcriptomic data at atlas and repository scale. Anything multimodal (spatial, protein, paired RNA/ATAC *training corpora*) is deliberately deferred to the sibling page, and the tooling that turns these resources into trainable tensors belongs to the formats-and-frameworks page.

Sources: [README.md](/README.md#L332-L334), [README.md](/README.md#L57-L60), [README.md](/README.md#L351-L364)

## The Inventory: 13 Resources, Three Functional Tiers

The 13 entries are not homogeneous. Reading their self-descriptions side by side, they resolve cleanly into three tiers that differ in *what kind of artifact they are*: a scientific reference (an atlas), an engineered system (a platform or database), or a storage primitive (an archive). The README records each entry with a year tag, venue, one-line description, and paper link — one entry additionally carries a live portal link:

| # | Resource | Year · Venue | Self-description (verbatim from README) | Tier |
|---|----------|--------------|------------------------------------------|------|
| 1 | **Tabula Sapiens 2.0** | 2026 · Cell | "A comprehensive transcriptomic atlas of human cell types" | 1 |
| 2 | **scBaseCount** | 2025 · bioRxiv | "An AI agent-curated, uniformly processed, and continually expanding single-cell data repository" | 2 |
| 3 | **hECA v2.0** | 2025 · Scientific Data | "An AI-ready ensemble cell atlas of single-cell RNA and ATAC sequencing data" | 1 |
| 4 | **scCompass** | 2025 · Advanced Science | "An Integrated Multi-Species scRNA-seq Database for AI-Ready" | 2 |
| 5 | **CZ CELLxGENE Discover** | 2025 · Nucleic Acids Research | "A single-cell data platform for scalable exploration, analysis and modeling of aggregated data" | 2 |
| 6 | **Expression Atlas** (update) | 2024 · Nucleic Acids Research | "Insights from sequencing data at both bulk and single cell level" | 2 |
| 7 | **Single Cell Portal** | 2023 · bioRxiv | "An interactive home for single-cell genomics data" | 2 |
| 8 | **Tabula Sapiens** | 2022 · Science | "A multiple-organ, single-cell transcriptomic atlas of humans" | 1 |
| 9 | **hECA** | 2022 · iScience | "The cell-centric assembly of a cell atlas" | 1 |
| 10 | **DISCO** | 2022 · Nucleic Acids Research | "A database of deeply integrated human single-cell omics data" | 2 |
| 11 | **UCSC Cell Browser** | 2021 · Bioinformatics | "Visualize your single-cell data" | 2 |
| 12 | **SRA** | 2010 · Nucleic Acids Research | "The Sequence Read Archive" | 3 |
| 13 | **GEO** | 2002 · Nucleic Acids Research | "Gene Expression Omnibus" | 3 |

```mermaid
flowchart LR
    subgraph T1["Tier 1 · Reference atlases (4)"]
        TS2["Tabula Sapiens 2.0"]
        TS1["Tabula Sapiens"]
        H2["hECA v2.0"]
        H1["hECA"]
    end
    subgraph T2["Tier 2 · Aggregation & discovery platforms (7)"]

    subgraph T3["Tier 3 · Raw archives (2)"]
        GEO["GEO"]
        SRA["SRA"]
    end
```

The classification above is derived purely from each entry's README description — for example, DISCO is placed in Tier 2 because it self-identifies as "a database of deeply integrated" data rather than a primary atlas, and UCSC Cell Browser in Tier 2 because its stated function is visualization rather than curation. Note also a formatting convention that matters when scanning this file: entries are listed in **strict reverse-chronological order**, so the newest resources (2026, 2025) appear at the top and the two archives anchor the bottom.

Sources: [README.md](/README.md#L337-L349)

## Tier 1 — Curated Reference Atlases
