Four entries constitute the reference-atlas tier, and they form two distinct **versioned lineages**, which is the tier's most instructive structural pattern:

| Lineage | First release | Current release | Character of the upgrade |
|---------|--------------|-----------------|---------------------------|
| Tabula Sapiens | [2022 Science](https://doi.org/10.1126/science.abl4896) — "a multiple-organ, single-cell transcriptomic atlas of humans" | [2026 Cell](https://www.cell.com/cell/fulltext/S0092-8674(26)00937-2) — "a comprehensive transcriptomic atlas of human cell types" | From organ coverage → comprehensive *cell-type* coverage |
| hECA | [2022 iScience](https://doi.org/10.1016/j.isci.2022.104318) — "the cell-centric assembly of a cell atlas" | [2025 Scientific Data](https://www.nature.com/articles/s41597-025-06426-2) — "an AI-ready ensemble cell atlas of single-cell RNA and ATAC sequencing data" | From assembly concept → AI-ready, RNA + ATAC ensemble |

Both lineages illustrate the same trajectory: a foundational human atlas published as primary research (Science, iScience) is later re-released as versioned infrastructure in venues that signal dataset-as-product intent (Cell for the flagship revision; *Scientific Data* — a journal explicitly for describable, reusable datasets — for hECA v2.0). The hECA lineage additionally shows modality expansion: v2.0 spans "single-cell RNA **and ATAC** sequencing data," making it the only Tier 1 entry that reaches beyond transcriptomics — though its transcriptomic core keeps it in this page's scope, its full multi-omic role is better understood alongside the sibling corpora page.

Sources: [README.md](/README.md#L337-L345)

## Tier 2 — Aggregation and Discovery Platforms

Seven entries form the platform tier, and their descriptions reveal a **shift from "browse the data" to "train on the data"** across the 2021–2025 window:

| Resource | Year | Primary function (per README) | Modeling-relevant signal |
|----------|------|-------------------------------|---------------------------|
| **CZ CELLxGENE Discover** | 2025 | "Scalable exploration, analysis **and modeling** of aggregated data" | Only entry in the section with a live `[[portal]]` link |
| **scBaseCount** | 2025 | "AI **agent-curated**, uniformly processed, continually expanding" | Automation + uniform preprocessing + growth by design |
| **scCompass** | 2025 | "Integrated **Multi-Species** scRNA-seq Database for AI-Ready" | Cross-species scope, explicit AI-readiness |
| **DISCO** | 2022 | "Deeply integrated human single-cell omics data" | Integration as the core value |
| **Single Cell Portal** | 2023 | "An interactive home for single-cell genomics data" | Human-facing interactivity |
| **Expression Atlas** | 2024 | "Sequencing data at both **bulk and single cell** level" | Bridges bulk and single-cell contexts |
| **UCSC Cell Browser** | 2021 | "Visualize your single-cell data" | Visualization utility |

Three descriptions deserve emphasis. First, CZ CELLxGENE Discover is phrased in explicitly computational terms — "exploration, analysis and **modeling** of aggregated data" — and it is the sole resource in this section accompanied by a live portal link (`cellxgene.cziscience.com`), which makes it the most direct entry point from this page to working infrastructure. Second, scBaseCount's "AI agent-curated, uniformly processed, and continually expanding" is the only description in the entire section that names an *operational pipeline* rather than a static dataset — uniform processing plus continuous expansion is precisely the property profile a pretraining corpus demands. Third, scCompass is the section's only multi-species entry, complementing the otherwise human-centric Tier 1.

> [!TIP]
> When building a pretraining pipeline from this page, CZ CELLxGENE Discover is the pragmatic first stop: it is the only Tier 2 resource whose README description names *modeling* as a first-class capability and the only one with a live `[[portal]]` link (README L341) — every other entry links to a paper alone. For programmatic access, start from the portal and use the paper (NAR 2025) as the schema reference.

Sources: [README.md](/README.md#L338-L348), [README.md](/README.md#L341)

## Tier 3 — Raw Data Archives

The tier-3 pair — **GEO** (Gene Expression Omnibus, 2002) and **SRA** (Sequence Read Archive, 2010) — are the section's oldest entries by more than a decade, and their presence in a 2026-curated foundation-model reading list is not vestigial. They serve a different role from Tiers 1–2: they are the **provenance layer**. Atlases and platforms aggregate and process raw submissions that ultimately live in these archives, so they are where a developer goes to trace a processed cell back to its original sequencing run, retrieve raw reads for reprocessing under a different pipeline, or submit new data that future atlases will aggregate. Their inclusion directly beneath the AI-ready platforms makes the dependency direction legible: everything above them, in some sense, compiles down from them.

Sources: [README.md](/README.md#L348-L349)

## A 24-Year Arc: From Submission Archives to AI-Ready Repositories

Because every entry carries a year tag, the section doubles as a timeline of how the field's data infrastructure evolved. Read in chronological order, the sequence is: raw archives (2002–2010) → visualization (2021) → curated human atlases and integrated databases (2022) → interactive portals (2023) → cross-context aggregation (2024) → **explicitly AI-ready platforms** (2025) → comprehensive atlas revision (2026):

```mermaid
timeline
    title Transcriptomic data infrastructure milestones (README year tags, L337–L349)
    2002 : GEO — raw submission archive
    2010 : SRA — raw read archive
    2021 : UCSC Cell Browser — visualization
    2022 : Tabula Sapiens · hECA · DISCO — curated atlases & integrated databases
    2023 : Single Cell Portal — interactive access
    2024 : Expression Atlas update — bulk + single-cell aggregation
    2025 : CZ CELLxGENE Discover · scCompass · hECA v2.0 · scBaseCount — AI-ready platforms
    2026 : Tabula Sapiens 2.0 — comprehensive atlas revision
```

The pattern is consistent with the repository's overall thesis: as foundation models matured (see the model families documented from [Taxonomy of Single-Cell Foundation Models](4-taxonomy-of-single-cell-foundation-models) onward), the data layer reorganized itself around their needs. The vocabulary shift in the resource descriptions is the evidence — "AI-ready" appears in three of the four 2025 entries (scCompass, hECA v2.0) and 2026's flagship atlas revision, a term entirely absent from the pre-2024 entries. The infrastructure did not merely grow; it *rebranded around model consumption*.

Sources: [README.md](/README.md#L337-L349)

## Choosing a Resource: Developer Decision Guide

The three tiers are complements, not competitors — each answers a different engineering question. The following decision table maps common pretraining and analysis tasks to the section's resources, with every recommendation grounded in the README's own descriptions:

| If you need… | Start with | Why (grounded in README description) |
|--------------|-----------|--------------------------------------|
| A human cell-type reference for annotation / embedding evaluation | Tabula Sapiens 2.0 | "Comprehensive transcriptomic atlas of human cell types" |
| A large aggregated pretraining pool | CZ CELLxGENE Discover; scBaseCount | Explicitly built for "modeling of aggregated data"; "uniformly processed, continually expanding" |
| Cross-species transcriptomic data | scCompass | The section's only "Multi-Species" database |
| RNA + ATAC ensemble at atlas scale | hECA v2.0 | "AI-ready ensemble cell atlas of single-cell RNA and ATAC" |
| Continuously growing, uniformly preprocessed data | scBaseCount | "Continually expanding" with uniform processing |
| Interactive data exploration before committing | Single Cell Portal; UCSC Cell Browser; CELLxGENE | "Interactive home"; "visualize your single-cell data" |
| Bulk–single-cell contextual comparison | Expression Atlas | Covers "both bulk and single cell level" |
| Raw reads / provenance tracing | GEO; SRA | The archival substrate beneath all processed resources |

A final structural observation for maintainers and heavy users of this list: the atlas resources here are **living, versioned artifacts**, not frozen snapshots — the Tabula Sapiens and hECA lineages each carry a superseded first release and an active current release within this single section. When citing these resources in reproducibility documentation or dataset manifests, pin the specific version and year rather than the project name, since the README itself distinguishes them as separate entries.

> [!TIP]
> Treat this section's reverse-chronological ordering as a freshness signal when scanning the raw file: line 337 (2026) to line 349 (2002) means the top of the subsection is where newly curated AI-ready resources accumulate. If you are diffing the README over time to detect new data resources, watch lines 337–341 — that is where the 2025–2026 additions landed.

Sources: [README.md](/README.md#L336-L349)

## Where to Go Next

This page covered the single-modality transcriptomic supply side. The natural continuations, in the order they appear in the catalog:

- **[Multimodal Pretraining Corpora](15-multimodal-pretraining-corpora)** — the sibling subsection (README L351–L355) covering paired-omics and spatial training corpora such as SCARF/X-Omics, SpatialCorpus-110M, and SToCorpus-88M. Go here when your pretraining needs exceed transcriptomics alone.
- **[Analysis Frameworks and Data Formats](16-analysis-frameworks-and-data-formats)** — the third data-foundations subsection (README L357–L364): Scanpy/AnnData, Seurat, scvi-tools, and scalable loaders. Go here to convert the resources on this page into trainable tensors.
- **[Perturbation Atlases and Datasets](10-perturbation-atlases-and-datasets)** — perturbation-scale data (Tahoe-100M, X-Atlas/Orion, PerturBase) lives under the Genetic Perturbation cluster, deliberately separated from these observational atlases. Go here for intervention data.
- **[Infrastructure and Model Platforms](19-infrastructure-and-model-platforms)** — when atlas-scale data requires serving and query layers (e.g., the Arc Virtual Cell Atlas work cataloged there), the infrastructure cluster picks up where this page ends.


# Multimodal Pretraining Corpora


This page documents the **multimodal and spatial pretraining corpora** cataloged by the `awesome-foundation-model-single-cell-papers` repository. While the model-centric pages of this documentation track classify foundation models by architecture and modality, this page focuses on the **raw data fuel** — the large-scale, multi-omic corpora that make multimodal and spatial pretraining possible. The section is deliberately compact: four curated entries spanning paired transcriptome–chromatin data, massive spatial corpora, and single-cell proteomics, each mapped to the foundation model it was built to train.

## Position in the Catalog
This page is the middle node of the repository's **Data Foundations** track, sandwiched between single-omic atlas repositories upstream and data-engineering frameworks downstream. The parent chapter is defined as "Large-scale atlases, multimodal corpora, and data frameworks used for pretraining and preprocessing single-cell foundation models," and the catalog explicitly reserves this page for the multimodal corpora subcategory. Understanding this position prevents content drift: corpora here are pretraining *inputs*, not analysis *tooling*.

```mermaid
flowchart LR
    P14["Page 14<br/>Transcriptomic Atlases<br/>and Repositories"] --> P15["Page 15<br/>Multimodal Pretraining<br/>Corpora ⭐"]
    P15 --> P16["Page 16<br/>Analysis Frameworks<br/>and Data Formats"]
    style P15 fill:#2d6a4f,color:#fff
```

The repository itself is a single curated README — the entire catalog lives in one file, with this corpus section at lines 351–355:

```
.
├── LICENSE
├── README.md          ← full catalog; corpus section: L351-L355
└── figs/
    └── evo_tree.png   ← evolutionary tree of scFMs (context image)
```

![Evolutionary tree of single-cell foundation models](https://github.com/OmicsML/awesome-foundation-model-single-cell-papers/blob/main/figs/evo_tree.png?raw=true)

Sources: [README.md](README.md#L57-L60), [README.md](README.md#L332-L334), [README.md](README.md#L22-L24)

## Boundary Rules: What Belongs Here (and What Doesn't)
The Data Foundations chapter applies a three-way partition, and each boundary is worth stating precisely. **Single-omic transcriptomic atlases** (Tabula Sapiens 2.0, CZ CELLxGENE Discover, hECA, DISCO, GEO/SRA) live on the previous page — they are massive but single-modality. **Processing and loading tooling** (Scanpy/AnnData, scvi-tools, Seurat, scDataset, Pertpy) lives on the next page. Only entries whose defining feature is *modality composition beyond a single omic* — paired RNA+ATAC measurements, spatial transcriptomics, single-cell proteomics — qualify for this page. This mirrors the repository's model taxonomy, where multimodal scFMs are defined as models that "jointly encode complementary modalities — transcriptomic, epigenomic, proteomic, perturbational and spatial."

Sources: [README.md](README.md#L336-L349), [README.md](README.md#L351-L355), [README.md](README.md#L357-L364), [README.md](README.md#L147-L149)

## The Corpus Inventory
The section contains exactly four entries. Three follow a **model-bound naming convention** — the corpus is named after (or paired with) the specific foundation model it trains — while the fourth is a standalone community knowledgebase:

| Corpus | Venue / Year | Modality Composition | Scale | Bound Model | Entry Type |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| **SCARF / X-Omics** | bioRxiv 2025 | scRNA-seq + scATAC-seq (paired) | 2.7M cells | SCARF | Model-bound corpus |
| **SpatialCorpus-110M** | Nature Methods 2025 | Spatial transcriptomics | 110M (encoded in name) | Nicheformer | Model-bound corpus |
| **SToCorpus-88M** | ICML 2025 | Spatial transcriptomics, multi-scale | 88M (encoded in name) | SToFM | Model-bound corpus |
| **SPDB** | Nucleic Acids Research 2024 | Single-cell proteomics | Knowledgebase (curated) | None | Community resource |

Sources: [README.md](README.md#L351-L355)

## Model-Bound Corpora: Named Fuel for Named Models
The dominant pattern in this section is **corpus–model co-release**: a foundation model paper ships alongside a named, versioned pretraining corpus, so the data lineage of the published model is explicit. The data flow is unambiguous:

```mermaid
flowchart LR
    subgraph C["Pretraining Corpora — this page"]
        C1["SCARF / X-Omics<br/>2.7M paired cells<br/>RNA + ATAC"]
        C2["SpatialCorpus-110M<br/>spatial corpus"]
        C3["SToCorpus-88M<br/>multi-scale spatial corpus"]
        C4["SPDB<br/>proteomics knowledgebase"]
    end
    subgraph M["Consumer scFMs — Multimodal and Spatial Models"]
        M1["SCARF<br/>RNA+ATAC foundation model"]
        M2["Nicheformer<br/>single-cell + spatial FM"]
        M3["SToFM<br/>multi-scale spatial FM"]
    end
    C1 -->|pretrains| M1
    C2 -->|pretrains| M2
    C3 -->|pretrains| M3
    C4 -.->|proteomic context<br/>no bound model| M
```

> [!TIP]
> The corpus–model pairing creates a **traceability contract**: if you are reproducing SCARF, Nicheformer, or SToFM, you do not need to reverse-engineer their training data mixture — fetch the corpus artifact registered under the same paper. This is why the catalog records them as named corpora rather than folding them into generic atlases.

Sources: [README.md](README.md#L351-L355), [README.md](README.md#L147-L149)

### SCARF / X-Omics — 2.7M Paired RNA + ATAC Cells
Listed as "SCARF / X-Omics: a 2.7M-cell scRNA-seq/scATAC-seq pretraining corpus," this is the section's only **paired-measurement** entry: each cell carries joint transcriptomic and chromatin-accessibility readouts. Its consumer model, SCARF (Single Cell ATAC-seq and RNA-seq Foundation model), is cataloged separately in the *Multi-omics: RNA, ATAC and Protein* subsection of the multimodal model landscape, making this corpus the concrete data counterpart to that architecture.

Sources: [README.md](README.md#L352), [README.md](README.md#L197)

### SpatialCorpus-110M — Nicheformer's Pretraining Corpus
Cataloged under Nature Methods 2025 as the "Nicheformer pretraining corpus," SpatialCorpus-110M carries its scale in its own name — 110 million spatially resolved cells. Nicheformer is described in the model catalog as "a foundation model for single-cell and spatial omics," meaning the corpus serves dual coverage: it trains representations that span both dissociated single-cell data and spatially contextualized tissue data.

Sources: [README.md](README.md#L353), [README.md](README.md#L180)

### SToCorpus-88M — SToFM's Multi-Scale Spatial Corpus
The ICML 2025 entry pairs SToCorpus-88M with SToFM, which the model catalog describes as "a Multi-scale Foundation Model for Spatial Transcriptomics." The corpus naming again encodes scale (88M), and its consumer model differs architecturally from Nicheformer by targeting **multi-scale** spatial representation — from subcellular molecular structure up through tissue-level organization — which is the distinctive axis this corpus supports.

Sources: [README.md](README.md#L354), [README.md](README.md#L179)

## SPDB: The Knowledgebase Alternative
The fourth entry breaks the model-bound pattern. SPDB (2024, Nucleic Acids Research) is described as "a comprehensive resource and knowledgebase for proteomic data at the single-cell resolution." It is not tied to any specific foundation model in the catalog; instead, it functions as shared community infrastructure — a curated aggregation of single-cell proteomics data that any future proteomic or RNA+protein multimodal model (such as co-assayed RNA+protein approaches like CAPTAIN) could draw from. For developers, treat SPDB as a **discovery layer** rather than a ready-made training corpus: you assemble the pretraining set from it, rather than downloading a fixed corpus artifact.

> [!TIP]
> When evaluating whether a new multimodal corpus belongs on your reading list, classify it first as **model-bound** (fixed artifact, exact reproducibility) or **knowledgebase** (queryable aggregation, assembly required). The catalog's four entries cleanly illustrate both categories.

Sources: [README.md](README.md#L355), [README.md](README.md#L196)

## Structural Pattern: The Scale–Pairing Trade-off
A quantifiable pattern emerges across the four entries: the only corpus built on **paired measurements** is the smallest by roughly two orders of magnitude, while the spatial corpora — unpaired, single-omic-per-spot data — reach 88M–110M scale. This is verifiable directly from the documented figures (2.7M vs. 88M vs. 110M) and reflects a real experimental constraint: jointly assaying RNA and ATAC in the same cell is technically expensive, whereas spatial transcriptomics platforms generate data at industrial scale. The practical consequence for developers planning multimodal pretraining is a fork in the road:

| Strategy | Example Corpus | Scale Achievable | Information Gained |
|---|---|---|---|
| Paired co-assay pretraining | SCARF / X-Omics | 2.7M cells | Within-cell RNA↔ATAC coupling |
| Large-scale single-omic spatial pretraining | SpatialCorpus-110M, SToCorpus-88M | 88M–110M cells | Tissue context at massive scale |

Sources: [README.md](README.md#L352-L354)

## Suggested Reading Progression
To contextualize this page within the Deep Dive track, we recommend this progression. Start with the **taxonomy** to see where multimodal corpora fit in the model design landscape; then study the **consumer models** that these corpora train; return here with that context; and finish with the **frameworks** page to learn how such corpora are loaded and processed at scale:

1. [Taxonomy of Single-Cell Foundation Models](4-taxonomy-of-single-cell-foundation-models) — the classification framework this catalog follows
2. [Multimodal and Spatial Models](7-multimodal-and-spatial-models) — the model-side counterpart of every corpus documented here
3. [Transcriptomic Atlases and Repositories](14-transcriptomic-atlases-and-repositories) — the single-omic predecessor: where massive RNA-only pretraining data lives
4. [Analysis Frameworks and Data Formats](16-analysis-frameworks-and-data-formats) — the engineering layer: AnnData, scDataset, and the tooling that ingests these corpora


# Analysis Frameworks and Data Formats


This page maps the **"Data formats and frameworks"** subsection of the curated list *Awesome Foundation Models for Single-Cell*. It collects **seven entries (2018–2026)** that form the software substrate of single-cell foundation models: the file formats that store cell data, the analysis frameworks that manipulate it, and the emerging tooling that makes atlas-scale computation possible. If you are new to this field, treat this page as your **tooling orientation layer** — every foundation model paper you read elsewhere in this catalog assumes fluency with what is documented here.

Sources: [README.md](README.md#L357-L364), [README.md](README.md#L39-L70)

## Where This Page Sits in the Catalog
The repository organizes its data resources under a parent section, *Pretraining Datasets and Resources*, which is explicitly described as covering "large-scale atlases, multimodal corpora, and data frameworks used for pretraining and preprocessing single-cell foundation models." This three-part structure mirrors an actual data pipeline: raw sequencing data flows into curated **atlases** (covered in [Transcriptomic Atlases and Repositories](14-transcriptomic-atlases-and-repositories)), gets packaged into **pretraining corpora** (covered in [Multimodal Pretraining Corpora](15-multimodal-pretraining-corpora)), and is ultimately handled by the **formats and frameworks** on this page. Foundation models never consume raw sequencing output directly — they consume matrices shaped, cleaned, and loaded by the tools listed here, which is exactly why this section exists as the final step of the data foundation.

```mermaid
flowchart TD
    RAW["Raw sequencing archives<br/>GEO · SRA"] --> ATL["Atlases and repositories<br/>Page 14: Transcriptomic Atlases"]
    ATL --> COR["Pretraining corpora<br/>Page 15: Multimodal Corpora"]
    COR --> DF["Data formats and frameworks<br/>THIS PAGE"]
    DF --> ANN["Format layer:<br/>AnnData"]
    DF --> PY["Python frameworks:<br/>Scanpy · scvi-tools · Pertpy"]
    DF --> RLANG["R framework:<br/>Seurat"]
    DF --> SCALE["Atlas-scale tooling:<br/>scDataset · scAtlasPy · scAtlasTb"]
    ANN --> PY
    PY --> FM["Single-cell foundation models:<br/>pretraining and inference"]
    RLANG --> FM
    SCALE --> FM
```

Sources: [README.md](README.md#L332-L334), [README.md](README.md#L336-L355)

## The Core Stack: AnnData, Scanpy, and Seurat
The two oldest entries in this section are also the most fundamental. **Scanpy / AnnData** (2018, *Genome Biology*) is cataloged as enabling "large-scale single-cell gene expression data analysis," and **Seurat** (2019, *Cell*) as providing "comprehensive integration of single-cell data." Conceptually, both revolve around a data object that pairs a **gene-expression count matrix** (genes × cells) with rich **annotations** — cell metadata, gene metadata, and derived results like embeddings and clusters. AnnData is the Python-side format; Seurat defines its own object in R. For a beginner, the practical takeaway from this catalog's structure is clear: the Python ecosystem (Scanpy → scvi-tools → Pertpy) chains together around AnnData, while Seurat is the dominant choice in R-centric interactive analysis workflows.

| Dimension | Scanpy / AnnData | Seurat |
|---|---|---|
| Language | Python | R |
| Catalog entry | 2018, *Genome Biology* | 2019, *Cell* |
| Data object | AnnData | Seurat object |
| Typical role | Programmatic pipelines, foundation-model workflows | Interactive analysis and exploration |
| Beginner guidance | **Start here** — this is the field's default stack | Read if your lab is R-based |

> [!TIP]
> Learn the AnnData object model once, and most of this catalog unlocks: the Python-side frameworks here (scvi-tools, Pertpy) and even the terabyte-scale training tooling cataloged on the infrastructure page are built around the same data object, so format fluency transfers directly to model work.

Sources: [README.md](README.md#L363-L364)

## Probabilistic Modeling with scvi-tools
The **scvi-tools** entry (2022, *Nature Biotechnology*) is described in the catalog as "a Python library for probabilistic analysis of single-cell omics data." For beginners, this entry marks the conceptual bridge between *analysis* and *foundation models*: scvi-tools packages probabilistic deep-learning models for single-cell data in a form researchers can actually train and apply. It is the framework where the data formats above meet trainable neural models — the same pattern later scaled up by the foundation models cataloged in the model-landscape pages. The catalog also shows this ecosystem maturing into infrastructure: **scvi-hub**, an actionable repository for model-driven single-cell analysis, is cataloged separately under infrastructure work, which makes it a natural follow-up destination.

Sources: [README.md](README.md#L362), [README.md](README.md#L451)

## Perturbation Analysis with Pertpy
**Pertpy** (2025, *Nature Methods*) is the task-specific entry: an "end-to-end framework for perturbation analysis." Perturbation analysis asks how cells respond when genes are disrupted — the same problem addressed by the dedicated models, atlases, and benchmarks cataloged in the perturbation cluster of this repository. Pertpy's inclusion here is architecturally meaningful: it shows the data-frameworks layer growing task-specific tooling that operates on the same data objects as the rest of the stack. Read this entry in parallel with the modeling-side pages rather than in isolation, because the framework and the models solve the same problem from complementary directions.

Sources: [README.md](README.md#L361)

## The 2026 Frontier: Atlas-Scale Data Engineering
The three newest entries share a single theme: **the in-memory ceiling**. Classic frameworks assume your dataset fits in RAM; modern pretraining corpora cataloged in this repository reach tens of millions of cells, and that assumption breaks. The catalog reflects this with:

- **scDataset** (2026, ICML) — "Scalable Data Loading for Deep Learning on Large-Scale Single-Cell Omics": solves the loading problem for model training itself.
- **scAtlasPy** (2026, bioRxiv) — "Atlas-scale single-cell analysis beyond in-memory paradigm": moves whole-atlas analysis out of RAM.
- **scAtlasTb** (2026, bioRxiv) — "Building optimized single-cell reference atlases": optimizes how reference atlases are constructed and stored in the first place.

| Tool | Year · Venue | Problem attacked | Pipeline stage |
|---|---|---|---|
| scAtlasTb | 2026 · bioRxiv | Optimizing reference atlas construction | Storage / preparation |
| scAtlasPy | 2026 · bioRxiv | Analysis beyond in-memory limits | Analysis |
| scDataset | 2026 · ICML | Scalable loading for deep learning | Training input |

> [!TIP]
> Watch the years, not just the names: all three 2026 entries in this section cluster on scale-out problems, and the infrastructure page independently catalogs sibling efforts like AnnData streaming and GPU-accelerated analysis. Memory and scale are where the field currently feels pain — a strong signal for where beginner skills will pay off.

Sources: [README.md](README.md#L358-L360), [README.md](README.md#L448-L450)

## The Seven Entries at a Glance
The table below lists every entry in this section in the repository's own order (newest first), with a beginner-oriented reading priority derived from the architectural layering above.

| Entry (as cataloged) | Year · Venue | Layer | Beginner priority |
|---|---|---|---|
| scAtlasPy: Atlas-scale single-cell analysis beyond in-memory paradigm | 2026 · bioRxiv | Atlas-scale analysis | Advanced — after Scanpy fluency |
| Building optimized single-cell reference atlases with scAtlasTb | 2026 · bioRxiv | Atlas storage/preparation | Advanced |
| scDataset: Scalable Data Loading for Deep Learning on Large-Scale Single-Cell Omics | 2026 · ICML | Training data loading | Intermediate — needed before training |
| Pertpy: an end-to-end framework for perturbation analysis | 2025 · Nature Methods | Task framework | Intermediate — pair with perturbation pages |
| scvi-tools: a Python library for probabilistic analysis of single-cell omics data | 2022 · Nature Biotechnology | Probabilistic modeling | Core — second stop |
| Seurat: Comprehensive integration of single-cell data | 2019 · Cell | Analysis framework (R) | Core for R users |
| Scanpy / AnnData: large-scale single-cell gene expression data analysis | 2018 · Genome Biology | Core stack + format | **First** |

Sources: [README.md](README.md#L357-L364)

## Your Reading Path
For a developer starting from zero, the catalog supports a clean progression. Begin with orientation pages, then walk the Data Foundations trio in pipeline order, and only then branch into the application areas this tooling serves:

```mermaid
flowchart LR
    START["Overview<br/>page 1-overview"] --> TAX["Taxonomy of Models<br/>page 4-taxonomy"]
    TAX --> P14["Transcriptomic Atlases<br/>page 14"]
    P14 --> P15["Multimodal Corpora<br/>page 15"]
    P15 --> HERE["Analysis Frameworks and Data Formats<br/>page 16 — you are here"]
    HERE --> P9["Perturbation Prediction<br/>page 9"]
    HERE --> P17["Benchmarking Studies<br/>page 17"]
    HERE --> P19["Infrastructure and Platforms<br/>page 19"]
```

Concretely: learn **AnnData/Scanpy** first, add **scvi-tools** when you want to train models, pick up **Pertpy** alongside the perturbation cluster, and save the 2026 scale-out tools for when you genuinely hit memory limits. The surrounding catalog then extends each branch: perturbation work continues in [Perturbation Prediction Frameworks](9-perturbation-prediction-frameworks), [Perturbation Atlases and Datasets](10-perturbation-atlases-and-datasets), and [Perturbation Benchmarks](11-perturbation-benchmarks); evaluation practices live in [Benchmarking Studies and Critiques](17-benchmarking-studies-and-critiques); and deployment-facing tooling continues in [Infrastructure and Model Platforms](19-infrastructure-and-model-platforms).

Sources: [README.md](README.md#L39-L70)

## Where to Go Next
This page closes the Data Foundations trilogy. Your two most valuable immediate moves: first, solidify the sibling context by reading [Transcriptomic Atlases and Repositories](14-transcriptomic-atlases-and-repositories) and [Multimodal Pretraining Corpora](15-multimodal-pretraining-corpora) — the data these frameworks operate on; second, follow the tooling forward into [Infrastructure and Model Platforms](19-infrastructure-and-model-platforms), where the format and scale work documented here continues at deployment scale. If your destination is model-building itself, proceed to the model landscape starting with [Unimodal scRNA-seq Models](5-unimodal-scrna-seq-models).

# Benchmarking Studies and Critiques



This page maps the **trust layer** of the single-cell foundation-model ecosystem: the benchmark suites, task-specific evaluations, metric audits, and skeptical critiques curated in the repository's *Benchmarks and critical evaluations* subsection. The list positions itself explicitly as "the science of evaluation" alongside the models themselves — a deliberate counterweight to the model landscape documented in [Unimodal scRNA-seq Models](5-unimodal-scrna-seq-models), [Multimodal and Spatial Models](7-multimodal-and-spatial-models), and [LLM-Based Cell Models](8-llm-based-cell-models). Boundary discipline matters here: perturbation-specific benchmarks are cataloged separately under [Perturbation Benchmarks](11-perturbation-benchmarks), and privacy-preserving techniques belong to [Privacy-Preserving Approaches](18-privacy-preserving-approaches), so this page covers only general-purpose evaluation of single-cell foundation models.

Sources: [README.md](README.md#L366-L368), [README.md](README.md#L370-L429)

## Scope and Position in the Catalog

The repository organizes evaluation content under a single top-level section — *Benchmarks and Evaluation* — whose stated scope is "benchmarks, reusability reports, and critical evaluations of single-cell foundation models, plus the science of evaluation and data-privacy considerations." That section splits into two subsections: **Benchmarks and critical evaluations** (59 entries, lines 370–429), which is the subject of this page, and **Data privacy and accessibility** (4 entries), which maps to the neighboring page on privacy-preserving approaches. The section-level framing matters for navigation: evaluation is treated as a first-class discipline in this catalog, not an appendix to the model pages.

Sources: [README.md](README.md#L366-L368), [README.md](README.md#L431-L435)

## The Evaluation Landscape at a Glance

The growth trajectory of this subsection is itself a finding. Entries cluster by publication year as 4 (2023) → 8 (2024) → 21 (2025) → 26 (2026), meaning nearly 80% of the evaluation literature in this list appeared within the last two years — evaluation science is the fastest-compounding segment of the catalog. Publication venues reinforce this signal: the section concentrates heavily in *Nature Methods* (benchmarking biomedical foundation models; scaling studies; multitask integration benchmarking), *Nature Biotechnology* (metric critiques; open-problem benchmarking), *Nature Communications*, *Genome Biology*, and *Nature Machine Intelligence*, with peer-reviewed ML-venue entries at NeurIPS, ICLR, KDD, AAAI, and WSDM. The pattern is consistent: the field's flagship methods journals have become the primary venue for auditing the field's flagship models.

| Year | Entries | Share of section | Character of the entries |
|---|---|---|---|
| 2023 | 4 | ~7% | First-wave audits: reusability reports, deep dives, early LLM evaluations |
| 2024 | 8 | ~14% | Standardized harnesses (BioLLM, scEval), first scaling studies, metric critiques begin |
| 2025 | 21 | ~36% | Metric science matures; task benchmarks proliferate; LLM-facing evaluation arrives |
| 2026 | 26 | ~44% | Dedicated suites (VCBench, SCMBench), scaling-law interrogations, negative results |

Sources: [README.md](README.md#L370-L429)

Conceptually, the 59 entries decompose into a **four-layer evaluation stack**, where each layer answers a different question about the same underlying claim — that foundation-model pretraining transfers to downstream single-cell biology:

```mermaid
flowchart TB
    FM["Single-cell foundation models<br/>catalog pages 5-8"]
    FM --> Q{"Does pretraining transfer<br/>to downstream biology?"}
    Q --> L1["Layer 1: Benchmark suites<br/>multi-task controlled comparisons"]
    Q --> L2["Layer 2: Task benchmarks<br/>one capability measured deeply"]
    Q --> L3["Layer 3: Metric science<br/>audit of the instruments themselves"]
    Q --> L4["Layer 4: Critiques and scaling studies<br/>stress-test of core premises"]
    L1 --> O["Context-dependent verdicts:<br/>utility varies by task and setting"]
    L2 --> O
    L3 --> O
    L4 --> O
    O --> N["Next-generation evaluation:<br/>unsupervised, OOD-aware, in-the-wild"]
```

Sources: [README.md](README.md#L370-L429)

## Layer 1: Benchmark Suites

The suite layer provides controlled, multi-task comparison harnesses. The most recent entries are purpose-built for foundation models: **VCBench** positions itself as a multi-dimensional benchmark for single-cell foundation models, **SCMBench** pits domain-specific models against foundation models specifically for multi-omics integration, and **CellBench-LS** targets the low-supervision regime that most realistic deployments inhabit. Framework-level entries — **BioLLM** (Patterns 2024) and **BMFM-RNA** (2025) — go further, offering standardized infrastructure for *building and* benchmarking transcriptomic models, which collapses the traditional separation between model development and evaluation tooling.

| Suite | Venue | Coverage focus | Distinctive angle |
|---|---|---|---|
| VCBench | bioRxiv 2026 | Single-cell foundation models | Multi-dimensional evaluation |
| SCMBench | Nature Communications 2026 | Multi-omics integration | Domain-specific vs. foundation models |
| scTranslation | KDD 2026 | Cross-modality translation | Comprehensive modality-translation benchmark |
| CellBench-LS | bioRxiv 2026 | Low-supervision scenarios | Label-scarce evaluation regime |
| BioLLM | Patterns 2024 | scFMs broadly | Standardized integration + benchmarking framework |
| BMFM-RNA | arXiv 2025 | Transcriptomic FMs | Open framework for building and evaluating |
| scEval | Advanced Science 2024 | LLMs in sc-analysis | LLM utility assessment |
| Multitask integration benchmark | Nature Methods 2025 | Multimodal omics integration | Multi-task protocol |

Sources: [README.md](README.md#L371-L396), [README.md](README.md#L409-L423)

## Layer 2: Task-Specific Benchmarks

Where suites trade depth for breadth, task benchmarks do the reverse: each entry interrogates one capability with domain-appropriate protocols. The cell-type-annotation thread is the densest, spanning a WSDM systematic evaluation of foundation models on classification, **scTab**'s cross-tissue scaling study, a hierarchical cross-entropy loss study for atlas-scale annotation, and an early investigation of foundation models on imbalanced cell-type data. Clinical translation is measured by **scDrugMap** (drug response prediction), an empirical evaluation for cancer outcome prediction, and a study showing foundation models predict durable CAR T response despite imperfect cell annotation — the latter being evidence that imperfect preprocessing tolerances matter more than leaderboard deltas in deployment.

| Capability under test | Representative entries |
|---|---|
| Cell-type classification/annotation | WSDM 2025 systematic evaluation; scTab (Nat Commun 2024); hierarchical cross-entropy (Nat Comput Sci 2026); imbalanced-data study (2023) |
| Clustering | scCluBench (AAAI 2026) |
| Multimodal integration | SCMBench (2026); multitask benchmarking (Nat Methods 2025) |
| Modality translation | scTranslation (KDD 2026) |
| Drug response / clinical endpoints | scDrugMap (Nat Commun 2025); cancer outcomes (2025); CAR T response (2026) |
| GRN inference | GeneRNIB living benchmark (2025) |
| Gene embeddings and function | Sequence/expression/network/text embedding comparison (2025); LLM gene-set function (2023); gene-importance scoring (Nat Biotechnol 2026) |
| Spatial transfer | STP-BENCH (2026); multi-scale spatial variation (2026); cross-modality reusability report (NMI 2025) |
| Dynamics and reconstruction | Zero-shot dynamics reconstruction (2026); latent-to-expression reconstruction (2026) |
| DNA language models | BEND (ICLR 2024) |
| LLM biological understanding | CellVerse (NeurIPS 2025); AnnDictionary (Nat Commun 2025); scEval (2024) |
| Virtual-cell perturbation response | In-the-wild perturbation benchmarking (2026) — adjacent to [Perturbation Benchmarks](11-perturbation-benchmarks) |

Sources: [README.md](README.md#L373-L429)

> [!TIP]
> When benchmarking your own model, reserve perturbation-response evaluation questions for the dedicated frameworks cataloged in [Perturbation Benchmarks](11-perturbation-benchmarks) (e.g., PerturBench, PertEval-scFM) — this page's general-purpose suites (VCBench, SCMBench) deliberately exclude that axis to avoid double-counting and metric entanglement.

## Layer 3: Metric Science — Auditing the Instruments

The most intellectually distinctive thread in this section does not evaluate models at all — it evaluates the *rulers*. Three 2024–2025 entries converge on the same conclusion from different angles: "Metric Mirages in Cell Embeddings," "Shortcomings of silhouette in single-cell integration benchmarking" (Nature Biotechnology), and "Limitations of cell embedding metrics assessed using drifting islands" (Nature Biotechnology). Collectively they establish that the standard quantitative vocabulary of integration and embedding quality — silhouette scores, embedding-space separation heuristics — can diverge from biological reality. A 2026 entry extends this line constructively: robustness to *nuisance perturbations* enables **unsupervised evaluation**, sidestepping annotation-dependence entirely. For benchmark designers, this layer is a prerequisite reading list; for benchmark consumers, it explains why rankings frequently disagree.

```mermaid
flowchart LR
    A["Critique surfaces an instrument flaw<br/>e.g. metric mirages"]
    B["Instrument redesigned<br/>e.g. drifting-islands probe"]
    C["Re-benchmarking revises conclusions<br/>e.g. parameter-free baselines win"]
    D["Methods adapt<br/>e.g. OOD-aware representations"]
    A --> B --> C --> D --> A
```

Sources: [README.md](README.md#L398-L399), [README.md](README.md#L378), [README.md](README.md#L424)

## Layer 4: Critiques — Stress-Testing Core Premises

The critique layer is where the catalog earns its credibility. The entries read as a systematic adversarial audit of the field's founding claims, and their verdicts — legible directly from the titles — are frequently negative:

| Premise under test | Published verdict | Entry |
|---|---|---|
| Pretraining beats trivial baselines | "Parameter-free representations outperform single-cell foundation models on downstream benchmarks" | 2026 arXiv |
| Attention maps encode regulation | "Attention-derived edge scores add no incremental value over gene-level features" | BMC Genomics 2026 |
| Sparse autoencoders uncover regulatory logic | "Organized biological knowledge but minimal regulatory logic" | 2026 arXiv |
| More pretraining data → proportionally better models | "Much pain with little gain" (Nat Methods 2026); "When do scaling laws hold?" | 2026 |
| Zero-shot transfer is reliable | "Zero-shot evaluation reveals limitations" | Genome Biology 2025 |
| Universal embeddings are within reach | "Batch effects remain a fundamental barrier" | 2025 |
| Embeddings are uniformly stable | "Glitch genes: embedding geometry predicts functional fragility" | 2026 |
| Deployment claims survive practice | "Accessible and reproducible deployment reveals the practical boundaries" | 2026 |
| The premise itself is sound | "Fundamental Limitations of Foundation Models in Single-Cell Transcriptomics" | 2025 |

The lineage matters for calibration: the audit began early and repeatedly. The 2023 *reusability report* on transformers learning "transcriptional grammar" and the contemporaneous "Deep Dive into Single-Cell RNA Sequencing Foundation Models" established the skeptical genre before the 2024 "Deeper evaluation of a single-cell foundation model" (Nature Machine Intelligence) formalized single-model forensic evaluation. The 2026 entries then close the loop at scale — not one model, but the paradigm, under test.

Sources: [README.md](README.md#L371-L396), [README.md](README.md#L397-L429)

> [!TIP]
> The single most consequential methodological insight from this layer for practitioners: always baseline against parameter-free representations (PCA-family) before crediting pretraining for downstream gains — the 2026 literature demonstrates this control is not optional if you intend your benchmark to survive review.

## Scaling Science: Data, Diversity, and Ablation Infrastructure

A dedicated sub-cluster interrogates the scaling premise quantitatively. The dataset-size question appears twice with a visible preprint-to-journal arc: a 2024 bioRxiv preprint, "Evaluating the role of pre-training dataset size and diversity on single-cell foundation model performance," and a 2026 Nature Methods publication of near-identical title — the three-year gap suggests the question resisted easy resolution. The verdicts that did land are bracing: scaling up training dataset size yields "much pain with little gain" (Nature Methods 2026), and the companion preprint asks directly "when do scaling laws hold?" — implying the answer is conditional. Complementing data-scaling are architecture-level ablation studies: HEIMDALL provides a modular framework for tokenization ablation, "Delineating the effective use of self-supervised learning in single-cell genomics" (Nature Machine Intelligence 2024) maps which SSL objectives actually pay off, and "Biology-driven insights into the power of single-cell foundation models" (Genome Biology 2025) grounds capability claims in biological rather than proxy metrics.

Sources: [README.md](README.md#L383-L385), [README.md](README.md#L402-L411), [README.md](README.md#L419-L421)

## Robustness, Distribution Shift, and Deployment Realism

The final evaluative axis asks whether published gains survive contact with messy data. The findings here form a coherent threat model: batch effects persist as a "fundamental barrier to universal embeddings" (2025); embedding geometry contains predictable "glitch genes" marking functional fragility (2026); utility is "context-dependent" across analytical tasks (2026); and real-world RNA-seq integration stresses models beyond curated benchmark conditions (2026). Countermeasures appear alongside the threats — USHER guides representations through distribution shifts, and nuisance-perturbation robustness doubles as an unsupervised evaluation signal. The through-line: **robustness measurement is becoming both a diagnostic and a training objective** in this literature.

Sources: [README.md](README.md#L378-L381), [README.md](README.md#L389-L392), [README.md](README.md#L401-L406)

## Interpretability as Evaluation

Two 2025–2026 sparse-autoencoder studies treat mechanistic interpretability as an evaluation instrument: the 2025 entry reports SAEs "reveal interpretable features," while the 2026 follow-up delivers the sharper verdict that models encode "organized biological knowledge but minimal regulatory logic." Combined with the attention-edge-score critique (BMC Genomics 2026) and gene-importance scoring via foundation-model interpretation (Nature Biotechnology 2026), this cluster establishes a pattern: **what a model can explain is now a benchmarked property**, separable from what it can predict.

Sources: [README.md](README.md#L375-L386), [README.md](README.md#L394-L405)

## Meta-Benchmarking and Open Problems

The section closes its loop with entries that benchmark the benchmarking enterprise itself: "Defining and benchmarking open problems in single-cell analysis" (Nature Biotechnology 2025) and "The current landscape and emerging challenges of benchmarking single-cell methods" (Briefings in Bioinformatics 2025) provide field-level roadmap documents, while "Benchmarking biomedical foundation models" (Nature Methods 2026) situates single-cell evaluation within the broader biomedical-AI evaluation discipline. These are the natural entry points for researchers designing new protocols rather than consuming existing ones.

Sources: [README.md](README.md#L371), [README.md](README.md#L397), [README.md](README.md#L416-L417)

## Suggested Reading Pathways

For advanced readers, the evidence supports three targeted progressions through the catalog. **The evaluator's path**: [Taxonomy of Single-Cell Foundation Models](4-taxonomy-of-single-cell-foundation-models) → this page's metric-science and critique layers → [Surveys and Open Challenges](21-surveys-and-open-challenges) for field-level framing. **The builder's path**: model pages ([Unimodal scRNA-seq Models](5-unimodal-scrna-seq-models), [Multimodal and Spatial Models](7-multimodal-and-spatial-models)) → scaling-science entries here → [Infrastructure and Model Platforms](19-infrastructure-and-model-platforms) for deployment tooling. **The trust-and-governance path**: this page → [Privacy-Preserving Approaches](18-privacy-preserving-approaches) → the virtual-cell accountability literature in [Virtual Cell Perspectives and Roadmaps](12-virtual-cell-perspectives-and-roadmaps), which inherits this page's evaluation vocabulary at system scale.


# Privacy-Preserving Approaches



This page curates the repository's **"Data privacy and accessibility"** records — the trust-oriented counterpart to the model-centric catalog. It contains exactly four cataloged entries that form a complete narrative arc: an empirical threat characterization (identity leakage from count matrices), two federated defenses positioned at different stages of the single-cell pipeline, and a strategic governance horizon for medical-scale foundation models. The section sits inside the *Evaluation and Trust* cluster of the review's taxonomy, meaning privacy is treated here as an **evaluation axis** rather than a model design family — a deliberate architectural choice that shapes how you should read the papers.
Sources: [README.md](README.md#L10-L12), [README.md](README.md#L366-L368)

## Position in the Catalog's Trust Architecture

The section header makes the placement explicit: the parent *Benchmarks and Evaluation* section declares its scope as "Benchmarks, reusability reports, and critical evaluations of single-cell foundation models, plus the science of evaluation and **data-privacy considerations**." Privacy therefore arrives *after* the benchmarking critiques ([Benchmarking Studies and Critiques](17-benchmarking-studies-and-critiques)) and *before* deployment infrastructure ([Infrastructure and Model Platforms](19-infrastructure-and-model-platforms)) — the catalog encodes the sequence "measure the threat → trust the data → build the platform." Sources: [README.md](README.md#L366-L368), [README.md](README.md#L63)

```mermaid
flowchart LR
    subgraph ET["Evaluation and Trust cluster"]
        direction LR
        B["Benchmarking Studies<br/>and Critiques"] -->|"threat exposure<br/>becomes visible"| P["Privacy-Preserving<br/>Approaches ★"] -->|"trusted data pipelines<br/>need runtime"| I["Infrastructure and<br/>Model Platforms"]
    end
    style P fill:#e8f0fe,stroke:#1a73e8,stroke-width:2px
```

## The Four-Entry Threat-and-Defense Stack

The cataloged entries are not a flat list; read as a stack, they cover threat, defense, and governance:

| # | Catalog entry | Venue · Year | Role in trust stack |
|---|---|---|---|
| 1 | **Private information leakage from single-cell count matrices** | Cell · 2024 | Threat characterization — why the problem exists |
| 2 | **FedscGen: privacy-preserving federated batch effect correction of single-cell RNA sequencing data** | Genome Biology · 2025 | Defense — preprocessing stage |
| 3 | **CLIFTI-GPT: Privacy-preserving federated fine-tuning and transferable inference of foundation models on clinical single-cell data** | Research Square · 2025 | Defense — training and inference stage |
| 4 | **Foundation models for generalist medical artificial intelligence** | Nature · 2023 | Governance and scale framing |

Sources: [README.md](README.md#L431-L435)

The entry point is the **threat paper**: *Private information leakage from single-cell count matrices* (Cell, 2024) establishes that single-cell expression matrices are not de-identified data in any meaningful sense — the sparse, high-dimensional per-cell profile acts as a quasi-identifier, so the section's premise is that count matrices themselves are the attack surface, not just associated metadata. This reframing is what makes the two federated entries meaningful rather than incidental: if raw matrices can never safely leave an institution, collaboration protocols must be redesigned around *what* is transmitted.
Sources: [README.md](README.md#L434)

```mermaid
flowchart TD
    L["Threat: private information leakage<br/>from single-cell count matrices<br/>(Cell, 2024)"]
    L -->|"motivates defense at<br/>preprocessing"| F1["FedscGen — federated<br/>batch effect correction<br/>(Genome Biology, 2025)"]
    L -->|"motivates defense at<br/>training + inference"| F2["CLIFTI-GPT — federated<br/>fine-tuning and transferable<br/>inference (Research Square, 2025)"]
    F1 -->|"corrected features,<br/>still site-local"| F2
    F2 -->|"clinical-scale,<br/>governed deployment"| G["Governance horizon:<br/>generalist medical AI<br/>(Nature, 2023)"]
    P["Privacy-featured model:<br/>privacy-preserving tabular learning<br/>(arXiv, 2026 — cataloged under models)"]
    P -.complementary track.-> G
    style L fill:#fce8e6,stroke:#d93025
    style F1 fill:#e6f4ea,stroke:#188038
    style F2 fill:#e6f4ea,stroke:#188038
```

Sources: [README.md](README.md#L431-L435)

## Federated Defense: Two Stages, One Trust Boundary

The two federated papers occupy adjacent, composable stages of the pipeline rather than competing alternatives. **FedscGen** federates *batch effect correction* — the preprocessing step every multi-site scRNA-seq analysis requires — meaning the privacy boundary is enforced before any model training begins. **CLIFTI-GPT** federates *fine-tuning and inference* of foundation models on clinical single-cell data, meaning the boundary is enforced at the deployment end, where patient-level clinical data is most sensitive and regulatory exposure is highest. Together they imply a design in which raw count matrices never transit an institutional boundary at any pipeline stage.
Sources: [README.md](README.md#L433), [README.md](README.md#L432)

| Dimension | FedscGen | CLIFTI-GPT |
|---|---|---|
| Pipeline stage | Preprocessing (batch correction) | Fine-tuning + inference |
| Data domain | Single-cell RNA-seq | Clinical single-cell data on foundation models |
| Defining capability | Privacy-preserving correction across sites | Transferable inference without raw-data export |
| Trust boundary position | Upstream of model training | Downstream, at deployment |
| Venue · Year | Genome Biology · 2025 | Research Square · 2025 |

Sources: [README.md](README.md#L433), [README.md](README.md#L432)

> [!TIP]
> The catalog's ordering encodes a pipeline dependency: FedscGen-style federated correction produces harmonized but still site-local features, which are exactly the input regime CLIFTI-GPT-style federated fine-tuning assumes. Treat them as two layers of one federated lifecycle, not as alternative solutions to pick between.

The lifecycle implied by the two entries, with raw matrices confined to each site:

```mermaid
flowchart LR
    subgraph SA["Clinical site A"]
        A1["Local scRNA-seq<br/>count matrix"] --> A2["Federated batch<br/>correction (FedscGen stage)"] --> A3["Local fine-tuning +<br/>inference (CLIFTI-GPT stage)"]
    end
    subgraph SB["Clinical site B"]
        B1["Local scRNA-seq<br/>count matrix"] --> B2["Federated batch<br/>correction (FedscGen stage)"] --> B3["Local fine-tuning +<br/>inference (CLIFTI-GPT stage)"]
    end
    A2 -->|"shared: correction<br/>updates only"| S["Federated<br/>aggregation"]
    B2 -->|"shared: correction<br/>updates only"| S
    A3 -->|"shared: model<br/>updates only"| S
    B3 -->|"shared: model<br/>updates only"| S
    S --> M["Global clinical<br/>foundation model"]
    M -.->|"transferable inference<br/>returned to sites"| A3
    M -.->|"transferable inference<br/>returned to sites"| B3
    style A1 fill:#fce8e6,stroke:#d93025
    style B1 fill:#fce8e6,stroke:#d93025
```

Sources: [README.md](README.md#L432-L433)

## Governance Horizon and Cross-Catalog Signals

The final entry, *Foundation models for generalist medical artificial intelligence* (Nature, 2023), is the strategic anchor: the GMAI vision argues that medical foundation models will only reach clinical generality if governance, privacy-preserving infrastructure, and accessibility are designed in from the start — which is why the catalog files it under privacy rather than under the medical-AI surveys. It converts the preceding threat-plus-defense pairing into a deployment-level mandate, and it is the oldest entry in the section, predating both federated implementations.
Sources: [README.md](README.md#L435), [README.md](README.md#L431-L435)

One further privacy signal lives outside this section by design: **"Predictive single cell foundation model for gene regulation and aging with privacy-preserving tabular learning"** (arXiv, 2026) is cataloged under the scRNA-seq model families, because its primary contribution is model architecture with privacy as a training constraint rather than privacy as the object of study. Consult it via [Unimodal scRNA-seq Models](5-unimodal-scrna-seq-models) when you need the model-design perspective; the data-accessibility dimension of privacy sits with the atlas repositories in [Transcriptomic Atlases and Repositories](14-transcriptomic-atlases-and-repositories).
Sources: [README.md](README.md#L84), [README.md](README.md#L336-L349)

> [!TIP]
> When contributing new entries, respect this filing logic: papers whose contribution is a privacy *mechanism* (federated protocols, leakage analyses, governance frameworks) belong in this section; papers that merely *use* privacy-preserving training among other contributions belong under their model family. The section stays small and high-signal precisely because of this boundary.

## Recommended Reading Path and Navigation

For an advanced reader, the section rewards reading in threat-first order: start with the Cell 2024 leakage paper to internalize why count matrices are quasi-identifiers, then read FedscGen to see the preprocessing-stage defense, then CLIFTI-GPT for the training/inference-stage defense on clinical data, and close with the Nature 2023 GMAI paper to see how the pieces compose into a governance argument.
Sources: [README.md](README.md#L431-L435)

To continue through the catalog, move **backward** to the sibling critiques in [Benchmarking Studies and Critiques](17-benchmarking-studies-and-critiques) if your concern is evaluation reliability, or **forward** to [Infrastructure and Model Platforms](19-infrastructure-and-model-platforms) to see where privacy-preserving pipelines would physically run. For orientation on the full model landscape this trust cluster evaluates, return to the [Overview](1-overview) and the [Taxonomy of Single-Cell Foundation Models](4-taxonomy-of-single-cell-foundation-models).
Sources: [README.md](README.md#L39-L70)

# Infrastructure and Model Platforms



This page covers the systems layer of the single-cell foundation model (scFM) ecosystem: the platforms, model repositories, and scalable infrastructure that turn pretrained cell models from research artifacts into usable engineering services. It maps directly to the **"Infrastructure and platforms"** subsection of the curated reading list, within the broader "Infrastructure, Platforms and AI Agents" section. Entries covering AI-agent systems and lab-in-the-loop discovery are deliberately excluded here and treated on the following page.

Sources: [README.md](README.md#L437-L441), [README.md](README.md#L64-L67)

## Scope: Where Infrastructure Sits in the Landscape

The reading list frames this section as covering "platforms, model repositories, and scalable infrastructure for scFMs" — the connective tissue between the model landscape (documented across the catalog's core model pages) and real-world application. While models define *what* can be computed over single-cell data, infrastructure defines *how* it is stored, streamed, accelerated, served, and discovered. The evolutionary tree below situates the model families that this infrastructure ultimately serves.

![Evolutionary tree of single-cell foundation models](https://github.com/OmicsML/awesome-foundation-model-single-cell-papers/blob/main/figs/evo_tree.png?raw=true)

Sources: [README.md](README.md#L437-L439), [README.md](README.md#L11-L24)

## The Layered Architecture of the scFM Infrastructure Stack

Across its thirteen entries, the section exhibits a consistent layered pattern recognizable to anyone who has built ML serving systems. At the bottom sits the **corpora layer** (the Human Cell Atlas and the Arc Virtual Cell Atlas with its 2.5B transcriptional profiles). Above it, a **data serving layer** handles quality control, annotation aggregation, terabyte-scale batching, and querying. A **compute layer** provides GPU acceleration and token-budget efficiency. Finally, a **model delivery layer** exposes models through hubs, browsers, and unified inference interfaces, with a standalone **registry layer** for tool discovery. The diagram below traces this dependency flow.

```mermaid
flowchart TD
    A["Corpora Layer<br/>Human Cell Atlas · Arc Virtual Cell Atlas (2.5B profiles)"]
    B["Data Serving<br/>cellNexus · annbatch · Lamin queries · batch correction"]
    C["Compute<br/>rapids-singlecell · BioNeMo · AdaGeneBudget"]
    D["Model Delivery<br/>scvi-hub · SaProtHub · scUnify · CytoVerse"]
    E["Registry<br/>Toolome"]
    F["Practitioners<br/>developers · analysts · labs"]
    A --> B --> C --> D --> F
    E -.->|discovery metadata| F
```

> [!TIP]
> Reading this section as a stack rather than a flat list is the key interpretive move: entries like `annbatch` and `cellNexus` are prerequisites for the delivery-layer tools, since hub-served models still need terabyte-scale training data moved through them.

Sources: [README.md](README.md#L441-L454)

## Data Serving: From Billion-Profile Atlases to Training Batches

The data serving entries attack the scale problem from complementary angles. **annbatch** (2026, arXiv) unlocks terabyte-scale training of biological data stored in AnnData — the de facto container format — by turning on-disk corpora into streaming training batches. **cellNexus** (2026, bioRxiv) builds quality control, annotation, aggregation, and analytical layers on top of Human Cell Atlas data, addressing the curation side of scale. The **Lamin blog entry** (2026) demonstrates a query layer over the 2.5B transcriptional profiles of the Arc Virtual Cell Atlas, showing how billion-profile corpora become addressable. Finally, the Nature Computational Science piece on **informed batch correction** (2026) tackles the harmonization problem that any cross-dataset training pipeline must solve before data can be pooled at scale.

| Entry | Venue/Year | Data-Serving Role | Primary Artifact |
|---|---|---|---|
| annbatch | arXiv 2026 | Streaming training batches from AnnData at terabyte scale | Data loader |
| cellNexus | bioRxiv 2026 | QC, annotation, aggregation layers for Human Cell Atlas | Data platform |
| Lamin / Arc VCA queries | Lamin Blog 2026 | Query access to 2.5B transcriptional profiles | Query interface |
| Informed batch correction | Nat. Comput. Sci. 2026 | Principled integration of heterogeneous batches | Methodology |

> [!TIP]
> Note the boundary: `annbatch` is listed here rather than on the data-formats page because its contribution is *training-scale ingestion* of existing AnnData containers, not format definition itself. Keep that distinction in mind when cross-referencing.

Sources: [README.md](README.md#L444-L448), [README.md](README.md#L64-L67)

## Compute Acceleration and Token-Efficient Inference

The compute entries address cost from two directions: hardware-level parallelism and model-level token economics. **rapids-singlecell** (2026, arXiv) provides GPU-accelerated single-cell analysis at scale, moving the standard analysis stack onto device memory. **BioNeMo** (2024, arXiv) contributes a modular, high-performance library for AI model development in drug discovery — the framework-level option when teams need to train rather than merely run models. **AdaGeneBudget** (2026, bioRxiv) operates at a finer granularity: cell-adaptive gene-token allocation makes scFM inference efficient by spending the token budget where each cell's biology demands it, rather than uniformly across the vocabulary. Together these entries form a cost-control toolkit spanning kernel, framework, and tokenization levels.

| Entry | Venue/Year | Acceleration Level | Mechanism |
|---|---|---|---|
| rapids-singlecell | arXiv 2026 | Kernel / analysis stack | GPU acceleration of single-cell operations |
| BioNeMo framework | arXiv 2024 | Training framework | Modular high-performance model development |
| AdaGeneBudget | bioRxiv 2026 | Model input | Cell-adaptive gene-token allocation |

Sources: [README.md](README.md#L442-L453)

## Model Hubs, Browser Access, and Unified Inference

The delivery layer is where the section's democratization thesis becomes concrete, and it splits into four distinct access models. **scvi-hub** (2025, Nature Methods) is an actionable repository for model-driven single-cell analysis — the closest analogue to a Hugging Face-style hub native to the scvi-tools ecosystem. **SaProtHub** (2025, Nature Biotechnology) and **ColabFold** (2022, Nature Methods) are protein-domain entries, but the list includes them as architectural blueprints: SaProtHub democratizes protein language model training, sharing, and collaboration, while ColabFold remains the canonical example of making heavyweight models accessible to all. **CytoVerse** (2026, bioRxiv) removes installation entirely by running single-cell AI foundation models in the browser. **scUnify** (2026, bioRxiv) abstracts away model choice with a unified framework for zero-shot inference of scFMs. **Toolome** (2026) closes the loop as a registry — a directory of AI tools for biology recording license, paper, and release date for each single-cell foundation model.

| Entry | Venue/Year | Access Model | What the User Gets |
|---|---|---|---|
| scvi-hub | Nat. Methods 2025 | Model repository | Downloadable, model-driven analysis |
| SaProtHub | Nat. Biotechnol. 2025 | Collaborative hub | Shared protein LM training/fine-tuning |
| ColabFold | Nat. Methods 2022 | Notebook service | Zero-setup protein folding |
| CytoVerse | bioRxiv 2026 | Browser runtime | In-browser scFM inference |
| scUnify | bioRxiv 2026 | Unified inference API | Zero-shot inference across scFMs |
| Toolome | Website 2026 | Directory/registry | License, paper, release metadata per model |

Sources: [README.md](README.md#L442-L454)

## Positioning Within This Catalog

This page is the fourth subsection within the ecosystem cluster of the deep-dive catalog, sitting between the evaluation-and-trust pages and the agentic systems that build on top of this infrastructure. The natural reading path starts upstream: the [Analysis Frameworks and Data Formats](16-analysis-frameworks-and-data-formats) page defines the containers (like AnnData) that the serving layer here streams, and the core model pages — [Unimodal scRNA-seq Models](5-unimodal-scrna-seq-models), [Single-Cell ATAC-seq Models](6-single-cell-atac-seq-models), [Multimodal and Spatial Models](7-multimodal-and-spatial-models), and [LLM-Based Cell Models](8-llm-based-cell-models) — define the artifacts this delivery layer serves. Downstream, [AI Agents for Discovery](20-ai-agents-for-discovery) covers the agentic systems that consume this infrastructure to automate analysis, and [Surveys and Open Challenges](21-surveys-and-open-challenges) zooms back out to the field-level perspective. If your concern is whether these platforms can be trusted at scale, pair this page with [Benchmarking Studies and Critiques](17-benchmarking-studies-and-critiques); if governance of shared clinical data matters to you, [Privacy-Preserving Approaches](18-privacy-preserving-approaches) is the companion read.


# AI Agents for Discovery



This page documents the agentic-AI layer of the single-cell foundation model ecosystem as cataloged by the OmicsML reading list. The repository is a curated, continuously updated collection of foundation-model research for single-cell genomics, structured as a single `README.md` with anchor-based navigation. The "AI Agents for Discovery" scope covers two README subsections — *AI agents for single-cell discovery* (16 entries) and *Lab-in-the-loop and active discovery* (2 entries) — targeting advanced developers who build agent orchestration on top of single-cell analysis stacks.

Sources: [README.md](README.md#L10-L16), [README.md](README.md#L64-L67)

## Position in the Catalog and Ecosystem

The page sits in the **Ecosystem and Applications** block of the catalog, immediately after [Infrastructure and Model Platforms](19-infrastructure-and-model-platforms) and before [Surveys and Open Challenges](21-surveys-and-open-challenges). In the README, both live inside the parent section *Infrastructure, Platforms and AI Agents*, which groups three subsections: infrastructure platforms (owned by page 19), the AI-agent catalog, and lab-in-the-loop discovery. This placement is architecturally meaningful: agents are positioned as the orchestration tier *above* the infrastructure and platform tier, consuming tools and data rather than providing them.

Sources: [README.md](README.md#L437-L454), [README.md](README.md#L64-L67)

The architecture below reconstructs the dependency graph implied by the catalog's grouping. Every named system and role is taken verifiably from entry titles: analysis agents orchestrate the analysis frameworks cataloged on page 16, annotation teams delegate the cell-labeling task, and the lab-in-the-loop subsection closes the cycle back to physical experiments.

```mermaid
flowchart TB
    Q["Research question<br/>from the human scientist"]

    subgraph AG["Agentic layer — this page"]
        direction TB
        GEN["General-purpose science agents<br/>autonomous research · expert-level code · team science"]
        ANA["Single-cell analysis agents<br/>CellAgent · scPilot · CellVoyager · CellAtria · ELISA"]
        FRAME["Multi-agent automation frameworks<br/>ToolsGenie 2.0 · PantheonOS"]
        ANNOT["Annotation agent teams<br/>CASSIA · CyteType · CellTypeAgent"]
    end

    subgraph SUB["Execution substrate — catalog context"]
        direction TB
        TOOLS["Analysis frameworks & data formats<br/>catalog page 16"]
        INFRA["Infrastructure & platforms<br/>catalog page 19"]
    end

    LAB["Wet-lab experiments<br/>perturbation screens & assays"]

    Q -->|"natural-language brief"| ANA
    GEN -.->|"decompose into verifiable subtasks"| ANA
    ANA -->|"orchestrate"| TOOLS
    ANA -->|"delegate annotation"| ANNOT
    FRAME -.->|"auto-generate pipelines"| TOOLS
    TOOLS --> INFRA
    ANA -->|"candidate findings & experiment proposals"| LAB
    LAB -->|"new datasets"| INFRA
```

A practical note for contributors: all content for this page lives under two README anchors, `ai-agents-for-single-cell-discovery` and `lab-in-the-loop-and-active-discovery`, both registered in the top-of-file catalog block, so pull requests adding new agent papers should update the entry list and keep the catalog block synchronized.

Sources: [README.md](README.md#L64-L67), [README.md](README.md#L456-L476)

## Functional Taxonomy of the Cataloged Agents

The 16 agent entries cluster cleanly by capability, using only what the entry titles state. This clustering is the fastest way for a developer to locate an architectural reference: the clusters differ in **unit of autonomy** (a single analysis session vs. a full research program), in **interaction mode** (natural language vs. programmatic pipelines), and in **verification surface** (annotation labels vs. open-ended findings).

Sources: [README.md](README.md#L456-L472)

| Cluster | Entries | Cataloged systems | Primary capability |
|---|---|---|---|
| General-purpose autonomous science | 5 | Autonomous biomedical research agent; expert-level empirical-software system; well-scoped verifiable agentic systems; Agentic Laboratories of the Future; in-silico team science | End-to-end research execution beyond single-cell-specific tasks |
| Single-cell analysis agents | 5 | CellAgent, scPilot, CellVoyager, CellAtria, ELISA | Natural-language-driven analysis, autonomous insight generation, data ingestion and standardization |
| Multi-agent automation frameworks | 2 | ToolsGenie 2.0, PantheonOS | Scalable, extensible, evolvable bioinformatics automation |
| Annotation agent teams | 3 | CASSIA, CyteType, CellTypeAgent | Evidence-based, interpretable, trustworthy cell-type annotation |
| Domain viewpoint | 1 | From equations to agents (precision oncology) | Strategic framing of agentic virtual cells in oncology |

Sources: [README.md](README.md#L456-L472)

**General-purpose autonomous science.** Five entries operate at the level of the scientific method itself rather than at the level of a single analysis: an agent performing autonomous biomedical research (Science 2026), a system helping scientists write expert-level empirical software (Nature 2026), a study of agentic systems on well-scoped verifiable problems, a perspective on agentic laboratories as world models for discovery, and an analysis of "in silico team science" (Nature Biotechnology 2026). For system architects, this cluster defines the outer envelope: what a fully autonomous research loop is expected to attempt in computational biology, and where its boundaries of reliability are drawn.

Sources: [README.md](README.md#L457-L463)

**Single-cell analysis agents.** The five-domain-specific entries split into three recurring roles visible from their titles: *orchestrators* that accept natural-language briefs and execute multi-step analyses (CellAgent, ICLR 2025; scPilot, NeurIPS 2025), *autonomous discovery engines* that generate new insights from raw biological data without step-by-step instruction (CellVoyager, Nature Methods 2026; ELISA, with expression-grounded interpretable reasoning), and *data-engineering agents* that handle the unglamorous ingestion-and-standardization front end of scRNA-seq pipelines (CellAtria, npj Artificial Intelligence 2026). These are the systems most directly reusable as references when building an analysis copilot over the tool stacks cataloged on [Analysis Frameworks and Data Formats](16-analysis-frameworks-and-data-formats).

Sources: [README.md](README.md#L461), [README.md](README.md#L464-L465), [README.md](README.md#L471-L472)

**Annotation agent teams.** Three entries attack the single highest-volume, most verifiable task in single-cell analysis: cell-type annotation. CASSIA (Nature Communications 2025) is explicitly a multi-agent LLM for automated *and interpretable* annotation; CyteType frames multi-agent AI as evidence-based annotation; CellTypeAgent targets trustworthiness. The pattern across all three is the same: decompose one annotation decision into roles that gather evidence, propose labels, and critique — a design worth studying before inventing a bespoke multi-agent topology.

Sources: [README.md](README.md#L468-L470)

**Multi-agent automation frameworks.** ToolsGenie 2.0 (scalable, extensible bioinformatics automation) and PantheonOS (an *evolvable* multi-agent framework for automatic genomics discovery) represent the infrastructure-flavored end of the spectrum: rather than solving one analysis, they provide the runtime substrate on which other agents execute. They are the natural companion reads to the platforms cataloged on page 19.

Sources: [README.md](README.md#L466-L467)

> [!TIP]
> The catalog's own evaluation framing — "agentic systems are adept at solving well-scoped, verifiable problems in computational biology" — doubles as a design heuristic. Prefer agent architectures whose success criteria are machine-checkable (annotation accuracy, pipeline validity, ingestion correctness) over open-ended "discovery" claims; three of the four functional clusters converge on exactly such tasks.

Sources: [README.md](README.md#L456-L472)

## Boundary Map: Agents vs. Adjacent Catalog Pages

Several README entries mention agents or agentic techniques but are deliberately *not* on this page, because the catalog organizes by **primary artifact** rather than by technique. Recognizing this rule prevents misfiled contributions and missed references: conversational copilots whose artifact is a language-model-based cell representation belong to [LLM-Based Cell Models](8-llm-based-cell-models); an agentic *builder* whose output is a virtual cell model belongs to [Cell World Model Implementations](13-cell-world-model-implementations); an agent-*curated* repository whose artifact is a dataset belongs to [Transcriptomic Atlases and Repositories](14-transcriptomic-atlases-and-repositories).

Sources: [README.md](README.md#L203-L205), [README.md](README.md#L215-L222), [README.md](README.md#L330), [README.md](README.md#L338), [README.md](README.md#L496)

| Agent-adjacent entry | Why it is agent-related | Catalog home |
|---|---|---|
| scChat, CellWhisperer, InstructCell | Conversational copilots — interactive assistants, not autonomous agents | [LLM-Based Cell Models](8-llm-based-cell-models) |
| CellForge: Agentic Design of Virtual Cell Models | Agentic technique, but the artifact is a virtual cell / world model | [Cell World Model Implementations](13-cell-world-model-implementations) |
| scBaseCount: "AI agent-curated" repository | Agent in the loop, but the artifact is a data repository | [Transcriptomic Atlases and Repositories](14-transcriptomic-atlases-and-repositories) |
| LLM4Cell: Survey of LLM and Agentic Models | Field-wide survey spanning agents and LLMs | [Surveys and Open Challenges](21-surveys-and-open-challenges) |

> [!TIP]
> When scanning the README for agent work, search by primary artifact, not by the keyword "agent": the term also appears in the description of a dataset (scBaseCount, L338) and a world-model builder (CellForge, L330), which the catalog files under data and virtual-cell pages respectively.

Sources: [README.md](README.md#L330), [README.md](README.md#L338)

## Lab-in-the-Loop and Active Discovery

The second subsection of this page contains only two entries, but they are structurally distinct from everything above: here, computation selects *which physical experiment to run next*, and the wet lab's measurement feeds back into the model. This is the closed loop that distinguishes agentic discovery from purely in-silico analysis — the agent (or active-learning framework) proposes experiments, the laboratory executes perturbation screens, and transcriptomic readouts update the selection policy.

Sources: [README.md](README.md#L474-L476)

```mermaid
flowchart LR
    M["Pretrained perturbation /<br/>phenotype model"] -->|"rank candidates"| S["Active selection:<br/>max-information perturbations"]
    S -->|"top-k proposals"| W["Wet-lab execution:<br/>Perturb-seq / phenotypic screens"]
    W -->|"transcriptomic readout"| U["Model update:<br/>active-learning feedback"]
    U --> M
    W -.->|"discovered hits & modulators"| OUT["Biological discovery"]
```

| Entry | Venue / year | Role in the loop |
|---|---|---|
| Many needles in a haystack: Active hit discovery for perturbation experiments | ICML 2026 | In-loop selection of informative perturbations for hit discovery |
| Active learning framework leveraging transcriptomics identifies modulators of disease phenotypes | Science 2025 | Transcriptomics-guided active learning to prioritize disease-modulator experiments |

Sources: [README.md](README.md#L474-L476)

Both entries presuppose the perturbation-prediction substrate cataloged on [Perturbation Prediction Frameworks](9-perturbation-prediction-frameworks) and the screen datasets of [Perturbation Atlases and Datasets](10-perturbation-atlases-and-datasets): active selection is only as good as the model doing the ranking.
