Developers entering this area should treat pages 9–11 as the prerequisite stack and this subsection as the orchestration layer that converts those models into experimental plans.

Sources: [README.md](README.md#L241-L273), [README.md](README.md#L474-L476)

## Suggested Reading Path

For an advanced developer approaching this page cold, the catalog supports a deliberate progression: orient in the model landscape first, understand the substrate agents will orchestrate, then study the agents themselves, and finish with the field-level surveys that contextualize open problems.

1. **[Overview](1-overview)** — the review's framing of the single-cell foundation model landscape.
2. **[Taxonomy of Single-Cell Foundation Models](4-taxonomy-of-single-cell-foundation-models)** — the model families (pages 5–8) that agentic systems increasingly invoke as callable tools.
3. **[Analysis Frameworks and Data Formats](16-analysis-frameworks-and-data-formats)** — the tool libraries (Scanpy, Seurat, scvi-tools) that analysis agents orchestrate.
4. **[Infrastructure and Model Platforms](19-infrastructure-and-model-platforms)** — the deployment substrate this page's agents run on top of; read immediately before this page.
5. **[AI Agents for Discovery](20-ai-agents-for-discovery)** — this page.
6. **[Surveys and Open Challenges](21-surveys-and-open-challenges)** — including the LLM4Cell survey covering large language and agentic models for single-cell biology, the field-wide synthesis of everything cataloged here.


# Surveys and Open Challenges



This page documents the **Surveys and Perspectives** section of the repository — the synthesis layer at the end of the catalog, where the collection shifts from inventorying *artifacts* (models, datasets, benchmarks, platforms) to inventorying *interpretation*. It contains **36 curated survey and position papers** that narrate the field's trajectory and codify its unresolved problems. The section is stored as a single flat list in the repository's README, with entries ordered newest-first and linked directly to their source publications. This page's catalog title ("Surveys and Open Challenges") corresponds to the README anchor `#surveys-and-perspectives`.

Sources: [README.md](/README.md#L478-L517), [README.md](/README.md#L39-L70)

## Scope Boundary: What Belongs Here

The section opens with an explicit **routing rule**, and it is the only catalog section that defines its scope by exclusion relative to another section: surveys focused on the *virtual cell paradigm specifically* are redirected to the "Virtual Cell, World Models and Digital Human" section, while this section retains surveys "more focused on single-cell foundation models in general". For an intermediate developer navigating the catalog, this distinction is the single most important piece of context — if a survey's framing centers on cellular world models or digital organisms, it lives in [Virtual Cell Perspectives and Roadmaps](12-virtual-cell-perspectives-and-roadmaps) (README lines 296–313); if it synthesizes the scFM landscape broadly, it lives here.

```mermaid
graph TD
    Q{"Survey's primary focus?"}
    Q -->|"Virtual cell paradigm specifically"| VC["Virtual Cell Reviews subsection<br/>README.md#L296-L313"]
    Q -->|"Single-cell foundation models in general"| SR["Surveys and Perspectives<br/>README.md#L478-L517<br/>36 entries"]
    SR --> T1["2026 cohort: 13 entries"]
    SR --> T2["2025 cohort: 14 entries"]
    SR --> T3["2024 cohort: 9 entries"]
```

> [!TIP]
> The routing rule at README.md#L479-L480 works in one direction only: a survey that merely *mentions* virtual cells still belongs in this section if its scope covers single-cell foundation models broadly. Check where the paper's central thesis sits, not its keyword density.

Sources: [README.md](/README.md#L478-L480), [README.md](/README.md#L292-L313)

## Entry Format and Ordering Conventions

Each of the 36 entries follows the repository's uniform citation anatomy: a chronological marker in brackets, a bolded title, and a resource-type tag linking to the publication — `[Year Venue] **Title** [[paper]](link)`. Unlike every other major catalog section, this one contains **no subsections**: it is a single, non-hierarchical list. The ordering is strictly **newest-first** (2026 → 2025 → 2024), which means the field's bleeding edge occupies the top of the list and its foundational retrospectives accumulate at the bottom. All 36 entries carry the `[[paper]]` resource tag; other sections of the repository additionally use `[[website]]`, `[[blog]]`, or `[[portal]]` tags, but none appear here. One formatting variance exists: the first entry (line 482) omits bold on its title, making it the sole deviation from the bolded-title convention used by the remaining 35 entries.

> [!TIP]
> Because ordering is reverse-chronological, a line-number binary search is an efficient retrieval strategy: lines 482–494 hold the 2026 frontier, lines 495–508 the 2025 consolidation, and lines 509–517 the 2024 foundational surveys. Jump directly to the cohort matching your currency needs instead of scanning all 36 entries.

Sources: [README.md](/README.md#L482-L517)

## Thematic Taxonomy of the Collection

Although the section is stored as one chronological list, its contents resolve cleanly into **five recurring themes**. This taxonomy is analytical — the repository itself does not subdivide the list — but it maps how the survey literature partitions the problem space: whole-field synthesis, forward-looking challenge statements, architecture-level methodology, spatial omics as a vertical domain, and specialized application areas. The counts below are exhaustive and mutually exclusive, summing to the section's 36 entries.

| Theme | Count | Example entries (README lines) | Value for developers |
|---|---|---|---|
| Field-wide scFM surveys | 12 | LLM4Cell (L496); Transformers in single-cell omics (L511); Foundation models in omics research: a comprehensive survey (L489); Harnessing the deep learning power of foundation models in single-cell omics (L510) | Orientation maps of the full landscape; fastest path to a structured mental model |
| Open challenges & position papers | 11 | Fifteen challenges for generative AI applications to cell biology (L484); The Human Cell Atlas from a cell census to a unified foundation model (L515); Overcoming barriers to the wide adoption of single-cell LLMs (L500) | Explicit problem statements that define open research and engineering directions |
| Architecture & generative modeling surveys | 4 | Flow matching for generative modelling (L490); Tokenization and deep learning architectures in genomics (L505); Transformers and genome language models (L499); Multimodal foundation transformer models for multiscale genomics (L498) | Design-level guidance on tokenization, transformer variants, and generative training paradigms |
| Spatial omics surveys | 5 | Multimodal spatial omics (L486); Spatial omics at the forefront (L493); Predicting spatial transcriptomics from histology images (L487); A perspective on developing foundation models for spatial transcriptomic data (L507) | Vertical-domain synthesis connecting histology, spatial assays, and computational integration |
| Specialized application surveys | 4 | Computational strategies for cross-species knowledge transfer (L497); LLMs for drug discovery and development (L502); Mini-review on perturbation modelling across single-cell omic modalities (L516); Decoding Cell Fate (L506) | Bridge material linking scFMs to drug discovery, perturbation biology, and cross-species transfer |

```mermaid
graph LR
    ROOT["Surveys and Perspectives<br/>36 entries"]
    ROOT --> A["Field-wide scFM surveys<br/>12 entries"]
    ROOT --> B["Open challenges and<br/>position papers<br/>11 entries"]
    ROOT --> C["Architecture and generative<br/>modeling surveys<br/>4 entries"]
    ROOT --> D["Spatial omics surveys<br/>5 entries"]
    ROOT --> E["Specialized application surveys<br/>4 entries"]
```

Sources: [README.md](/README.md#L482-L517)

## The Open-Challenges Cluster

The catalog page's "Open Challenges" designation is carried substantively by the eleven position and challenge papers in this section. These entries do not survey what exists — they specify what remains unsolved. The most concrete artifact is **"Fifteen challenges for generative AI applications to cell biology"** (2026 Cell), an enumerated problem list, while **"Why machines don't speak biology: Toward native biological language models"** (2026 Cell) argues a foundational representation-level thesis. Adoption-focused challenges appear in **"Overcoming barriers to the wide adoption of single-cell large language models in biomedical research"** (2025 Nature Methods), and architectural evolution is framed by **"From modality-specific to compositional foundation models for cell biology"** (2026 Cell Systems). Roadmap-class entries anchor the cluster's older stratum: the Human Cell Atlas repositioned as a unified foundation model (2024 Nature), causal cell-and-tissue modeling via a Perturbation Cell and Tissue Atlas (2024 Cell), and reference mapping as the future of automated single-cell analysis (2024 Cell).

This cluster also connects back to the repository's own synthesis artifact: the catalog's structure follows the companion review **"The Landscape of Single-Cell Foundation Models: Design Principles, Applications, and Open Challenges"**, currently under review at Cell and citable via the BibTeX block at README lines 30–37. The section's external surveys complement that in-house review with independent perspectives on the same open problems.

Sources: [README.md](/README.md#L483-L494), [README.md](/README.md#L500-L515), [README.md](/README.md#L26-L37)

## Temporal Cohorts and Venue Landscape

The section's 36 entries distribute across three temporal cohorts, and the cohort structure itself is informative: the 2026 stratum (13 entries) shows the survey wave maturing into comprehensive syntheses and challenge enumerations; the 2025 stratum (14 entries) is the largest, marking peak consolidation; the 2024 stratum (9 entries) contains the foundational retrospectives that defined the field's vocabulary. Venue concentration is equally telling — the collection draws overwhelmingly from the **Nature portfolio** and **Cell Press**, signaling that the survey literature has consolidated into top-tier venues rather than remaining in preprint form (the 2025 cohort contains exactly one arXiv entry, LLM4Cell).

| Cohort | Entries | README lines | Character |
|---|---|---|---|
| 2026 | 13 | L482–L494 | Comprehensive surveys, challenge enumerations, spatial omics wave |
| 2025 | 14 | L495–L508 | Consolidation: multimodal FMs, adoption barriers, tokenization reviews |
| 2024 | 9 | L509–L517 | Foundational retrospectives defining the field's framing |

| Venue cluster | Entries | Examples |
|---|---|---|
| Nature portfolio (Nature, Nature Methods, Nature Biotechnology, Nature Machine Intelligence, Nature Reviews Genetics, Nature Reviews Molecular Cell Biology) | 12 | L485, L490, L491, L494, L495, L497, L498, L499, L500, L510, L511, L515 |
| Cell Press (Cell, Cell Systems, Cancer Cell, Patterns) | 8 | L483, L484, L486, L492, L493, L502, L513, L514 |
| Briefings in Bioinformatics | 4 | L482, L488, L489, L517 |
| Other journals and venues | 12 | National Science Review, CSBJ, Quantitative Biology, Genome Biology, arXiv, ACL, Bioinformatics, Experimental & Molecular Medicine, EXO |

Sources: [README.md](/README.md#L482-L517)

## Recommended Reading Progression

As the catalog's synthesis layer, this section works best as either a **starting orientation** or a **capstone consolidation** — read it first to acquire the field's vocabulary, or last to situate everything you have already cataloged. If your goal is understanding open problems before studying implementations, read this page, then descend into the core model landscape via [Taxonomy of Single-Cell Foundation Models](4-taxonomy-of-single-cell-foundation-models). If you arrived here after traversing the catalog, proceed to the adjacent related-work page [Related Pathology and Bulk Models](22-related-pathology-and-bulk-models) to close out the boundary domains. Challenge statements about evaluation methodology in this section pair naturally with the empirical counterpart in [Benchmarking Studies and Critiques](17-benchmarking-studies-and-critiques), and roadmap discussions touching agentic systems connect forward to [AI Agents for Discovery](20-ai-agents-for-discovery).

| Step | Catalog page | Rationale |
|---|---|---|
| Orient | [Overview](1-overview) → [Evolutionary Tree of Models](3-evolutionary-tree-of-models) | Establish the landscape vocabulary this section's surveys assume |
| Synthesize | [Surveys and Open Challenges](21-surveys-and-open-challenges) *(this page)* | Acquire field-wide framing and open problem statements |
| Cross-reference | [Virtual Cell Perspectives and Roadmaps](12-virtual-cell-perspectives-and-roadmaps) | The parallel survey collection for virtual-cell-scoped perspectives, per the routing rule |
| Empirical counterpart | [Benchmarking Studies and Critiques](17-benchmarking-studies-and-critiques) | Challenge statements here vs. measured evidence there |
| Continue catalog | [Related Pathology and Bulk Models](22-related-pathology-and-bulk-models) | Next page in sequence; the catalog's final related-work boundary |

The repository actively maintains this list: contributions, missed papers, and broken links are solicited via issues or pull requests. If you identify a survey absent from the 36 entries, this section is designed to absorb it.


# Related Pathology and Bulk Models



This page documents the final two sections of the curated reading list: **Foundation Models for Pathology (related work)** and **Foundation Models for Bulk Transcriptome**. These sections are deliberately positioned at the end of the catalog as *adjacent* research areas — they apply the same "foundation model" playbook (large-scale pretraining, transferable representations) to biological data types that are **not single-cell**: digitized tissue images and mixed-population gene expression profiles. For a beginner, this page explains what these neighboring fields are, what the listed papers contribute, and how they relate back to the single-cell core of the catalog.

Sources: [README.md](README.md#L519-L533), [README.md](README.md#L69-L70)

## Why These Sections Exist

The repository's stated scope is a reading list of foundation-model research for **single-cell genomics**, structured around a companion review titled *"The landscape of single-cell foundation models: design principles, applications, and open challenges"*. The pathology section is explicitly framed in the file itself: its entries are *"outside the scope of the single-cell review above but are kept here as closely related work"* — the bulk transcriptome section sits immediately after it under the same logic. In other words, these are curated **on-ramps**: if you came to single-cell foundation models from a pathology or bulk-omics background (or want to migrate in the other direction), the maintainers signal that these five plus three papers are the canonical bridges.

> [!TIP]
> The "(related work)" label is a scope boundary, not a quality judgment. Everything else in this catalog feeds the single-cell review; these two sections are appendices of intentionally adjacent material. When citing or extending this list, keep that separation intact.

The following concept map shows where this page sits relative to the catalog's core:

```mermaid
flowchart TB
    subgraph CORE["Catalog core: single-cell foundation models"]
        SCFM["scFMs pretrained on single-cell atlases<br/>(pages 5–8 of the catalog)"]
    end
    subgraph THISPAGE["This page: related work at adjacent scales"]
        PATH["Pathology FMs<br/>whole-slide images + text reports"]
        BULK["Bulk transcriptome FMs<br/>one mixed signal per tissue sample"]
    end
    SCFM -- "bulk = mixture of many cells<br/>(deconvolution link)" --> BULK
    SCFM -- "cells live inside tissue<br/>(histology link)" --> PATH
```

Reading the diagram left to right: the core catalog models learn representations from **individual cells**, while the two related sections operate one scale up — pathology models look at **tissue images**, and bulk models look at **aggregated molecular signals** from many cells at once.

Sources: [README.md](README.md#L11-L11), [README.md](README.md#L69-L70), [README.md](README.md#L519-L521)

## Foundation Models for Pathology

**Computational pathology in one paragraph**: pathologists diagnose disease by examining tissue under a microscope; when that tissue is digitized into massive images called *whole-slide images* (WSIs), machine learning can be applied to them. A pathology foundation model is pretrained on large collections of these images — sometimes paired with text such as diagnostic reports — so it learns general visual representations of tissue morphology that transfer to many downstream tasks (classification, detection, survival prediction).

The repository lists **five papers** (2023–2024, all published in top-tier venues) with no intro text beyond the scoping note. Here is the verbatim inventory, organized by what each paper's title tells you:

| # | Paper focus (year, venue) | Input data | Task pattern |
|---|---|---|---|
| 1 | Joint segmentation, detection and recognition of biomedical objects **across nine modalities** (2024, Nature Methods) | Biomedical images, 9 imaging modalities | Multi-task universal vision model |
| 2 | **Whole-slide** foundation model for digital pathology **from real-world data** (2024, Nature) | Whole-slide images | Slide-level pretraining at scale |
| 3 | **General-purpose** foundation model for computational pathology (2024, Nature Medicine) | Pathology images | General-purpose image encoder |
| 4 | **Visual-language** foundation model for computational pathology (2024, Nature Medicine) | Pathology images + text | Image–text alignment |
| 5 | Visual-language model trained on **medical Twitter** data (2023, Nature Medicine) | Pathology images + social-media captions | Weakly-supervised image–text alignment |

Sources: [README.md](README.md#L519-L527)

Three design patterns emerge from this list, and they mirror the pretraining-strategy taxonomy used for single-cell models elsewhere in the catalog. First, entries 1–3 represent **vision-only pretraining**: the model sees images alone and learns representations through tasks like masked modeling or supervised prediction — the pathology analog of unimodal scRNA-seq models. Second, entries 4–5 represent **vision-language pretraining**: images are paired with free text (reports, or in the 2023 paper, the alt-text that clinicians wrote on social media), and the model learns a *joint* space where an image and its description land close together. Third, the spread of data sources is instructive: entry 2 emphasizes **real-world data** (routine clinical archives) and entry 5 uses **social media**, showing that the field scrounges scale wherever it can find it — a theme beginners will recognize from the data-hungry single-cell world.

> [!TIP]
> The repository provides paper links only — no code or model weights — so you must search the literature for implementations. Four of these papers are widely known in the community under model acronyms (the whole-slide model as Virchow, the general-purpose encoder as UNI, the vision-language models as CONCH and PLIP), which makes finding their open-source releases straightforward once you know the mappings.

Sources: [README.md](README.md#L519-L527)

## Foundation Models for Bulk Transcriptome

**Bulk transcriptomics in one paragraph**: a bulk RNA-seq experiment measures, for every gene, the *average* expression across the millions of cells in a tissue sample — you get one mixed signal per sample rather than one profile per cell. This is cheaper, older, and far more common in clinical settings (hospitals routinely profile tumors in bulk), which is why foundation models for bulk data matter even in a single-cell-centric catalog. Entry 3 of this section also introduces **DNA methylation** — an epigenetic layer measuring chemical marks on DNA — as a second bulk modality.

The section contains **three papers**, all from 2026, and unlike the pathology section it has no introductory note:

| # | Paper (year, venue) | Input data | Contribution |
|---|---|---|---|
| 1 | **BulkFormer**: large-scale foundation model for bulk transcriptomes (2026, Cell Systems) | Bulk gene expression | Dedicated large-scale bulk FM |
| 2 | Generalizable AI predicting **immotherapy outcomes across cancers and treatments** (2026, Nature Medicine) | Transcriptomic profiles | Clinical outcome prediction, cross-cancer transfer |
| 3 | **Bimodal masked language modeling** for bulk RNA-seq and DNA methylation (2026, ICML) | Bulk RNA-seq + DNA methylation | Two-modality joint pretraining |

Sources: [README.md](README.md#L529-L533)

The youth of this section is its most notable structural fact: every entry is dated 2026, while the pathology section's entries all date from 2023–2024. Bulk-transcriptome foundation models are thus a **newer frontier** — the field has one flagship named model (BulkFormer), one clinical-application demonstration (immunotherapy outcomes, notable because it claims *generalizability across cancers and treatments*), and one methodological contribution (bimodal masked language modeling, published at a machine-learning venue rather than a medical journal). The venue spread — Cell Systems, Nature Medicine, ICML — signals that this area is jointly claimed by biology, medicine, and ML communities, exactly like the single-cell field itself.

Sources: [README.md](README.md#L529-L533)

## Pathology vs. Bulk: A Side-by-Side View

Because this page combines two sections, a direct comparison clarifies why they are kept together as "related work" despite being quite different in nature:

| Dimension | Pathology section | Bulk transcriptome section |
|---|---|---|
| Data type | **Images** (whole slides, multi-modal microscopy) ± text | **Molecular vectors** (gene expression, methylation) |
| Entry count | 5 papers | 3 papers |
| Year range | 2023–2024 (mature) | 2026 (emerging) |
| Venues | Nature Methods, Nature, Nature Medicine | Cell Systems, Nature Medicine, ICML |
| Pretraining signal | Visual appearance; image–text pairs | Expression patterns; two-omics co-modeling |
| Relationship to single-cell | Cells live **inside** the tissue these models see | Bulk profiles are **mixtures** of single-cell profiles |

The pairing is not arbitrary: both sections represent foundation models applied to data where the **single cell is not the unit of observation** — either because the unit is an image of tissue, or because the unit is a molecular average over many cells. That shared contrast with the catalog's core is what earns them the "related work" designation.

Sources: [README.md](README.md#L519-L533), [README.md](README.md#L69-L70)

## Connecting Back to the Single-Cell Core

Neither section is an island. The catalog itself shows the interfaces: pathology images appear inside the main single-cell landscape wherever models jointly model **spatial data and histology** (the "Spatial, Proteomics and Histology" grouping under multimodal scFMs), and bulk-to-single-cell translation is the implicit bridge that makes bulk foundation models clinically relevant — a bulk model can be validated or refined using single-cell references, and single-cell models can be aggregated to simulate bulk profiles. The critical-evaluation literature in the catalog similarly warns against assuming representations transfer freely across these scale boundaries.

For your reading path, this page is catalog position 22 of 22 — the deliberate end of the tour. Sensible continuations:

- Deepen the modality interface: [Multimodal and Spatial Models](7-multimodal-and-spatial-models) covers the single-cell models that already touch histology, the closest core-catalog neighbor to the pathology section.
- Ground your expectations: [Benchmarking Studies and Critiques](17-benchmarking-studies-and-critiques) collects the evaluation literature that applies equally to related-work models.
- Zoom back out: [Evolutionary Tree of Models](3-evolutionary-tree-of-models) offers the visual map of how the whole landscape fits together, or restart with [Overview](1-overview).
- Continue the frontier theme: [Surveys and Open Challenges](21-surveys-and-open-challenges) catalogs where the field — including its adjacent disciplines — says it is heading next.
